What SDL3 Is — and What It Isn't

SDL3 is a portable low-level runtime, and it is deliberately incomplete as a game engine. That gap is the syllabus of this course.

  • SDL3 gives you the machine room: windows, events, 2D renderer, GPU access, audio streams, input, files, threads
  • It is not an engine: no scene graph, no sprites, no physics, no UI widgets in the core
    • —Those layers are exactly what we build — the Sable engine of this course
  • Design center: a C ABI with small headers and predictable semantics across 10+ platforms
  • First stable release: SDL 3.2.0, January 2025 — a mature API you can build a career on
Common Pitfall — Expecting batteries

Newcomers search for SDL_Sprite or SDL_PlaySound. The equivalents live in the companion libraries (SDL3_image, SDL3_ttf) and in the modules we write ourselves in Chapters 4-12.

The SDL3 Family: Core + Companions

The core stays minimal by policy; satellites extend it for common content formats. They all speak the same C calling convention and error-reporting style.

  • SDL3 core — windowing, events, 2D renderer, the new SDL_GPU API, audio, input, IO, threads
  • SDL3_image — decodes PNG/JPG/BMP and friends into SDL_Texture (IMG_LoadTexture)
  • SDL3_ttf — TrueType rendering for HUDs and menus (TTF_OpenFont, TTF_RenderText_Blended)
  • Community satellites (net, rtf…) are migrating to SDL3 — evaluate them the same way we do the core
  • Rule of thumb: prefer core SDL3; reach for a companion only when it saves real code
Deep Dive — Course dependency set

This course uses core SDL3 plus SDL3_image and SDL3_ttf. Audio decoding stays hand-rolled in Chapter 10 so you understand what a mixer actually does.

Why SDL3 for Engine Study

You could study engine architecture atop a AAA framework — but opacity is the enemy of learning. SDL3 is thin enough to see through.

  • Thin enough to learn from — every subsystem maps to OS calls you can observe with a debugger
  • Real enough to ship — Valve tooling and countless ports run on it daily
  • One API across Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS and the browser — no #ifdef forests
  • The new SDL_GPU API teaches modern pipeline thinking: command buffers, passes, fences
  • C ABI means freedom of language: we use C++ for structure, the C API for calls
Best Practice — Learn the C API first

Even in C++ code, call SDL3 exactly as C does for your first projects. Wrapping too early hides semantics you will need the day something breaks at 2 AM.

Graphics: What SDL3 Gives You on Day One

The 2D renderer alone covers Chapters 3-12; the GPU API is our ticket to shaders and 3D in Chapters 11-14.

  • Immediate-mode 2D renderer: SDL_RenderTexture, SDL_RenderTextureRotated, flips at subpixel precision
  • Render targets for off-screen compositing — the backbone of Chapter 9 transitions
  • Resolution independence: SDL_SetRenderLogicalPresentation with letterboxing
  • Per-renderer vsync: SDL_SetRenderVSync(renderer, 1) — but design to delta time regardless
  • SDL_GPU: shader pipelines, compute, buffers and textures over Vulkan / Metal / D3D12 backends

Audio, Input, Files & Threads

The non-graphics half of the runtime — where cross-platform pain actually lives, and where SDL3 earns its keep.

  • Audio: open a logical device, bind any number of SDL_AudioStreams — SDL mixes them for you
  • Input: one unified event queue — keyboard, mouse, touch, gamepads backed by SDLs controller database
  • Files: SDL_IOStream abstraction; SDL_GetBasePath() (read-only assets) vs SDL_GetPrefPath() (writable saves)
  • Threads, mutexes and atomics — portable concurrency primitives you will need for asset loading
  • A properties API for capability queries without breaking ABI — the SDL3 answer to feature creep
Performance Tip — The event pump is your heartbeat

SDL_PollEvent() both fetches events and pumps platform internals. Call it every frame, even when nothing seems to happen — some window managers require it to stay responsive.

Meet the Course Project: Canyon Dash

A side-scrolling platformer — deep enough to exercise every subsystem, small enough to finish.

  • Layered parallax canyons, translucent water overlays, decorative props — Chapter 5
  • A player with coyote-time jumps, collectibles, power-ups, moving hazards — Chapter 6
  • Menus, options, persistent saves and screen transitions — Chapters 7 and 9
  • Particles, parallax dust, procedural water bobbing — Chapter 8
  • A 3D physics playground reusing the same engine core — Chapters 13 and 14
Deep Dive — Why one vertical project

Each chapter adds one layer to the same codebase. By Chapter 14 you can trace any feature — a jump, a coin pickup, a screen fade — from gameplay code down through the engine to the exact SDL3 call that executes it.

Prerequisites: Minimum vs Comfortable Kit

Nothing below is exotic. The minimum kit is genuinely enough to finish Chapter 14; the comfortable kit is what a working studio would hand you.

AMinimum viable kit
  • A C/C++ compiler: MSVC, Clang or GCC
  • CMake 3.24+ for portable, generator-agnostic builds
  • Git for versioning and for pulling dependencies
  • A terminal and any text editor
  • SDL3 fetched by the build (no manual installs)
BComfortable kit
  • An IDE with a real debugger (VS, CLion, VS Code + C/C++)
  • vcpkg or CMake FetchContent — one dependency strategy, applied consistently
  • Sanitizers (-fsanitize=address,undefined) for memory hygiene
  • Emscripten SDK for instant browser builds — Chapter 2 deploys there
  • A second machine or VM for cross-platform spot checks
Best Practice — Lock your toolchain

Record compiler and dependency versions in CMakePresets.json and commit it. Six months from now, "works on my machine" must mean "works from the repo".

Dependency Strategy A — vcpkg Manifests

vcpkg consumes a manifest that travels with your repository and installs prebuilt binaries at configure time.

key points
  • The manifest is versioned with the game — every checkout gets identical dependencies
  • Binary caching means dependencies install in seconds after the first build
  • Point CMake at the vcpkg toolchain file once; classic find_package just works

Dependency Strategy B — CMake FetchContent

FetchContent pulls and compiles SDL3 from source at configure time — no external package manager at all.

Best Practice — Pin, never float

Always pin dependency versions (GIT_TAG, vcpkg baseline). CI plus pinned tags is the difference between a build system and a lottery.

Performance Tip — Cache FetchContent

First configure compiles SDL3 from scratch. Point FETCHCONTENT_BASE_DIR at a shared cache outside the repo so teammates and CI only pay that cost once.

hello_sdl3.c — Your First Main Loop

The smallest honest SDL3 program: a window, an event loop, a colored clear, a clean shutdown. Every game you ever ship is this shape, just busier.

Common Pitfall — Ignoring the bool

SDL3 moved to bool returns. SDL_Init, SDL_RenderTexture, SDL_PollEvent — they all speak true/false now. Silent failure looks identical to success until frame 3000.

vcpkg vs FetchContent — Choosing a Strategy

Both are excellent. Pick per-project, apply consistently, and never let the two strategies fight over the same library.

Avcpkg (registry)
  • Prebuilt binaries from a curated registry — fast installs
  • vcpkg.json manifest travels with the repo
  • Scales well to many third-party dependencies
  • Requires the toolchain file on every configure
BCMake FetchContent (source)
  • Pulls and builds from git — no extra tools, CMake only
  • Exact version control via GIT_TAG pins
  • Perfect for one or two heavyweight dependencies
  • First configure is slower — cache it aggressively
Common Pitfall — Mixing strategies

Mixing a registry install and a vendored source build of the same library is the classic route to duplicate symbols and ABI mismatches. One library, one source of truth.

IDEs, Debuggers & Diagnostics

SDL3 meets you where your debugger lives — but you have to actually open it.

  • Any debugger beats printf: break on SDL_assert failures and inspect live state
  • VS Code: C/C++ extension + CMake Tools; CLion and Visual Studio work out of the box
  • Sanitizers: -fsanitize=address,undefined catches the memory bugs C++ invites
  • Emscripten builds run in a browser tab — SDL_Log output appears in devtools console
  • SDL_GetError() is the last gasp of a failed call — treat it like a stack trace fragment
Common Pitfall — Stale error strings

SDL_GetError() reflects only the most recent failed call. Log it immediately at the failure site, or you will read a misleading string three functions later.

Course Project Layout — Folder Conventions

The repository grows for 14 chapters. Fix the shape now, in empty folders, so structure never becomes a retroactive chore.

key points
  • Engine vs game is a folder boundary — src/sable must never include from src/game
  • Assets are data, not source: they ship with the package, not the compiler

2.1 — The Promise: One Codebase, Every Target

Write the game once in C and C++17 against SDL3, then ship the same source to desktops, phones and browsers. This chapter is about earning that sentence honestly.

One codebase
src/ + assets/

Six shipping targets in this course — every one runs Canyon Dash from the same source.

details
  • Desktop — Windows, macOS and Linux: the development hosts, with full OS access
  • Mobile — Android and iOS: sandboxed storage, enforced lifecycles, touch-first input
  • Web — WebAssembly through Emscripten: the browser as a full runtime target
  • Same entry point, same assets/ folder, same Sable engine — only packaging differs
  • The price of admission: respect the rules of each host, or the host will eject you

2.2 — One Codebase, Multi-Target Builds

Canyon Dash compiles from one source tree into six packages. The trick is a thin platform layer that keeps per-target knowledge out of the game entirely.

If a game file ever needs to know the platform, the platform layer is too thin.

details
  • Sable splits into a portable core (src/sable/) and a platform layer (src/sable/platform/)
  • Game code in src/game/ contains zero target #ifdef — it talks to interfaces only
  • Per-target reality lives in entry points, packaging and a handful of adapter files
  • CMake presets pick compilers and flags per host; platforms/ holds the wrappers
  • Chapter 1's folder tree reserved platforms/ for exactly this moment

2.3 — What SDL3 Actually Abstracts

SDL3 is a translation layer: one flat C API over radically different operating systems. Knowing exactly what it absorbs tells you where bugs can hide.

  • Windows become SDL_Window across Win32, Cocoa, X11, Wayland and the browser canvas
  • The 2D renderer picks each host's best backend; SDL_GPU speaks Vulkan, Metal and D3D12
  • Input collapses into one event queue: keyboards, mice, touch, gamepads, sensors
  • Audio becomes logical devices with bound streams instead of platform callbacks
  • Hidden machinery: message pumps, GL context creation, device enumeration, DPI math
Deep Dive — One call, three worlds

Chapter 1's SDL_RenderFillRect rides Direct3D on Windows, Metal on macOS and WebGL in the browser. One call, three worlds — and when a frame comes out black, the backend is your first suspect, not your code.

2.4 — Engine Backends & Sable's Platform Layer

Every SDL3 port reaches the operating system through a backend chosen at build time. Sable adds one boundary of its own so the engine core stays target-blind.

Sable core (target-blind)
GameApp · AssetManager · WorldController
portable C++17
Sable PAL
Lifecycle
pause · resume · quit
Storage
base + pref paths
Entry

SDL3 backends
Win32 · Cocoa · X11/Wayland
desktop
JNI · UIKit

Consoles differ by toolchain and certification, not by your code — the C ABI is the same.

details
  • Desktop backends: Win32, Cocoa, X11 and Wayland — selected when SDL3 is compiled
  • Android bridges into Java through JNI; iOS reaches UIKit and its app lifecycle
  • The web target compiles SDL3 itself to WebAssembly under Emscripten
  • Consoles ship locked, NDA-covered toolchains — SDL's console ports speak the same ABI
  • Sable's PAL boundary is deliberately tiny: lifecycle, storage paths, entry point
Deep Dive — The console exception

PlayStation, Xbox and Switch support exists, but it lives under NDA: you cannot read those backends without being a licensed developer. Designing against SDL's public ABI is what keeps your code portable the day the locked toolchain arrives.

2.5 — The Application Lifecycle

Desktop apps own the machine until they exit. Mobile apps do not: the OS backgrounds, resumes and kills them at will — so the app becomes a state machine.

States
init
SDL_Init
running
the main loop
suspended
the OS owns the CPU
Transition events
will enter bg
did enter bg
will enter fg
did enter fg
Exit
terminating
final save · teardown

"Will" events are your last chance to act; "did" events confirm the transition landed.

details
  • Flow: init → running → background → foreground → terminating
  • Backgrounding suspends your loop: audio stops, timers freeze, GPU contents may drop
  • Resuming must resync the clock — a stale delta time teleports the player
  • SDL3 delivers every transition as an event, identically on all targets
  • Desktop rarely fires them; mobile and web fire them constantly — one path covers all
Common Pitfall — The desktop contract

If saving only happens in the quit handler, mobile players lose progress to every phone call and notification. Treat each SDL_EVENT_APP_WILLENTERBACKGROUND as a potential final goodbye: flush saves, hush audio, stop simulating.

2.6 — Handling Lifecycle Events in GameApp

The five lifecycle events arrive on the same queue as keystrokes. One switch in GameApp turns them into named engine hooks the rest of the code can override.

key points
  • One switch turns five SDL events into named engine callbacks
  • "Will" hooks carry urgency; "did" hooks carry confirmation
  • The same dispatch runs on desktop — it simply fires far less often
  • Subclasses of GameApp override the hooks; the switch never changes
Best Practice — Background means save now

The OS grants little time after SDL_EVENT_APP_WILLENTERBACKGROUND. Saving settings takes milliseconds; spending them here is what keeps a five-minute Canyon Dash run alive across an incoming call.

2.7 — Logging That Travels

printf writes to a console your players will never see. SDL_Log routes to wherever each platform actually keeps its output — learn it before you need it at 2 AM.

  • SDL_Log lands in IDE consoles, adb logcat, Xcode and browser devtools alike
  • Categories tag lines by subsystem — SDL_LOG_CATEGORY_APPLICATION is ours
  • Priorities rank every line from verbose to critical; filters follow the build type
  • Debug builds call SDL_SetLogPriorities(SDL_LOG_PRIORITY_DEBUG) and see everything
  • Release builds clamp to warnings and errors — chatter costs performance and privacy
  • printf dies quietly on Android and Web: no console, no output, no clue

2.8 — A Log Output Function That Files Everything

SDL3 lets you replace the default log sink with your own callback. We mirror every line to stdout and to a timestamped file players can actually send us.

key points
  • The callback fires for every SDL_Log line that survives priority filtering
  • Timestamps come from SDL_GetTicksNS() — one clock, every platform
  • The file lives under SDL_GetPrefPath("sable", "canyon-dash"), writable everywhere
  • Swap the priority threshold per build type — a one-line change
Best Practice — Ship the log

Ask for the log file instead of a screenshot of a black screen. Timestamped lines from this callback have closed more support tickets than any debugger: "what happened in the last 3 seconds" becomes a grep.

2.9 — Graceful Shutdown

Any app can start; a professional one ends well. Shutdown is a sequence, not an exit call — and sometimes the right move is refusing to die for one more moment.

  • Tear down in reverse creation order: screens → engine modules → renderer → window → SDL_Quit()
  • Chapter 1's hello_sdl3.c already followed the pattern — now it becomes policy
  • Refuse to die mid-save: an event filter can veto SDL_EVENT_QUIT until the write lands
  • The same veto answers SDL_EVENT_WINDOW_CLOSE_REQUESTED from the pause menu
  • On mobile you rarely choose the exit — SDL_EVENT_TERMINATING chooses for you
Common Pitfall — Dying mid-save

A half-written settings.json is worse than none: the next launch parses garbage and load-or-defaults silently resets the player's options. Finish the write, SDL_CloseIO the stream, then let the quit event through.

2.10 — Persisting Settings: Load or Default

Settings are the first cross-platform system every game needs. The pattern is one file under the pref path: parse what exists, default what does not, write on change.

key points
  • Load-or-defaults: a missing or corrupt file is a normal state, never a crash
  • SDL_GetPrefPath creates the directory — join paths onto its trailing separator
  • Parsing rides on cJSON, the same library our level files use in Chapter 4
  • Write, then SDL_CloseIO — closing is what flushes on every platform
Best Practice — Defaults are not failures

A first run with no settings file is a success, not an error path. Start from defaults and overwrite field by field as JSON provides them — the file becomes self-healing when new keys ship.

2.11 — Runtime Checks: Platform & Version Gates

Sometimes code must know where it runs or what it runs on. SDL3 answers with one runtime call, plus version gates for the features you depend on.

  • SDL_GetPlatform() returns a stable name string — "Windows", "Android", "iOS", "Linux"
  • Compile-time: the SDL_VERSION macro bakes the header version into your binary
  • Runtime: SDL_GetVersion(&SDL_Version) reports the library actually loaded
  • Gate features on the runtime value — your binary may meet an older DLL or framework
  • Capability queries ride the properties API: string-keyed typed values, ABI-safe
  • Sable rule: platform checks live in the PAL only — game code stays blind

2.12 — Threads: Workers for the Heavy Lifting

A three-second level load on the main thread is three seconds of frozen window. SDL threads move that work off-stage — under one golden rule.

key points
  • The worker owns file IO and decoding; the main thread owns everything SDL video
  • Results cross through a mutex-guarded queue plus SDL_CreateCondition signaling
  • SDL_WaitThread joins before teardown — never destroy state under a live worker
  • Web needs Emscripten pthreads (SharedArrayBuffer) or falls back to synchronous loads
Common Pitfall — The golden rule

SDL3 serializes video state: calling SDL_RenderTexture or SDL_PollEvent from a worker is undefined behavior on several backends. Workers may touch files, memory and math — the window, renderer and event queue belong to the thread that created them.

2.13 — Graphics: Delta Time, VSync, High DPI

The renderer must behave identically on a 60 Hz monitor, a 120 Hz phone and a throttled browser tab. The discipline that survives all three is delta time.

key points
  • Design to delta time; treat vsync as a request — 120 Hz phones and 30 Hz tabs both exist
  • High-DPI buys the real pixel grid; logical presentation keeps the 960×540 design space
  • React to SDL_EVENT_WINDOW_RESIZED instead of caching sizes at startup
  • One clamped delta after a mobile resume prevents the classic teleport bug
Performance Tip — Vsync is a preference, not a promise

SDL_SetRenderVSync(renderer, 1) is best-effort: compositors, battery savers and hidden browser tabs override it freely. A frame must simulate correctly at any cadence — motion multiplied by delta time, always, everywhere.

2.14 — Audio: Low-Latency SFX, Streamed Music

A jump must sound within milliseconds of the button; a theme song can trickle through a buffer. SDL3 binds both to one logical device and mixes them for you.

Logical device
SDL_AudioDeviceID
default playback
Bound streams
SFX voice
jump.wav · resident
SFX voice
carrot.wav · resident
Music stream
fed in chunks
Output
hardware mixer
SDL mixes all bound streams

The mixer is SDL's job, not ours — Chapter 10 builds the SfxVoice pool and MusicStreamer on top.

details
  • Open one logical playback device — SDL mixes every stream bound to it
  • SFX: SDL_LoadWAV at load time, buffers resident, pushed per trigger
  • Music: a long-lived SDL_AudioStream fed decoded chunks — bounded memory
  • SDL_SetAudioStreamGain per stream is the volume control, not a custom mixer
  • On background: pause the device; on resume: clear stale music buffers
Performance Tip — Resident SFX, streamed music

Decode-on-play is the classic audio hitch: a stall during level load is fine, a stall mid-jump is not. Golden carrots get small preloaded buffers; the theme gets fed in chunks so a four-minute track never sits in RAM decoded.

2.15 — Input: One Event Queue, Every Device

Keyboard, mouse, touch and gamepads all land in the same SDL queue. Sorting them once, in one place, is what keeps input code portable.

key points
  • Keyboard, mouse, touch and gamepads all arrive on one queue — dispatch, do not poll
  • Touch coordinates are normalized 0..1 — scale into the 960×540 logical space
  • Gamepad axes span -32768..32767; normalize before gameplay math sees them
  • Haptics are one call: SDL_RumbleGamepad with 0..0xFFFF magnitudes

2.16 — Storage: Base Path vs Pref Path

Assets are sacred and immutable; user data is personal and writable. SDL3 splits them into two roots — and confusing them is the number one portability bug.

ASDL_GetBasePath() — read-only
  • Where the OS installed your program and its assets
  • Ships assets/atlases/canyon.atlas and assets/levels/level-01.json
  • Read via SDL_IOFromFile(path, "rb") — never write here
  • Read-only in the wild: Program Files, bundles, APKs, web packs
  • Returns a path ending with a separator — join directly
BSDL_GetPrefPath() — writable
  • The per-user directory each OS expects apps to use; SDL creates it
  • Holds settings.json, saves, telemetry — and our log file
  • Write via SDL_IOFromFile(path, "w") plus SDL_WriteIO
  • A different physical home on every platform — never hardcode it
  • Canon call: SDL_GetPrefPath("sable", "canyon-dash")
Common Pitfall — Writing next to the executable

That trick works in a debug build from your build folder and dies the day the game installs into Program Files, an app bundle or an APK. SDL_GetBasePath() territory is read-only in the real world — user data belongs under SDL_GetPrefPath().

2.17 — The Network Module

Canyon Dash is offline-first — but leaderboards, telemetry and shared levels want the network. Each platform shapes what HTTP and sockets may do.

  • libcurl is the portable HTTP workhorse — same calls on desktop, mobile and web
  • WebSockets suit live channels; pick a small C library — SDL_net has no WebSocket layer
  • SDL_net itself remains a community satellite: verify its SDL3 migration before relying on it
  • Payloads are JSON — cJSON already ships with our toolchain from Chapter 4 onwards
  • Offline is a state, not an error: every request must fail gracefully
  • Network IO runs off the main thread, exactly like asset loading

2.18 — The Portable Entry Point

One main function runs on every target. The desktop keeps its while loop; the browser needs the loop handed over — SDL_main.h and one ifdef make both live in one file.

key points
  • SDL_main.h rewrites main() per platform: WinMain, JNI glue, web bootstrap
  • Desktop keeps the classic while loop; the browser gets emscripten_set_main_loop_arg
  • fps=0 follows requestAnimationFrame — the browser sets the cadence, not us
  • Web truth: the call never returns, so persistence rides lifecycle events, not exit paths

2.19 — Running the Demo on Every Target

Code is half the story. Each target wants its package, its icon and its quirks respected before Canyon Dash ships there.

  • Desktop: CMake presets per host; ship assets/ beside the binary
  • Android: a Gradle project wraps the NDK build; manifest and icons in platforms/android/
  • iOS: an Xcode project with launch screen and Info.plist from platforms/ios/
  • Web: Emscripten packs assets into a .data bundle — SDL_GetBasePath() finds them
  • Browser quirk: audio stays silent until the first user input unlocks the device
  • Icons, manifests and splash screens are packaging — they never touch src/

2.20 — Debugging Across Platforms

A bug that only reproduces on one platform is still your bug. Build the observability that lets you see it from anywhere.

  • SDL_assert halts in debug builds, logs in release — assert liberally
  • SDL_GetError() discipline: read it at the failure site, immediately (Chapter 1 rule)
  • Sanitizers on desktop catch what phones and tabs would hide
  • Tail the log file from slide 2.8: adb logcat on device, devtools console on web
  • Dev-mode hot-reload: watch assets/ timestamps, reload atlases without restarting
  • Treat warnings as errors on every target from day one
Common Pitfall — It's just a warning

The warning MSVC shrugs at, GCC may escalate — and Emscripten may turn into a codegen difference. A cross-platform project running warnings-as-errors on all targets from day one is far cheaper than a port-week archaeology dig.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 2 Recap

  • One codebase, six targets — Sable's platform layer keeps #ifdef out of the game
  • SDL3 translates windows, rendering, audio, input and files onto each OS backend
  • The lifecycle state machine: save on will, recover on did, die clean on terminating
  • SDL_Log with a custom output function leaves the same trail on every target
  • Storage splits read-only SDL_GetBasePath() from writable SDL_GetPrefPath()
  • Discipline: main-thread video, delta-time graphics, resident SFX, one input queue
Chapter 3 — Configuring the Game: structure, patterns, and the loop
Ch 3Chapter 3

Configuring the Game

01Project structure: the engine/game boundary as a build rule
02Architecture patterns: inheritance trees, ECS, and the Sable hybrid
03The trinity: GameApp, WorldController, WorldRenderer
04constants.h — the canon numbers of Canyon Dash
05The main loop: fixed timesteps, the accumulator, delta hygiene
06Camera2D, render layers, and debug controls

3.1 — The Engine/Game Boundary

Chapter 1 fixed the folder tree; this chapter turns it into law. The line between src/sable and src/game is the most valuable sentence in the codebase.

src/game — Canyon Dash
world/
rules · spawns
screens/
menus · flow
actors/
player · hazards
src/sable — the engine
app/
loop · lifecycle
scene/
camera · layers
assets/
load · atlases
shared foundation
SDL3 runtime
window · render · audio · events
assets/ data
levels · atlases · audio

Includes flow downward only — game → sable → SDL3. Data flows up as return values, never as #include.

details
  • src/sable is the engine: loops, rendering, assets, audio — it has never heard of carrots
  • src/game is Canyon Dash: rules, level flow, tuning, and content glue
  • The one-way rule: game code may include sable; sable must never include game
    • —An upward include means engine code learned game content — refactor it the same day
  • CMake turns the rule into law: sable builds as a static library with exactly one client
  • Assets are data, not code — nothing in assets/ ever appears on an include path
  • Engine tests link sable alone: regressions reproduce without any game content
Best Practice — Compile the boundary into the build

Model the split as two CMake targets from day one. The linker then enforces the one-way rule for free — a stray include from sable into game fails the build before it fails code review.

3.2 — Architecture Patterns for Game Code

Before writing classes, decide how classes relate. Three architectures dominate 2D game code — and each one buys a different kind of safety.

  • Actor inheritance: one deep Actor base class; subclasses override virtuals to specialize
    • —Shines for: small casts, fast prototyping, readable call stacks
  • Entity-Component: entities are bare IDs; behavior emerges from components that systems iterate
    • —Shines for: thousands of entities, editor-driven composition, data-oriented hot paths
  • Model-View-Controller: state, presentation, and input as separate citizens — our loop is already shaped like it
  • Sable picks a pragmatic hybrid: actor classes that compose helpers, plus a hard MVC split at the renderer
  • The right question is not which pattern is best — it is which failure mode this team can afford

3.3 — OOP Actor Inheritance vs Entity-Component

The classic trade in game architecture: deep class trees versus flat composition. Study both sides before committing.

AOOP actor inheritance
  • One Actor base: transform, update order, type tags, virtual tick
  • Subclasses specialize cleanly: PlayerActor, SpikeActor, CritterActor
  • Readable call stacks; jump-to-definition works everywhere
  • Pain: the "flying, swimming, spiked" actor forces multiple inheritance or duct tape
  • Pain: one new field on the base recompiles the whole world
BEntity-component composition
  • An entity is just an ID; behavior emerges from attached components
  • Sprite, Body, Emitter mix freely — no class explosions
  • New gameplay is a new component; existing types never change
  • Pain: indirection — "which system owns this bug?" gets harder to answer
  • Pain: storage, queries, and iteration order all need real machinery
Best Practice — Steal the middle

Sable keeps a shallow Actor base and composes helpers inside it: actors own a Camera2D or an AnimationPlayer instead of inheriting from them. Trees stay shallow, composition stays typed, and both pain columns shrink.

3.4 — Canyon Dash: The Class Map

One screen of architecture: GameApp coordinates, the controller simulates, the renderer presents. Every later chapter plugs into one of these boxes.

GameApp owns
WorldController
input → world state
WorldRenderer
state → pixels
AssetManager
textures — Ch 4
WorldController owns
Level
tile grid · AABBs
Actor + PlayerController
intent · motion
Camera2D
follow · clamp · zoom
WorldRenderer owns
Render layers
bg → actors → fx
Hud
lives · score · screen space
Debug overlays
F1 stats · F3 boxes

One frame, one direction: events feed the controller; the controller publishes state; the renderer snapshots it and never reaches back.

details
  • GameApp owns the loop and the pair; it never touches a carrot or a pixel directly
  • WorldController owns Level, Actors, and Camera2D — the entire simulation state
  • WorldRenderer owns layers, Hud, and debug overlays — it reads state and draws it

3.5 — constants.h: The Canon Numbers

Every tunable number lives in one header. A value that appears twice in the codebase will eventually disagree with itself.

key points
  • Values live once: designers tune the game by editing single lines, reviewed in git
  • Comments carry units — confusing px/s with px/s^2 is the classic gravity bug
  • The jump impulse clears just over three tiles at this gravity; tune the pair together, never one
  • Level bounds derive from tiles: 120 × 32 = 3840 px — the camera clamps against exactly this
Deep Dive — Why 960×540

Half of 1080p in both axes: clean integer 2× and 4× scale factors, 16:9 aspect, and only 518k pixels to fill — cheap for mobile GPUs. SDL_SetRenderLogicalPresentation letterboxes it onto any display you meet.

3.6 — GameApp: The Core Coordinator

Every game has one object that owns the process. In Sable it is GameApp — small, boring, and absolutely in charge.

  • Owns the main loop and its timestep policy — nothing else in the project spins the game
  • Owns subsystem lifetime: window, renderer, assets, audio — created in order, destroyed in reverse
  • Holds one controller/renderer pair per screen; Chapter 7 swaps them behind the ScreenManager
  • Translates OS events into engine facts: quit, focus loss, app backgrounding
  • Delegates everything else — no gameplay rules, no draw calls, no level knowledge
  • The test: GameApp compiles against sable and SDL only; if it includes game headers, the split is rotting
Common Pitfall — The coordinator becomes a god object

Every subsystem wants a reference to GameApp — resist. When everything can reach the coordinator, everything eventually does, and initialization order turns into archaeology. Pass dependencies explicitly at construction.

3.7 — GameApp: init, run, dispose

The full lifecycle in three methods: init brings the world up, run spins the loop, dispose tears it down in reverse. SDL_Init and SDL_Quit live here, and only here.

key points
  • Per frame, forever: pump → update → render → present — events before simulation, always
  • The per-frame delta here is deliberately naive; the accumulator loop (3.14) replaces it with fixed ticks
  • dispose() unwinds in exact reverse of init(); unique_ptr members make early exits safe
  • main() stays three lines: construct GameApp, drive the lifecycle, return its exit code
Common Pitfall — Leaking the early exit

A failed SDL_CreateRenderer must still destroy the window and call SDL_Quit(). Route every failure through dispose() — otherwise a crash leaves a zombie window and a locked audio device behind.

3.8 — WorldController: Pure Simulation

The controller is the game: everything that decides, moves, or scores. It has never heard of pixels-on-screen — only state and time.

  • Consumes input snapshots and dt; produces new world state — that is the entire contract
  • Owns Level, Actors, pickups, hazards, Camera2D, and the lives/score model
  • Zero rendering calls inside — not one SDL_Render*, not one texture lookup
  • A headless build links the controller with SDL_InitEvents alone and runs ticks in tests
  • Deterministic ticks make recorded input a replay, and a failing frame a unit test
  • Renderers are disposable — 2D today, SDL_GPU in Chapter 11; the simulation outlives them all
Best Practice — Narrow the SDL surface

Keep controller-side SDL down to SDL_GetKeyboardState — a snapshot that needs events initialized but no window. Everything else crosses the boundary as plain structs, so tests inject snapshots and run ticks in microseconds.

3.9 — WorldController::update: Input to Motion

One tick, read top to bottom: sample input, decide intent, integrate motion, advance everything else. Not one draw call in sight.

key points
  • The keyboard array refreshes during the event pump — sample it once, at the top, and trust that snapshot all tick
  • Edge detection (jump && !m_jumpHeld) turns a held key into a single press
  • Order is the physics: intent → integrate → collide — resolving before moving would erase motion
  • Units discipline: GRAVITY scales by dt, PLAYER_JUMP does not — one is a field, the other an impulse
Performance Tip — The snapshot is free; misusing it is not

SDL_GetKeyboardState hands you a pointer into SDL state: reading a key is one array index, no syscall. The cost appears when code polls it before the pump or from other threads — the data is only coherent right after SDL_PollEvent.

3.10 — WorldRenderer: Pure Presentation

The renderer is a pure function of the controller's state: same state in, same pixels out. It decides nothing — it only shows.

  • Reads positions, animation frames, and HUD numbers from a const snapshot of the controller
  • Owns draw order, blend modes, and the camera transform — presentation concerns only
  • Never mutates simulation state — the moment drawing changes the world, tests stop meaning anything
  • World layers draw through the camera; the HUD draws in fixed 960×540 logical space
  • Handles the 2D API today; an SDL_GPU version in Chapter 11 changes this file and nothing upstream
  • The renderer may skip frames, cache textures, or sort draws — none of it visible to gameplay

3.11 — WorldRenderer::render: World, then HUD

One frame in four moves: clear, enter world space through the camera, draw the layers back to front, reset to screen space for the HUD.

key points
  • The camera transform is two halves: scale (SDL applies it) and translate (toScreen subtracts it)
  • One funnel: every world draw passes through toScreen, so camera math lives in exactly one function
  • The reset before the HUD is load-bearing — UI drawn in world space pans with the player
  • A second SDL_RenderPresent costs a full frame budget and shows nothing new
Common Pitfall — HUD in world space

Forget the scale reset and the score floats over the desert, drifting with every camera pan. Memorize the symptom: UI that moves when the world moves means a transform leaked past its section.

3.12 — The Main Loop: One Tick at a Time

The loop is the game's heartbeat — and its timestep is a design decision, not an implementation detail. Just multiply by delta is where jumps start lying.

  • Variable timestep: simulate with the measured elapsed time — smooth motion, unstable everything else
  • Integration error scales with dt: the same jump reaches different apexes at 30 and 144 fps
  • Collisions tunnel: one large step can hop a fast actor clean through a thin spike
  • Fixed timestep: constant 60 Hz ticks — the run is identical on every machine
    • —Same input and tick count produce the same world: replays, demos, and lockstep networking fall out for free
  • Box2D (Chapter 11) requires fixed steps outright — variable dt makes its solver jitter
  • The renderer still runs at display rate; making both true is the hybrid on the next slide
Deep Dive — Why delta breaks jump height

Semi-implicit Euler runs v += g*dt then y += v*dt, so position uses the post-gravity velocity — per-step error scales with dt. Halve the frame rate and the apex genuinely moves. A fixed dt (or fancier integration) is the only thing that pins the arc.

3.13 — Fixed vs Variable Timestep

Both loops ship real games. The choice is about which guarantees you need — and what you will pay for them.

AVariable timestep
  • Simulate with measured elapsed time — motion tracks the display exactly
  • One update per frame: the simplest loop that can exist
  • Jump arcs and physics drift with frame rate; spikes get tunneled through
  • Replays and lockstep networking need extra bookkeeping to work
  • Fits: menus, slow-paced games, visual toys — low physics stakes
BFixed timestep
  • Simulate in constant 60 Hz ticks; render at whatever rate the display runs
  • Deterministic: same input sequence, same world, every single time
  • Collision and solver math stay inside their tested bounds
  • Costs: an accumulator loop plus interpolation for smooth rendering
  • Fits: platformers, physics games, replays — Canyon Dash, in short
Best Practice — The hybrid is the industry answer

Fixed simulation at 60 Hz, a render every vsync, and draw positions interpolated between the last two ticks using the accumulator leftover as alpha. Determinism and 144 Hz smoothness in one loop — we build exactly this next.

3.14 — The Accumulator Loop

The industry-standard loop: measure the frame, bank it in an accumulator, spend it in fixed 60 Hz ticks, render what is left. Three guards keep it honest.

key points
  • SDL_GetTicksNS() hands you Uint64 nanoseconds — monotonic, wrap-free, precise across hours-long sessions
  • The clamp (250 ms) bounds the debt a single stall can create
  • The step cap (5) is the spiral-of-death breaker: slow machines drop time, never freeze
  • acc / STEP becomes the interpolation alpha — how far between tick n-1 and n this frame lands
Common Pitfall — The spiral of death

When one tick costs more than 16.6 ms, the accumulator grows, the next frame runs more ticks, the machine falls further behind — a slow-motion freeze. Clamp plus cap is the circuit breaker; test it by forcing a 30 ms tick in a debug build.

3.15 — Delta Smoothing and Clamping

Between the timer and the simulation sits a small policy layer: how much of the measured frame time do you actually believe?

  • Clamp first: cap the raw frame delta (250 ms here) — a single stall must not teleport actors
  • Smoothing: an exponential or moving average damps timer noise from jittery vsync and OS scheduling
  • Smoothed dt may feed presentation only — camera easing, particle drift — never the fixed ticks
  • Every millisecond of smoothing is a millisecond of input latency; players feel three frames of it
  • Canyon Dash policy: clamp always, smooth never — the fixed-step loop already absorbs the jitter
Performance Tip — Smoothing buys shimmer, costs latency

Averaging hides vsync jitter but also delays the response to real slowdowns while adding straight-up input lag. With fixed ticks your cadence already follows the display — skip the filter unless you can measure the shimmer you are fixing.

3.16 — Loading Test Assets

Before the art pipeline arrives in Chapter 4, the game needs something to draw. Stand-in textures keep the loop honest without pretending to be pretty.

  • The placeholder set: flat-color 32 px tiles, a marked player box, numbered pickups — ugly on purpose
  • IMG_LoadTexture(renderer, "assets/atlases/canyon.png") decodes a file straight into a texture
  • Prefix every path with SDL_GetBasePath() — relative paths only work where the debugger launched you
  • SDL_SetTextureScaleMode(tex, SDL_SCALEMODE_NEAREST) keeps pixel art crisp at integer zooms
    • —The default is LINEAR: at 2× scale it averages your pixels into mud
  • SDL_SetTextureBlendMode(tex, SDL_BLENDMODE_BLEND) on anything that draws over the world
  • Track placeholders in one registry so the real art pass (Chapter 4) replaces them wholesale
Common Pitfall — LINEAR by default

SDL textures default to SDL_SCALEMODE_LINEAR. Pixel art behind a 960×540 logical presentation means blur everywhere. Call SDL_SetTextureScaleMode immediately after IMG_LoadTexture — every texture, every time.

3.17 — Render Layers, Back to Front

Canyon Dash draws in six passes, back to front — the painter's algorithm. Order is not style; for anything with alpha, it is correctness.

far
1 Background
sky · mesas — opaque
2 Water overlay
translucent · animated
mid
3 Props
cacti · rocks · spikes
4 Actors
player · critters · pickups
near
5 Particles
dust · splash · sparkles
6 HUD
screen space · camera-free

Everything above layer 1 blends — the alpha between layers is what makes the order matter.

details
  • Painter's algorithm: later draws land on top — water over rocks is what reads as depth
  • Only the background is opaque; every layer above it blends with SDL_BLENDMODE_BLEND
  • Particles draw above actors so splash and dust wrap the action instead of hiding under it
  • The HUD ignores the camera entirely — it belongs to the fixed 960×540 logical screen
Performance Tip — Order is also batching

Back-to-front is a visual requirement; within a layer, keep draws grouped by texture. The 2D renderer batches consecutive work on the same texture — every needless texture switch is a state change you paid for nothing.

3.18 — Debug Controls: F1 and F3

Two debug keys carry this project: F1 for a stats overlay, F3 for collider drawing. They cost an afternoon and save weeks.

  • F1 — stats: fps, tick count, actors, camera pos, draw calls — text arrives properly in Chapter 7
  • F3 — colliders: AABB outlines via SDL_RenderRect, red for hazards, green for solid tiles
  • Toggle on the edge: key down this tick and up last tick — level-triggered tests flap at 60 Hz
  • Gate behind a build flag: debug draws cost milliseconds and leak design intent in release builds
  • Add what you currently printf: coyote windows, respawn points, actor state names — one overlay, one key
  • F1 may ship — players love stats screens; F3 never leaves debug builds
Best Practice — Debug UI is engine UI

Build stats and colliders as renderer features behind one flag, not game hacks scattered across files. When Chapter 8 adds particles, F3 grows an emitter counter for free — debug tooling compounds.

3.19 — Camera2D: Smooth Follow and Look-Ahead

A camera that snaps to the player feels like security footage. Camera2D lerps toward a look-ahead target — smooth, stable, and frame-rate independent.

key points
  • t = 1 - exp(-SMOOTH·dt) — the smoothing rate is a property of the camera, not the player monitor
  • The naive pos += (target - pos) * 0.1f runs three times stiffer at 180 Hz than at 60 Hz
  • Look-ahead steers the view into oncoming ground: roughly a third of a second of velocity
  • Vertical look-ahead is halved — jumps should nudge the view, not yank it
  • Called from the controller tick: the camera is simulated state, replayed with everything else
Deep Dive — Why not plain lerp

Constant-alpha lerp is an exponential smoother whose speed depends on tick rate. Rewriting alpha as 1 - exp(-k·dt) decouples stiffness from fps — the same decay-curve fix used in audio envelopes and network interpolation. One formula, any rate.

3.20 — Camera Clamp and Zoom

Two finishing moves: clamp the camera to level bounds so edges never show void, and zoom around a chosen world point so the focus never slides.

key points
  • Clamp against LEVEL_W_TILES × TILE — the camera never reveals void beyond the canyon
  • When the view outgrows a small level, center it instead of clamping to nonsense
  • zoomAt re-anchors: the focused world point holds its screen position across the zoom
  • Tick order is a contract: look-ahead → lerp → clamp → zoom, every tick
Common Pitfall — Clamp after the lerp, every tick

Clamp the follow target instead of the camera position and the lerp keeps pushing past the edge while the clamp snaps back — edge jitter. Clamp the smoothed position itself, once per tick, after smoothing and before rendering.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 3 Recap

  • Structure: src/game includes src/sable, never the reverse — two CMake targets make it law
  • The trinity: GameApp coordinates, WorldController simulates, WorldRenderer presents — one-way data flow
  • constants.h holds the canon: 960×540 logical, 32 px tiles, 3 lives, carrot value 10
  • Fixed-step accumulator: clamp the frame, bank the time, tick at 60 Hz, cap the spiral, render with alpha
  • Camera2D: exponential-lerp follow, look-ahead, level clamp, zoom around a focus
  • Six render layers back to front; F1 and F3 debug tools stay behind a build flag
