Gathering Resources

01The asset pipeline: raw art to shipped packages
02Icons and splash screens on every platform
03Sprite atlases: packing, metadata, and the Atlas class
04The AssetManager: cache, sync and async loading, disposal
05Asset hygiene: directory rules, CI validation, hot reload
06Level data: formats, the JSON schema, and versioning

4.1 — The Asset Pipeline

Chapter 3 drew numbered stand-in rectangles; real games ship a pipeline. Raw art becomes processed, packed, installed data — and every hop is scripted.

raw — artist sources
sprites
aseprite · psd
tilesets
raw png
audio
wav stems
icon art
master 1024
process — tools/ scripts
trim
crop borders
quantize
palette fit
normalize
audio levels
rename
lowercase keys
pack
atlas pages
canyon.png
region tables
canyon.atlas
level data
level-01.json
ship
assets/
read-only data
platforms/
icons · splash
packages
per-target install

Every arrow is a script under tools/ — versioned with the code and re-runnable on a clean checkout.

details
  • Raw sources live outside the build: layered sprite files, uncompressed audio, the 1024 px icon master
    • —Artists own these; the game never opens them directly
  • Process: trim transparent borders, quantize to a palette, normalize audio levels, enforce naming rules
  • Pack: sprites merge into atlas pages; the region table is generated beside each page
  • Ship: assets/ rides every package; platforms/ carries icons, manifests, and splash screens
  • Every hop is a script under tools/ — the folder Chapter 1 reserved for exactly this work
Best Practice — The pipeline is code

A remembered sequence of export dialogs lives in one artist's head and dies with their laptop. The same steps as scripts under tools/, versioned with the code, re-run on every clean checkout — that is the difference between art that ships and art that rots.

4.2 — Icons and Splash Screens per Platform

The window icon is the first frame of your game. Every platform demands its own formats — all of them live in platforms/, none of them touch src/.

  • Desktop: Windows wants icon.ico, macOS icon.icns, Linux a set of PNGs plus a .desktop entry
  • Android: adaptive icons split into foreground and background layers under platforms/android/
    • —Legacy PNG sizes ship alongside the adaptive pair for old devices
  • iOS: the launch screen is a storyboard in platforms/ios/ — sized for every device at build time
  • Web: favicon, PWA manifest icons at 192 and 512 px, wired into the Emscripten shell HTML
  • Chapter 2 wired the packaging targets; this chapter supplies the pixels that fill them
  • One 1024 px master PNG generates every target — a tools/ script, never fourteen hand-exports
Common Pitfall — Shipping the default icon

A window with the SDL logo and a store listing with a missing 512 px icon are the same bug: assets forgotten until submission week. Generate every icon target in the pack script and fail the build when one is missing — reviewers and players judge the first frame.

4.3 — Why Sprite Atlases

An atlas is one texture holding many sprites plus a table saying who lives where. It exists because batching is the entire game of 2D performance.

  • SDL3 batches consecutive draws that share a texture — every switch to a new texture flushes the batch
  • Two hundred loose PNGs is two hundred flushes per frame; one atlas page is one
  • Memory: one allocation per page, no per-file padding, better cache locality for the renderer
  • UV space: sprites become regions addressed by coordinates inside the page — Chapter 11's shaders want them normalized
    • —Normalized u/v coordinates ship in SpriteRegion from day one
  • What breaks without atlases: mobile frame budgets die first, then level-load times balloon with per-file overhead
Performance Tip — Batching before micro-optimizing

Draw order that keeps same-texture runs long buys more frames than any per-sprite tuning. The 2D renderer pays a state change at every texture switch — atlases are how you make those switches rare enough to ignore.

4.4 — Packing Atlases: Tools and Settings

Packing is solved software. The decisions that matter are the export settings — page size, padding, trim — because they change what the region table must record.

  • TexturePacker (paid) is the industry default: GUI packing, trim, rotation, many export formats
  • Free alternatives: open-source packers such as free-tex-packer, or the 60-line script in tools/ this course uses
    • —A shelf packer is a sorted loop — writing one teaches more than configuring one
  • Max page size 2048: fits every target we ship; overflow splits into a second page, never a bigger one
  • Padding 2 px: neighboring pixels bleed through linear filtering without it
  • Trim crops transparent borders — region sizes are post-trim, so sprites anchor differently
  • POT vs non-POT: SDL3 accepts any page size; power-of-two still plays nicer with old GLES devices and compressed formats
Best Practice — Two pixels of peace of mind

Linear filtering samples a border zone around every region; without padding, a dune tile's left edge can bleed in the cactus beside it. Two pixels of duplicated border cost nothing and end the mystery specks.

4.5 — Atlas Metadata Formats

A page without a table is a mystery image. Every packer exports a companion describing each region — and the format choice shapes your tooling for years.

  • JSON: nested frames arrays; every tool speaks it, humans can read it, cJSON already links in our build
  • XML: the editor-era standard — verbose, but validators and an ecosystem
  • Plaintext tables: one line per region — greppable, diffable, parseable with a single sscanf
  • Canyon Dash chooses a plaintext .atlas file; every line is dune_tile 0 0 32 32
    • —The pair canyon.png + canyon.atlas travels together as one unit
  • Why simple wins for teaching: zero parser code, honest diffs in review, and hand-editing during jams
  • The upgrade path is real: when regions grow pivots and effects, a JSON schema arrives without touching the Atlas class
Deep Dive — Formats follow generators

Who writes the file decides the format. Hand-authored data earns human formats; machine-generated data can be as terse as it likes. The .atlas table is written by the packer and read by one loader — plaintext is the honest contract between two scripts.

4.6 — The Atlas Class

One page, one table, one map. The Atlas loads the PNG, parses the region lines, and hands the renderer addressable sprites by name.

key points
  • The page loads once with IMG_LoadTexture; SDL_GetTextureSize supplies the denominators for normalized UVs
  • SpriteRegion carries both addressings: pixel x/y/w/h for the 2D renderer, u/v for Chapter 11's GPU passes
  • Parsing is one strtok-sscanf loop: a name plus four floats, comments allowed with #
  • find() returns a pointer into the map — NULL means the name never shipped in the page
Common Pitfall — A stale table on a fresh page

Re-export the page and forget the table (or the reverse) and regions point into yesterday's layout: carrots draw as cactus fragments. Generate the pair atomically in one script step, and let the CI smoke test in 4.15 catch the drift.

4.7 — Drawing Sprites from the Atlas

Rendering a region is two rectangles: the srcrect that picks it out of the page, and the dstrect that places it in the world.

key points
  • SDL_RenderTexture takes the region as srcrect, the placement as dstrect — one draw, one line
  • Camera math stays with the caller: this helper draws where it is told, world space or screen space
  • The scale parameter grows pickups and shrinks dust — no separate art assets for size variants
  • Flipping rides SDL_RenderTextureRotated at zero angle — mirrored critters cost no texture space
Best Practice — Content bugs must not crash the process

A mistyped sprite name is data, not a fatal error. Log it once, draw nothing, keep the frame alive — then let the asset smoke test in CI turn it into a red build before any player sees it.

4.8 — The AssetManager

One class owns every SDL_Texture lifetime. Everything else borrows pointers — and borrowers, by contract, never destroy.

  • Load: base-path-prefixed loads, atlas pages, fonts — one entry point with consistent scale and blend defaults
  • Cache by key: loading canyon twice returns the same pointer; the second load is a hash hit
  • Unload: explicit for level-scoped packs; refcounting only earns its cost when screens share heavily
  • Dispose at shutdown: walk the cache in reverse creation order, then drop the whole store
  • The single-owner rule: no other file calls SDL_DestroyTexture — leaks and double-frees become impossible bug classes
Best Practice — One owner, many borrowers

When exactly one object can destroy a resource, destruction mistakes collapse into one file. Game code holds borrowed pointers; the manager decides their fate. This is the C++ rule of zero applied to C handles.

4.9 — Synchronous Loading

The synchronous core boots the game and loads small things: prefix every path once, cache by key, fail loudly without crashing.

key points
  • Every path joins SDL_GetBasePath() — Chapter 3's rule, now enforced in exactly one place
  • get<T>(key) picks the typed store — textures, atlases, fonts; NULL means not loaded yet
  • Failure returns NULL with a logged reason — callers fall back to a stand-in region, never crash
  • Synchronous loads happen at boot and level start only; the async path owns everything bigger
Common Pitfall — Relative paths work until they ship

Relative asset paths resolve wherever the debugger launched you, then break from a desktop shortcut, an APK, or the web bundle. The base path is the one true anchor — prefixing anywhere else is a bug farm.

4.10 — Asynchronous Loading: The Design

A level load on the main thread is a frozen frame — thirty textures at cold-cache prices. The design goal: keep the loading screen animating while work happens elsewhere.

  • The shape: a worker thread draining a request queue, feeding a result queue the main thread pumps
  • Both queues sit behind mutexes; a condition variable lets the worker sleep instead of spin
  • The worker touches files only; the render API stays on its owning thread — Chapter 2's golden rule
  • The pump converts delivered work into textures between frames — budgeted, not bursted
  • Web fallback: without pthreads the same API degrades to synchronous loads — design once, run anywhere
Deep Dive — Where load time actually goes

A texture load is three costs: cold IO (disk, or network on the web), decode (CPU — PNG is not free), and upload (a driver copy). The worker hides the first; the pump pays the last two in small slices. Measure which dominates before optimizing the wrong one.

4.11 — The Async Loader Worker

Chapter 2 sketched a worker for settings; the AssetManager finishes the design — request queue in, results out, a counter the loading bar can trust.

key points
  • The worker reads and frees: prefetch plus verification — the page cache is warm when the pump decodes
  • deliver() locks, pushes, increments, signals — progress is a counter, not a guess
  • pump() runs on the render thread: IMG_LoadTexture plus scale defaults, then the cache swap
  • Shutdown is Chapter 2's poison pill plus SDL_WaitThread — join before destroying the mutex
Performance Tip — One worker is plenty

An IO queue serialized on one thread outruns a pool of threads fighting over a cold cache — disks like company, not contention. Save the extra cores for Chapter 11's physics; the loading screen needs one good worker.

4.12 — Tracking Load Progress

A loading screen earns trust by telling the truth. The counter knows exactly how much work remains — let it say so.

  • Progress is arithmetic: loaded / total, counted at deliver time by the worker itself
  • onUpdate(loaded, total) callbacks drive the bar — the manager knows numbers, the screen draws them
  • Smooth the bar's motion, never the number: the target jumps honestly, the pixel width eases
  • Show task names while stalled: loading canyon.png beats a bar frozen at 87 percent
  • Chapter 7 turns this screen into a proper Screen with states — the callback interface is already it
Common Pitfall — The lying progress bar

Bars that animate to 90 percent and wait, or tick on a timer, train players to distrust every loader you ever ship. The honest counter sometimes stalls — so pair it with the current task name and let the animation admit it.

4.13 — Memory Cleanup and Disposal

Every asset the manager owns, it must outlive. Disposal is creation played in reverse — and SDL has opinions about the order.

  • Reverse of creation, every time: level packs before atlases, atlases before the renderer, renderer before the window
  • Explicit unload for level-scoped packs; the boot pack lives until dispose()
  • RAII wrappers: a TexturePtr alias over unique_ptr with an SDL_DestroyTexture deleter — C++17 cleans up C handles
  • The cache destructor asserts emptiness at shutdown — a leak caught on your desk, not a customer's
Common Pitfall — Tearing down out of order

Destroy the renderer while textures live — or the window while the renderer lives — and teardown becomes undefined behavior on some backends. GameApp::dispose already runs the reverse chain from Chapter 3; the manager simply slots into it.

4.14 — Organizing the Asset Directory

The assets tree from Chapter 1 fills in today — and its naming conventions are cross-platform law, not local preference.

  • assets/atlases/ — page and table pairs: canyon.png beside canyon.atlas, always siblings
  • assets/levels/ — level-01.json and successors: versioned, hand-editable, diffed in review
  • assets/audio/ splits sfx/ and music/ — Chapter 10 streams them differently
  • assets/ui/ — fonts, skins, menu art; shared by every screen Chapter 7 builds
  • Naming: lowercase kebab-case, ASCII only, no spaces, no version suffixes inside names
  • Names describe content, not history: cactus_large, never cactus_final_v2_really
Common Pitfall — Case sensitivity is a platform feature

Windows and macOS forgive mixed-case paths; Linux, Android, and the web bundle do not — the file simply is not there. Lowercase everything in the tree and in every string literal: a case mismatch works on your desk and breaks on the store.

4.15 — Testing and Validating Assets

Assets are code that fails at runtime — unless a test fails first. A smoke test that loads everything the game references is an afternoon that pays rent.

  • The smoke test: enumerate every level, parse it, load every atlas page and region it references
  • Assert invariants: regions inside page bounds, terrain rows matching widthTiles, no empty names
  • Headless run: the test links sable with events and IO only — no window, CI-friendly
  • The gate: a missing asset turns the build red — content bugs become compile-time bugs
  • The tests/ folder Chapter 1 reserved for asset smoke tests gets its first resident
Best Practice — Fail in CI, not on a player's device

A mistyped region name in level 7 costs a red build in CI and a shrug; the same bug in production costs a support ticket with a screenshot. The smoke test is one file — write it the same week you write the loader.

4.16 — Hot-Reloading Assets in Dev Builds

Chapter 2 promised timestamp-watching hot reload; here it is. Poll file mtimes once per second and swap the texture pointer behind the cache.

key points
  • One stat() per watched file per second — timestamps, not busy polling
  • replace() swaps the pointer between ticks — nothing mid-frame holds the stale texture
  • A failed reload (a half-written file) skips one second and retries — never swaps in garbage
  • Gated behind a build flag: dev builds watch, release builds never even link this file
Best Practice — Iteration speed compounds

An art tweak visible in one second — no restart, no level reload — changes how often artists try things. Tools that reward experimentation get used; tools that cost a reboot do not. Hot reload is a feature of the build, not of the game.

4.17 — The Level Data Landscape

Level data has four native habitats — human-readable files and machine-packed records — and the trade-offs between them. The choice is per data type, not per project.

  • JSON: the modern default — readable, diffable, tool-supported; cJSON parses it in microseconds at course scale
  • XML: the editor-era standard — Tiled and friends still speak it fluently
  • Plaintext tables: our .atlas format — terse, greppable, zero parser dependencies
  • Binary: fixed-layout structs — smallest, fastest, opaque to humans and to git diffs
  • Parse cost is a load-time cost: a 20 KB level parses in well under a millisecond — never a per-frame concern
  • The real trade is authoring: what designers edit by hand, and what only tools ever touch

4.18 — Level Data Formats

Human-readable and machine-packed formats are not rivals — they are instruments for different jobs. Match the column to the data.

AHuman-readable — JSON, XML
  • Git diffs line by line; review catches a moved spawn point instantly
  • Hand-editable: a designer nudges a prop with no tool round-trip
  • Tool ecosystems: validators, editors, converters, Tiled exporters
  • Cost: several times the bytes on disk, plus a parse at load time
  • Fits level files and config — anything humans open in an editor
BCompact — plaintext, binary
  • Plaintext tables parse with sscanf; binary maps straight onto structs
  • Smallest payload: one record per line, or fixed-size binary blocks
  • Survives size pressure: network saves, consoles with tight budgets
  • Cost: corruption hides from the eye — one flipped byte ships silently
  • Fits generated tables, save games, telemetry — machine audiences
Best Practice — Choose per data type

Canyon Dash ships three formats on purpose: JSON levels because designers hand-edit them, a plaintext .atlas because the packer writes it, and binary reserved for later chapters' saves and replays. One format for everything is how XML level files happen.

4.19 — The Level JSON Schema

The whole level as pure data: a header, terrain rows, background layers, props, and the actors Chapter 6 will bring to life. cJSON turns it into structs.

key points
  • The schema mirrors the scene catalog: terrain grid, background layers, props, dynamic actors — nothing else
  • Terrain rows are strings: one character per tile — # solid, = platform, w water
  • Tiles and actors parse here; backgrounds and props complete in Chapter 5's loader
  • Spawn positions are tile coordinates converted to pixels exactly once, at load time
Common Pitfall — Trusting the file's shape

A row shorter than widthTiles, a missing field, a negative coordinate: the loader pads, guards, and rejects — it never indexes out of bounds for a data file. Every read is bounded; every failure names the file in the log.

4.20 — Versioning Data Files

Every file that outlives a release needs a magic header and a version number — before the first format ever changes. Retrofitting versions is the expensive path.

  • The magic header CDLVL answers "is this even our file?" in five characters
  • The version field answers "which shape is this?" — checked before any field is read
  • Schema evolution: new fields arrive optional with defaults — old files load, new code fills the gaps
  • Migration: version 1 to 2 to current runs as a chain of small converters, each testable alone
  • Binary formats get the same treatment: magic bytes plus version at byte zero, fixed stride after
  • Our Chapter 2 settings file ships without a version field — add one before it grows a second key
Common Pitfall — Saves without versions brick players

A save file indistinguishable from next year's format cannot be migrated — only discarded, and players lose progress exactly once. The magic-plus-version pair costs two fields at write time and stays a support-ticket firewall forever.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 4 Recap

  • The pipeline is code: raw art → processed → packed atlases → shipped assets/ and platforms/
  • Atlases batch draws: one page per visual style, 2 px padding, a region table beside every page
  • Atlas parses the .atlas table; AssetManager is the single owner of every SDL_Texture
  • Async loading: a worker thread for IO, a render-thread pump for decode and upload, honest progress
  • Dispose in reverse creation order; validate every asset in CI; hot-reload pages in dev builds
  • Level data: JSON parsed with cJSON, magic header and version on every file that persists
Chapter 5 — Making a Scene: terrain, layers, and the HUD
Ch 5Chapter 5

Making a Scene

01Static world entities versus dynamic actors
02Tile rendering with camera culling
03Backgrounds, water overlay, and environmental props
04LevelLoader completion and the render order contract
05The HUD: score, lives, cached text, and the FPS monitor
06Scaling, resize, and the assembled scene

5.1 — Static versus Dynamic Entities

Chapter 4 turned levels into data; now the data becomes a scene. The first split in world code is what moves and what never does.

  • Static: terrain tiles, background bands, water overlay, props — placed once at load, zero per-tick cost
  • Dynamic: actors — player, critters, pickups with behavior; they tick, collide, and die (Chapter 6)
  • The level file is pure data: no behavior, no update order, no code — Chapter 4's JSON is inert by design
  • The split drives memory layout: static batches live in arrays; actors live in a polymorphic list
  • Static things draw in fixed passes; dynamic things draw after them, in simulation order
  • When a prop needs to move, it graduates to an actor — the categories are about behavior, not looks
Best Practice — Levels as data, engines as code

A designer moves a cactus by editing JSON and reloading; the same change in code costs a compile and a programmer. Every fact that can be data should be — the engine exists to interpret it.

5.2 — The Level Object Catalog

One screen shows everything level-01.json places. Four categories, all static, all described by Chapter 4's schema and parsed by LevelLoader.

terrain — the grid
solid dunes
# · collision
ledges
= · platform
water cells
w · hazard
backgrounds — three bands
mesas
scroll 0.15
ridge
scroll 0.4
clouds
drift · Ch 8
water overlay
surface band
bright · alpha 90
body band
deep · alpha 150
oscillation
±4 px sine
props — static decor
cacti
large · small
rock clusters
grounded
skull signs
landmarks

Everything on this slide is placed once by LevelLoader and never ticks — zero per-frame simulation cost.

details
  • Terrain: the 120×17 tile grid — # solid dunes, = ledges, w water cells
  • Backgrounds: three painted bands, far to near, each with its own scroll factor
  • Water overlay: two translucent bands anchored to the lowest water tile
  • Props: cacti, rock clusters, skull signs — a name plus placement data, nothing more
  • All four draw every frame; none of them tick, allocate, or query input

5.3 — Tile Rendering with Culling

Drawing the whole 120×17 grid is 2040 quads for 558 the camera can see. The window math is four divisions and four clamps.

key points
  • The window: from cam.pos / TILE to the view edge, plus one cell for the partial tile at the margin
  • At zoom 1 that is 31×18 candidate cells out of a 120×17 grid; at zoom 0.5, twice the cells
  • Each draw reuses Chapter 4's drawSprite: world position minus camera, zoom applied by the render pass
  • Empty cells skip before any rectangle is built — most of the grid is air
Performance Tip — Cull before the renderer ever sees it

Skipped draws cost nothing: 2040 grid cells become a 558-cell window, then roughly 350 real draws — all from one page, one batch. Loop-level culling is simpler than any spatial structure and plenty for a 2D grid this size.

5.4 — Background Layers and the Parallax Preview

Three painted bands turn a flat canyon into depth. Each moves at a fraction of the camera — that fraction is the parallax illusion.

  • Far to near: distant mesas, a mid ridge with silhouettes, drifting clouds above the action
  • The preview: each band draws offset by cam.pos.x * scroll — mesas at 0.15, the ridge at 0.4
  • Nearer bands move faster; the contrast between bands is what reads as distance
  • Backgrounds draw first in the world pass, behind terrain and everything else — no culling, they span the view
  • This is the flat version: seamless looping bands, zoom-aware widths, and cloud drift land in Chapter 8
  • The sky clear color from Chapter 3 is layer zero — painted by SDL_RenderClear for free
Deep Dive — Overdraw is the painter's tax

Back-to-front drawing means far layers get covered by near ones — wasted fill you pay for correctness. At 2D scale this is pocket change; in Chapter 13's 3D pipeline the same trade becomes culling and depth buffers. The habit of thinking about covered pixels starts here.

5.5 — The Water Overlay

Water in Canyon Dash is a translucent tint, not a simulation — two modulated bands that breathe slowly over the hazards.

  • Two bands: a bright surface strip over a deeper body band — one hue, two alphas
  • A dedicated 4×4 white texture: SDL_SetTextureAlphaMod for depth, SDL_SetTextureColorMod for hue
  • Gentle vertical oscillation: ±4 px on a slow sine, the surface band livelier than the body
  • Time-based, never frame-based: sin(t) off the controller's clock — Chapter 3's dt discipline
  • Anchored to the water line the loader computed — the lowest w tile in the grid
  • It draws after terrain, before props: hazards tinted, foreground props on top
Common Pitfall — Modulating the shared page

SDL_SetTextureAlphaMod and friends are per-texture state, not per-draw parameters. Modulate the atlas page and every sprite drawn after the water inherits the tint — mystery ghosts. Dedicated small textures carry modulated effects; the page stays untouched.

5.6 — Environmental Props

Props are scenery with an atlas name and a position — cacti, rock clusters, skull signs. The loader places them once; the renderer never asks again.

  • Placement is data: { name, x, y } in tile coordinates, converted to pixels at load
  • Drawing is drawSprite at p.x - cam.pos.x — the same camera math as the tiles
  • Sorted by x at load time: stable order, batch-friendly iteration down the level
  • Spike traps are props today — Chapter 6 straps hitboxes onto the dangerous subset
  • Depth reading: props draw after the water band, so cacti in pools read as foreground
  • The moment a prop needs a tick, it graduates to an actor — Chapter 6 door is open

5.7 — LevelLoader: The Completion

Chapter 4 parsed terrain rows and spawn lists; the completion adds the world's dressing — background layers, placed props, and the water line.

key points
  • Background layers carry their scroll factor in the file — designers tune depth in review, not in code
  • Props convert tile coordinates to pixels exactly once — the renderer never multiplies again
  • computeWaterLine scans for the lowest water cell — the overlay's anchor, decided by data
  • Every read stays guarded: the Chapter 4 bounds discipline carries through the completion
Common Pitfall — Unguarded reads from authored files

A level file is user input with good intentions: a missing scroll key, a null name, a prop outside the grid. Guard every field, log the file and index on failure, default the value — the game keeps booting while the level author fixes the typo.

5.8 — Assembling the World

The renderer now owns a full toolbox: terrain pass, background bands, water texture, prop list, HUD. The contract that orders them is this chapter's spine.

  • WorldRenderer composes: the Atlas from Chapter 4, a TerrainRenderer, the water texture, and the Hud
  • The render order contract: backgrounds and terrain → water → props → actors → particles → HUD
  • It is Chapter 3's six layers, now populated by real passes instead of stubs
  • Every world pass shares one camera funnel: scale by zoom, translate by cam.pos
  • The HUD closes the frame in screen space, camera-free by contract
Best Practice — The contract is a comment, not a convention

Six numbered passes, written as a comment block above renderWorld. New features slot into the list in review — "which pass?" always has an answer. Unwritten ordering conventions are how particles end up behind the background.

5.9 — WorldRenderer::renderWorld

One method assembles the frame: enter world space through the camera, draw the passes back to front, reset the transform, hand the screen to the HUD.

key points
  • The transform is Chapter 3's two halves: SDL_SetRenderScale takes the zoom, every draw subtracts cam.pos
  • The passes run back to front; actors and particles have reserved slots in Chapters 6 and 8
  • The reset before the HUD is load-bearing — screen space, scale one, offset zero
  • Water draws as two modulated bands from a dedicated texture — never the shared page

5.10 — Rendering Efficiently

A scene this size is cheap by design — but the disciplines that keep it cheap deserve names: batch, cull, and touch state rarely.

  • Group by page: terrain and props share canyon.png — one batch covers most of the frame
  • Cull early: the tile window from 5.3; props by x range against the camera
  • Set the transform twice per frame, never per sprite — scale changes flush batches too
  • Per-sprite mods are state changes: pre-baked region variants (dim lives icons) beat runtime modulation
  • Cached text, introduced in 5.13 — re-rendering TTF every frame is the classic 2D stall
  • Measure first: the F1 overlay from Chapter 3 shows the frame budget before opinions do
Performance Tip — The budget and the batch

At 60 Hz the frame budget is 16.6 ms; this scene spends well under a millisecond drawing on desktop. The two realistic killers are texture churn — a page switch between every sprite — and per-frame text rasterization. Both are already designed out.

5.11 — Game UI Overlay Design

The HUD is a different world: score, lives, messages, and debug stats — all in fixed screen space, all reading controller state they never own.

  • Elements: lives top-left, score top-right, transient messages center, fps as a debug overlay
  • Screen space: the fixed 960×540 logical viewport — never the camera, never window pixels
  • World space is everything simulated; UI drawn mid-camera-pan is the classic drift bug
  • Anchoring: corners for persistent identity, center for events, a 12 px margin everywhere
  • The HUD reads lives, score, and message state — controller-owned, updated by ticks
  • Chapter 7 grows this into widgets, screens, and menus — today it is four cached textures

5.12 — The HUD Skeleton

Anchored drawing in logical 960×540 space, no camera transform anywhere — the HUD trusts the pass above it to have reset the world.

key points
  • Logical coordinates only: anchors are constants against 960×540, no window math anywhere
  • The camera reset already happened in renderWorld — the HUD trusts the pass above it
  • Dimmed lives are a pre-baked region — ui_carrot_dim — not an alpha mod on the page
  • Message timing is controller state; the HUD only draws what the snapshot says

5.13 — Score Tracking with Cached Text

Scores change in events, not in draw code. Render text only when the string changes — then drawing it is one texture blit.

key points
  • The controller adds CARROT_VALUE on pickup events; the HUD notices the change and re-renders
  • The dirty flag is the whole cache: TTF_RenderText_Blended runs only when the string changes
  • A surface becomes a texture, the surface dies immediately — the texture owns its pixels
  • Anchored top-right: width from SDL_GetTextureSize, margin from the same 12 px constant
Performance Tip — Text is the classic stall

TTF_RenderText_Blended rasterizes and blends every glyph on every call — per frame that is milliseconds plus a texture allocation. Cache the result and change it only when the number does: one carrot pickup re-renders text once, not once per frame.

5.14 — Health and Lives Counters

Lives are canon — three of them — and the HUD row doubles as the game's health language: capacity, loss, and the jolt when it happens.

  • The row: MAX_LIVES carrot icons top-left; spent slots draw as dimmed regions, not absences
  • Dimmed icons keep the row readable as capacity — players count what is left at a glance
  • Big action numbers use atlas digits: digit_0 through digit_9 regions — no font in the hot path
  • TTF text waits for menus and settings screens — Chapter 7 territory
  • Decrement feedback: a one-frame shake and flash on the row — a Chapter 12 tween, hand-rolled today
  • Games with health bars reuse the pattern: a row of segments is just a bar you can count

5.15 — The Framerate Monitor

Chapter 3 promised an F1 stats overlay; the frame-time graph makes it honest. Averages lie — distributions tell the truth.

  • The counter: frames per second, smoothed over a 30-frame window
  • The graph: a ring buffer of the last 120 frame times, one bar per frame — spikes read instantly
  • The 99th percentile beats the average: one 100 ms stall per second leaves the mean near 60 and the feel in pieces
  • Show average, worst, and p99 together — the gap between them names the stutter source
  • The overlay must be cheap itself: cached text, pre-built bars, zero allocation per frame
  • The spikes you hunt: shader compiles, asset swaps, OS scheduling, debug draws left on
Deep Dive — Why p99, not the mean

Frame-time hitches are outliers, and the mean is outlier-blind: nine perfect frames and one disaster average into fine. The 99th percentile answers the player's actual question — how bad is it at its worst? Feel tracks the tail of the distribution, never its center.

5.16 — The FPS Counter

A fixed 30-slot ring, a sum, a cached string. The number moves twice a second; the texture re-renders only when it does.

key points
  • A fixed 30-slot ring: sum, divide, done — no allocation, no drift, no math library
  • The text re-renders only when the number changes — twice a second here, not sixty times
  • Same cached-texture pattern as the score: one TTF call per change, zero per frame
  • Frame times come from SDL_GetTicksNS deltas measured around the whole loop — the frame's true cost

5.17 — Layout Scaling and Anchoring

Anchors are promises about where things sit when the window changes shape. In logical space, those promises survive every display on earth.

  • The HUD anchors to the 960×540 logical edges with a 12 px margin — never to physical pixels
  • SDL_SetRenderLogicalPresentation letterboxes: draws in logical space cannot leak into the bars
  • Integer window scales land pixel-perfect; fractional scales letterbox — the presentation picks, not us
  • Anchor by meaning: identity at corners, events at center, transient state near the bottom
  • Mobile cutouts shrink usable area — query the safe area inset and grow margins on notched devices
  • Touch targets obey the same margin: buttons clear rounded corners and camera holes
Common Pitfall — Corners the hardware eats

HUD elements pinned to the raw top-left vanish under a phone notch or a laptop camera hole. The safe area is a platform question with a platform answer — inset the anchor margins there, and the same layout works on desk and device.

5.18 — Reacting to Resize

SDL_EVENT_WINDOW_RESIZED arrives with new pixel dimensions. The satisfying answer for the whole game: recompute nothing.

  • The window has been resizable since Chapter 3 — players will drag it
  • Logical presentation re-derives scale and letterbox every frame — the 960×540 design space never hears about it
  • Pointer events arrive mapped into logical coordinates — no manual division by window size
  • Fullscreen toggles ride the same event path — one handler, every size change
  • The exception proves the rule: pixel-sized render targets (Chapter 9 wipes) re-allocate — that is their chapter
  • Game code that divides by window pixels is code that breaks on the first resize
Best Practice — Design in logical coordinates only

One rule keeps resize a non-event: every position in the game lives in 960×540 space, and SDL maps it onto whatever glass is attached. The moment code peeks at physical size, resize becomes a feature — and features need tests.

5.19 — The Assembled Scene

Chapter 5's scoreboard: one scene, assembled from data, drawn in six ordered passes.

960×540
logical presentation
letterboxed onto any display

Chapter 3's contract, now populated

Tiles, props, and pickups all draw from one atlas page in one batch — the sprite count above is what gameplay adds on top of the grid.

5.20 — Visual Hierarchy: One Frame, Top to Bottom

Walk one frame the way the player's eye meets it — HUD first, motion second, depth last. Then read the same walk backwards as draw order.

  • Top layer, first glance: the HUD — highest contrast, never moving, always readable
  • Then motion: water bands breathing, clouds drifting, the player's own animation (soon)
  • Then depth: mesas crawling at 0.15× behind the ridge at 0.4× — parallax sells the space
  • The terrain grid sets rhythm and pace; the letterbox bars frame it like film
  • Props and hazards tint under or stand over the water — order communicates danger
  • The walkthrough and the render contract are one artifact read in two directions
Common Pitfall — Translucency order artifacts

A cactus drawn before the water reads submerged; drawn after, in front. Both look plausible — flipping between them mid-level looks broken. The contract settles it forever (water pass two, props pass three); hand-sorting translucent draws per frame is how the artifacts sneak back in.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 5 Recap

  • The level is pure data: static terrain, backgrounds, water, props — actors arrive in Chapter 6
  • Tile rendering draws the visible window: 558 candidate cells, not the 2040-tile grid
  • The render order contract: backgrounds and terrain → water → props → actors → particles → HUD
  • WorldRenderer::renderWorld sets the camera scale, draws the world passes, resets for the HUD
  • HUD text is cached: re-render only when the string changes — TTF per frame is a stall
  • Logical 960×540 absorbs resize: game code never divides by window pixels
Chapter 6 — Adding the Actors: collision, pickups, and the player
Ch 6Chapter 6

Adding the Actors

01The Actor base class and the cast of Canyon Dash
02AABB collision: gameplay boxes, helpers, push-out resolution
03Spatial hashing so hundreds of actors stay cheap
04The player controller: coyote time, jump buffering, friction
05Collectibles, power-ups, hazards, and the EventBus
06Health, death sequencing, and the game-over overlay

6.1 — The Cast of Canyon Dash

Chapter 5 built the stage — tiles, parallax, a scrolling camera. Now we cast the show: four actor families sharing one small base class.

Friendly
PlayerActor
coyote jump · hearts
Golden carrot
sine bob · +10 score
Feather
power-up · double jump
Hostile

Crumbling ledge

Underneath
Actor base
pos · vel · bounds · alive

PICKUP · DAMAGE · POWERUP · GAME_OVER

One base class, four families — differences live in update() overrides, never in type switches.

details
  • Actor is the single base: position, velocity, bounds, and an alive flag — nothing more
  • Player: the only actor that reads input; everything else is scenery or danger
  • Collectibles reward exploration: golden carrots bob and pull toward a nearby player
  • Power-ups rewrite one rule for a while: the feather unlocks a double jump for 10 s
  • Hazards punish contact: spiked cacti hurt, crumbling ledges shake, drop, and respawn

6.2 — The Actor Base Class

Every moving thing in the canyon inherits one small contract: where it is, how fast it moves, the box it occupies, and whether it still exists.

key points
  • Subclasses override update; the world ticks them all with the same fixed dt
  • bounds is offset from pos — carrot art can overhang the box freely
  • alive = false means retire: the world sweeps dead actors after the tick
  • worldBox() is the single pos-plus-bounds funnel — one place to breakpoint
Best Practice — Kill flags, not deletes

Never erase actors from the live vector during iteration. Mark alive = false and sweep once after the tick: iterators stay valid, order stays stable, and a carrot eaten mid-loop cannot corrupt the loop that ate it.

6.3 — Gameplay Boxes vs Sprite Art

Chapter 3 drew AABBs over tiles; actors get the same treatment with one extra rule players feel but never see — hitboxes are not the same size as art.

  • AABB = axis-aligned box, x/y/w/h — the cheapest collision test that still feels fair
  • The gameplay box is 8-12 px inset from the sprite: generous on pickups, strict on hazards
  • Pixel-perfect collision reads as unfair: one transparent pixel ends a perfect run
  • Bias every ambiguous case toward the player: carrot boxes grow, spike boxes shrink
  • F3 (Ch 3) draws actor boxes live — tune them with the game running, not in an image editor
  • Rotation breaks AABBs, so spinning carrots are art only (6.10) — the box stays axis-aligned
Common Pitfall — Art-sized hitboxes

A spiky cactus sprite that is 32 px wide with a 32 px box kills players who visibly cleared it. Inset hazard boxes 15-20% and grow pickup boxes by the same margin. Players forgive generous carrots; they never forgive generous spikes.

6.4 — AABB Helpers: Test and Push-Out

Two free functions carry the whole chapter: an overlap test, and a minimum-translation push-out that separates two boxes along the shallowest axis.

key points
  • intersects is four comparisons — every compiler turns it into branchless compares
  • The MTV picks the shallowest overlap axis: the direction the boxes barely touch
  • Push-out changes position only; what happens to velocity is the caller's policy
  • Ties resolve upward, so corner clips favor landing over wall bumps
Deep Dive — Why the shallowest axis

Resolving along the deepest axis teleports actors sideways through floors when they clip a corner. The shallowest axis matches player intuition: mostly-horizontal overlap means you brushed a wall; mostly-vertical means you hit a floor. Box2D makes the same choice when it picks contact normals.

6.5 — Spatial Partitioning

Two hundred actors tested against each other is about 20,000 pair tests per tick — 1.2 million per second. The tile grid we already have fixes the scaling.

brute force
200 actors
200 x 199 / 2 pairs
20,000 tests
per tick — 1.2 M/s
grid buckets
insert(actor)
tile coords -> bucket
query(rect)
visit 4-9 buckets
~12 candidates
per actor, typical

Same answers, three orders of magnitude fewer tests — the grid pays for itself at roughly 30 actors.

details
  • Naive collision is O(N x M): every actor against every other, every tick
  • A uniform grid buckets actors by tile coordinates — the level is already a 32 px lattice
  • Queries return the handful of actors in nearby buckets — neighbors at constant cost
  • Bucket size = TILE: platformer motion is local, so one-cell lookahead covers a full tick
  • Rebuild each tick: clearing and re-inserting 300 actors beats caching stale positions
Performance Tip — The 30-actor threshold

Below roughly 30 moving actors the grid costs more than it saves — insertion overhead dominates the tests it eliminates. Canyon Dash keeps it anyway: the interface is tiny, and a level with triple the actors changes zero lines of gameplay code.

6.6 — The Spatial Hash Grid

One hash map from packed tile coordinates to small vectors of actors: insert each tick, query with a rect, and collision work stops scaling with actor count.

key points
  • Keys pack (tileX, tileY) into one Uint64 — one hash lookup, no string keys
  • A big actor spans buckets and lands in all of them — insert covers the covered tiles
  • The stamp dedups: an actor stored in four buckets is returned once per query
  • Terra firma never enters the grid — solid tiles answer from the Level itself (6.14)
Performance Tip — Reserve before play

An unordered_map rehashes as it grows, and a rehash mid-tick is a stutter. Call m_buckets.reserve(1024) once at level load: a 120-tile-wide level touches well under a thousand buckets, so the table never resizes during play.

6.7 — Spawning Actors from Level JSON

The dynamic layer stops being an inert list: WorldController walks the spawn entries LevelLoader parsed in Ch 4, once at level start, and gives every one a body.

key points
  • The JSON stays data: adding ten carrots is a level-file edit, not a recompile
  • Unknown types log and skip — a typo in level 4 must not crash level 1
  • Dangerous props graduate here too: Ch 5 spike traps enter the world as Hazard actors
  • The player start is just another entry — respawn reuses the same point
Best Practice — Validate levels at load, fail loud

Every field the loader reads is a field a designer can typo. Chapter 4 already guards the parse; this loop guards the interpretation. A missing carrot should be a visible line in the log — not a crash the night before a playtest.

6.8 — The Player Controller by Design

The controller is three stages in strict order: input becomes intent, intent becomes velocity, velocity becomes position. Jump feel lives in two timers.

  • Input → intent → integration: sampled keys become acceleration, never instant velocity
  • Gravity is constant downward; a jump is a one-frame impulse that sets vel.y outright
  • Running accelerates toward PLAYER_RUN (220 px/s); friction carries the stop
  • Coyote time (~0.09 s): jumps pressed just after leaving a ledge still count
  • Jump buffering (~0.12 s): a press just before landing fires the instant feet touch
  • Both windows are named constants with units — not magic numbers buried in branches
Deep Dive — Why coyote time works

Players decide to jump when their eyes see the ledge — tens of milliseconds before the physics agrees the ground is gone. Coyote time forgives exactly that perceptual gap. Top platformers grant 6-10 frames of grace; we grant about 5 ticks (0.09 s): enough to feel honest, too short to double-jump for free.

6.9 — PlayerController::update

The whole feel of Canyon Dash in one function: coyote and buffer timers, ground versus air acceleration, and a grounded flag owned by the collision pass — never guessed.

key points
  • The feather power-up is one field: m_airJumps goes 0 → 1 for ten seconds, jump code unchanged
  • Air control weaker than ground control — full-strength air steering feels floaty
  • Terminal velocity (MAX_FALL) bounds the fall — unbounded falls tunnel through floors
  • The controller clears grounded; the terrain pass is the only code that sets it
  • Every number here lives in constants.h with its unit in the comment
Common Pitfall — Guessing grounded

Deriving grounded from "velocity is zero" or "a foot below looks solid" breaks on moving platforms and one-frame bounces. Let the vertical push-out decide: if the MTV pushed you up, you are standing. One flag, set where the physics actually happened.

6.10 — Collectibles That Feel Good

A carrot that sits still is a texture. A carrot that bobs, leans into its spin, and slides toward the player when close is a reward.

  • Idle motion: a sine bob of ±4 px around the spawn anchor — cheap, readable, alive
  • The sprite spins via SDL_RenderTextureRotated — art rotates, the AABB never does
  • Magnet pull inside ~96 px: the carrot drifts toward the player, easing in as it nears
  • Pickup uses a grown AABB overlap, not a distance check — same helpers as everything else
  • On pickup: alive = false, publish PICKUP, +10 score, sparkle burst (Ch 8 does the burst)
  • Respawning collectibles keep their spawn anchor and flip alive back after a delay
Best Practice — Juice the pickup moment

The pickup frame matters more than the item: pop the score into the HUD, freeze the carrot one tick, and cue the chime instantly (Ch 10). Players forgive a plain sprite when the feedback is rich — they never forgive a gorgeous sprite with dead feedback.

6.11 — Collectible::update

Forty lines of sine, magnet, and overlap: the carrot animates itself, chases a nearby player, and announces its own pickup through the event bus.

key points
  • The bob writes position, never velocity — a kinematic actor that gravity ignores
  • Magnet strength grows as distance shrinks — attraction that eases in, not snaps
  • Pickup grows the box by 6 px per side: the generosity rule from 6.3, in code
  • One publish, zero includes — the carrot never knows the HUD exists
Performance Tip — Do not fear the per-carrot math

A sinf and a sqrtf per carrot per tick is 300 calls each at 60 Hz — microseconds on any CPU this game targets. The expensive version is the one that queries the spatial grid per carrot for a player it already knows. Profile before optimizing arithmetic that was never slow.

6.12 — Power-Ups and Hazards

Power-ups rewrite one rule for a while; hazards enforce the rules with pain. Both must be legible at a glance — the screen is 960×540 and the player is moving.

  • The feather grants double jump for 10 s: m_airJumps = 1, a HUD timer, a tint on the player
  • Hazards deal one heart plus knockback — small, sharp, survivable
  • Spiked cacti are static AABBs; crumbling ledges shake 0.4 s, drop, then respawn after 3 s
  • Telegraph everything: shaking ledges, blinking timers, wind-up poses — no instant kills
  • Damage stays generous where pickups are strict: hazard boxes are inset, never grown
  • Power-up expiry warns twice: at 3 s the icon blinks, at 0 the tint fades out
Best Practice — One rule per power-up

A feather that grants double jump AND speed AND invincibility cannot be tuned or taught. One rule, one timer, one visual tell. Players understand it in a heartbeat, and stacking different feathers later stays a design choice instead of combinatorial chaos.

6.13 — Collision Response: Resolve, Then React

Separation and consequence are two different systems. The sweep pushes boxes apart; reactions — damage, pickups, crumbles — ride on top as trigger checks and events.

  • Resolve = geometry: push-out until boxes stop overlapping. React = gameplay: what the overlap meant
  • Sweep the Y axis first, then X: vertical resolution decides grounded — the stable platformer order
  • Landing means the MTV pushed up while falling → grounded, coyote refreshed, fall checked
  • Head bonk means the MTV pushed down while rising → zero the vertical velocity, keep the horizontal
  • React only after both axes are clean — reacting mid-sweep sees half-resolved positions
  • One-way platforms: skip the upward push when the player was below the top last tick — the lone exception
Common Pitfall — Resolving X first

X-first sweeps make ledges feel sticky: a player brushing a wall while falling gets pushed sideways out from under their own landing. Y first, then X — floor contact settles before walls matter. Every classic platformer sweeps in exactly this order.

6.14 — The Two-Pass Terrain Sweep

The pass that replaces Chapter 3's resolvePlayer: move and resolve each axis separately against candidate tiles straight from the level grid — the MTV does the talking.

key points
  • Candidates come from floor/ceil of box coords over TILE — a ~3x4 tile window, never the level
  • Landing requires push.y < 0 and falling — standing beside a block is not landing
  • Only a vertical MTV sets grounded and refreshes coyote; wall pushes never do
  • Pass 2 re-reads worldBox() — resolving X against the pre-Y position double-corrects
  • A pure horizontal push zeroes vel.x; the player slides along walls instead of sticking
Performance Tip — Terrain never needs the actor grid

The tile grid IS the partition for terrain: the player touches at most a dozen candidate tiles per pass, so two dozen AABB tests per tick. The spatial hash from 6.6 exists for actor-actor pairs — pickups, hazards, hazards versus critters. Two partitions, two jobs.

6.15 — Trigger Zones and the Event Bus

Not every overlap should push. Sensors — pickups, hazard contacts, level exits — overlap on purpose, and their consequences belong to whoever cares, not to the collision code.

  • A trigger zone is an AABB that never resolves: overlap is a signal, not a collision
  • Collision code answers "do these touch" — it must not know about score, sound, or saves
  • The EventBus decouples: publishers say what happened, subscribers decide what it means
  • Four events carry the whole game: PICKUP, DAMAGE, POWERUP, GAME_OVER
  • Subscribers: the HUD (pops and flash), the controller (hearts), audio hooks (Ch 10)
  • A fixed event list, no strings — a typo in an event name is a compile error, not a silent miss
Best Practice — Publish facts, not commands

Publish what happened — "a carrot was collected at x,y" — not what to do about it ("add 10 and play ding"). Facts survive design changes: the same PICKUP event later feeds achievements, counters, and audio without touching gameplay code again.

6.16 — The EventBus

Thirty lines, zero dependencies: a fixed enum of events, a handler list per event, publish loops the list. Everything gameplay "communicates" flows through here.

key points
  • The enum is the entire API — adding an event is one line plus its handlers
  • Handlers fire in subscription order; subscribe during init, before the first tick
  • Publish is synchronous: by return, every subscriber has run — no queues to drain
  • A handler that publishes back can recurse; defer to a queue if that day ever comes
Common Pitfall — The bus as a dump truck

The moment the bus carries "set player position to X", it has become a function call with extra steps and no type safety. Events are facts about the past. If a caller needs an answer back, it should not be an event — call the code directly.

6.17 — Health, Hearts, and Lives

Damage flows through one event into one owner: the WorldController decrements hearts, arms 1.2 s of invincibility, and only decides about lives when hearts hit zero.

  • Three hearts per life, three lives per run (Ch 3 canon) — hearts refill on respawn, lives do not
  • The DAMAGE handler: hearts--, knockback impulse, invincible = 1.2 s
  • Invincibility means ignore DAMAGE events, not skip drawing — the world keeps moving
  • Hearts at zero: lives--, respawn at the level start with hearts back to three
  • Lives at zero: publish GAME_OVER — nothing else in the simulation may decide that
  • The Hud subscribes for feedback — pops and flashes — while its Ch 5 dirty-flag digits stay pull-based
Deep Dive — Why 1.2 seconds

Invincibility must outlast the worst reasonable overlap: a knocked-back player skimming two cacti needs about 0.8 s to clear them. 1.2 s adds margin without letting players tank hazards on purpose. Tune it by playing, not by math — the 8 Hz flash cadence is what makes the state legible.

6.18 — Locking the Camera on Death

Death is a directed moment, not a state flag: the camera stops chasing, the world dims, a short sequence plays out, and only then does an overlay ask for a button.

  • On GAME_OVER: camera follow stops being called — the Ch 3 clamp still holds the frame
  • The player pops upward in the classic death arc, ignores terrain, spins via SDL_RenderTextureRotated
  • The world dims behind the action: one translucent black fill over everything but the HUD
  • A 1.6 s timeline: 0.2 s freeze, 0.9 s arc, 0.5 s fade into the overlay — timers, not state spaghetti
  • Input is gated off until the overlay owns it — no buffered jump leaks into the restart
  • The timeline lives in the controller but reads no input: the world froze when the event fired
Best Practice — Death is choreography

Resist the hard cut to a game-over screen. The 1.6 s between death and overlay is where players process what happened; cut it and every death feels like a bug instead of a consequence. Nintendo has shipped this beat in every platformer since the 1980s for exactly this reason.

6.19 — The Game-Over Overlay

A full-screen translucent fill, two centered text draws, and one gated input check — the simplest screen in the game, and the one players see most.

key points
  • Alpha 160 is about 63% black — dark enough to focus, light enough to read the world behind it
  • Centering is computed once in show() with SDL_GetTextureSize — not per frame
  • The blink makes the call to action visible without shouting — 1 Hz, 60% duty
  • m_finished is the gate: the timeline must end before input exists again
Common Pitfall — Draw order is the design

The dim rect must draw after the world and before the overlay text, or it either does nothing or eats the HUD it was supposed to preserve. Fix the order once — world, dim, text — in the layer list, and the overlay stops being a per-frame decision.

6.20 — Status the Player Can Read

Hearts, invincibility flash, score pops: the Hud from Ch 5 gains subscriptions — it renders what happened and touches no simulation state.

  • Hearts row: three small quads top-left in logical space — empty hearts draw dark, not missing
  • Invincibility flash: SDL_SetTextureAlphaMod(playerTex, alpha) at ~8 Hz — reset to 255 first
  • Score pops: "+10" rises 24 px and fades over 0.5 s — a tiny tween, formalized in Ch 12
  • Digits keep the Ch 5 dirty-flag cache; only transient feedback rides on events
  • The feather timer is a shrinking bar under the hearts — one rect, clipped by time
  • The HUD publishes nothing, ever — events flow one way into presentation
Common Pitfall — UI state leaks into simulation

The moment the controller asks "is the score popup done?" to gate a respawn, determinism dies: the simulation now depends on draw timing. Rule: events flow one way into the HUD. If the game must wait for feedback, the controller owns that timer and the HUD merely displays it.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 6 Recap

  • One Actor base: pos, vel, bounds, alive — differences live in update overrides, never type switches
  • AABB helpers: intersects plus minimum-translation push-out; gameplay boxes inset from art
  • Spatial hash grid on the 32 px tile lattice — neighbor queries stop scaling with actor count
  • Player feel: coyote time 0.09 s, jump buffer 0.12 s, Y-first sweep sets grounded from the MTV
  • EventBus with four events — collision code publishes facts, subsystems decide meaning
  • Hearts → lives → death timeline → gated overlay; the HUD subscribes and never reaches back
Chapter 7 — Menus and Options

Menus and Options

06Menu input: focus navigation, hold-to-repeat, touch passthrough

7.1 — Game State as Screens

A game is a stack of modes with different update, render, and input needs. The Screen abstraction turns "which mode am I in" from a forest of bools into a type.

flow
Boot
load + settings
Menu
title screen
Game
play
Pause
stacked over game
Game Over
stacked over game
a Screen owns
update(dt)
its own simulation
render(r)
its own layers
input
top of stack only
the manager
ScreenManager
push · pop · set
transitions
Ch 9 fades & wraps these calls

Only the top screen consumes input. Everything below stays alive, paused, and renderable.

details
  • States without architecture: inMenu && !paused && !gameOver — bool soup that only grows
  • A Screen is one mode: title, gameplay, pause, settings — each with its own loop body
  • The stack gives pause for free: gameplay stays alive underneath, paused and dimmed
  • Only the top screen consumes input — the pause menu never fights the player controller
  • set() replaces (menu → game); push()/pop() overlay (game → pause → game)
  • Transitions between screens arrive in Chapter 9; their hooks land in this chapter
Best Practice — Model modes, not flags

Every mode boolean you add doubles the states nobody tests. A Screen type makes impossible states unrepresentable: there is no code path where the pause menu and the title screen both read the keyboard, because only one of them is on top.

7.2 — The Screen Contract

Six virtuals define a screen's life: enter, leave, background, foreground, tick, draw. The manager calls them in a fixed order — screens never call each other.

key points
  • show() receives the manager — wiring a transition is one sm.set(...) call, no globals
  • pause() fires on the screen being covered; resume() when it surfaces again
  • update and render are pure virtual — a screen that does nothing is still a screen
  • hide() releases heavyweight assets, show() re-acquires them — always paired

7.3 — ScreenManager: A Stack of Modes

Fifty lines that end mode-bools forever: push, pop, set, and per-frame delegation — with the top screen alone receiving events.

key points
  • set = clear + push: boot → menu → game; pause is push + pop
  • pause() before a push, resume() after a pop — the covered screen freezes itself
  • Only top() updates and gets events — modality by construction, not by if-chains
  • render walks from the topmost opaque screen: gameplay is opaque, pause is not
  • Chapter 9 transitions wrap exactly these calls; nothing else in the engine changes
Best Practice — Screens own their transitions

A screen decides what comes next — sm.set(makeGameOverScreen(...)) — instead of a central switch interpreting an enum. The manager stays fifty lines forever, and the flow graph lives in the same file as the buttons that trigger it.

7.4 — Layout Engines: The Scene Graph Idea

Full UI toolkits are trees of widgets with local rectangles and inherited transforms. We borrow the idea, keep a flat cut of it, and stay under two hundred lines.

  • A scene graph: every widget has a local rect; screen rect = parent rect + local offset, recursively
  • Container widgets (rows, anchors) size and place children — layout is data, not hand-placed pixels
  • libGDX-style tables solve constraints (fill, expand, colspan) — a mini linear solver
  • Our cut: Anchor pins one child to a screen point, Row lays children out — no solver
  • Everything sizes in logical pixels on the 960×540 canvas — never native pixels
  • Why not a full engine? The menus are six screens; a solver would be the biggest file in src/sable
Deep Dive — What the transform walk buys you

The recursive parent-plus-offset walk is what makes nesting work: a slider inside a row inside a window computes its screen rect in three additions. The same walk in reverse turns a mouse click into "which widget" — hit testing and layout are one algorithm run in opposite directions.

7.5 — Widgets, Anchors, and Rows

Three types carry every menu in Canyon Dash: a base Widget, an Anchor that pins one child to one of nine screen points, and a Row that lays children out left to right.

  • Widget: rect, enabled, focused, a virtual draw — the atom every control shares
  • Anchor: nine points (corners, edge midpoints, center) on 960×540, plus margin
  • Logo anchors top-center at 96 px; version text anchors bottom-left with the build number
  • Row: children in a horizontal strip with a gap, vertically centered — the button stack
  • Nest freely: a Row of Anchors is legal — layout is just function composition
  • A 240 px button is a quarter of screen width on every display, because units are logical

7.6 — Widget Base and Hit Testing

The base class plus the transform walk: contains() in local space, resolve() against the parent — hit testing and layout as one algorithm.

key points
  • rect is local: the same button renders correctly in the title stack and the pause window
  • The parent rect flows down at draw and hit-test time — no stored pointers, no cycles
  • contains answers in local space after resolve — four comparisons
  • focused is visual state for draw; navigation sets it, widgets never steal it
Performance Tip — Linear hit tests are fine here

Sixty widgets hit-tested linearly per pointer move is nothing — never build a spatial index for UI. The real win is skipping draws outside the clip rect, and that only matters once a screen exceeds a few hundred widgets.

7.7 — Skin and Theme: Style as Data

A skin is a table of named styles — fonts, colors, frame regions — loaded from data. Widgets look themselves up in it; swapping one file reskins every screen.

  • A style = font id, text color, frame colors for normal/hover/pressed, padding
  • The skin loads from assets/ui/skin.json at boot — cJSON, the same reader as levels
  • Button frames draw as three strips: left cap, stretchable middle, right cap — one atlas region each
  • Widgets reference styles by name: skin.button("primary"), skin.label("footer")
  • Swapping skin.json for skin-neon.json reskins the entire game — zero code changes
  • Colors stay data as SDL_Color; SDL_SetRenderDrawColor per draw, never baked into widgets
Best Practice — Separate structure from skin

The moment a widget hardcodes RGB values, theme support is gone. Structure — anchors, rows, focus order — lives in code; appearance lives in one data file. Canyon Dash ships two themes this way, and a high-contrast accessibility theme is a third JSON, not a fork.

7.8 — Anatomy of the Main Menu

Five layers, back to front: animated background, decorative particles, logo, button stack, footer. Each is one widget subtree — the screen is their composition.

back
Parallax mesas
slow drift, Ch 5 stack
Particle field
dust — Ch 8 emitter
brand
Logo + subtitle
anchor top-center, 96 px
Version text
anchor bottom-left + build
interact
Button row
start · settings · quit
Focus ring
keyboard + gamepad visible

Every layer is a widget; the screen itself only owns composition and wiring.

details
  • Background: the Chapter 5 parallax stack drifting at a few px/s — alive, not a screenshot
  • Decorative dust: the Chapter 8 emitter with a menu-friendly spawn rate
  • The button row is one widget — focus moves inside it; the screen never sees keys
  • Pressing Start is sm.set(makeGameScreen(...)) — the entire navigation, one call

7.9 — Building the Menu Scene Graph

The whole title screen assembled in show(): anchors for the chrome, a row of three buttons, each wiring one ScreenManager call. Zero hardcoded pixels.

key points
  • Buttons receive callbacks, not commands — the menu never learns what a game screen is
  • Capturing the manager is safe: it outlives every screen in the stack
  • Quit goes through sm.requestQuit() — GameApp polls it each frame
  • All positions are anchor constants; no button knows a screen coordinate
Common Pitfall — The dangling callback

A button that captures its owning screen by reference is a use-after-free the moment that screen pops. Screens are transient and heap-owned; the manager is not. Capture the manager — the one object guaranteed to outlive every menu — and the bug cannot exist.

7.10 — The Button Widget

Three visual states, three input paths, one 44 px minimum height — the widget that teaches all the others: focus, hover, press, activate.

key points
  • 44 px on a 540 px logical screen is ~8% of height — a comfortable thumb target on phones
  • Hover (pointer) and focus (keyboard/gamepad) are separate states with the same visual
  • Click fires on release inside the widget — release-outside cancels; nobody mis-taps
  • The focus ring draws whenever focused, even when a pointer is also present
  • Disabled buttons still hit-test: they explain themselves instead of vanishing
Best Practice — The 44 px floor is not optional

Touch ergonomics research converged on roughly 9 mm physical targets; at phone DPI that lands near 44 px in our logical space. Smaller buttons work with a mouse and fail with thumbs. Ship one size that works for both — and pad the hit box, not the art, when visuals must be smaller.

7.11 — The Settings Window

Three sliders, one checkbox, one reset button, in a modal window over a dimmed menu — and every change applies live, because "restart to apply" is an admission of defeat.

  • Audio: master / SFX / music sliders, 0..1 each — Chapter 10 maps them onto stream gains
  • Display: fullscreen checkbox, applied live; Chapter 2 covered the platform quirks
  • Reset: one button restoring defaults — undo is the cheapest trust builder in a settings UI
  • Modal: pushes over the menu, dim layer behind, input routed by the stack — top only
  • Every control writes settings and applies them in the same handler — nothing deferred
  • Back pops the window and saves — debounced writes make even that cheap
Common Pitfall — "Restart to apply"

A setting that needs a reboot tells players your engine cannot reconfigure itself. Volume and fullscreen are changeable live in SDL3 — route them through one apply() that reads current values, and the restart dialog never ships.

7.12 — Slider and Checkbox Widgets

A slider is a value 0..1, a drag state, and two rects; a checkbox is a button with a state. Focus-safe means a drag ends the moment focus moves.

key points
  • One writer rule: setValue clamps, stores, notifies — no other line touches m_value
  • The drag ends on pointer-up or focus loss — the classic slider bug, prevented twice
  • Sliders keep the 44 px floor: the track is tall even when the art looks thin
  • A checkbox reuses button activation — one input path for every activatable widget
  • Both fire callbacks on change — settings apply live because widgets cannot stay quiet

7.13 — Persistence: Where Settings Live

Read-only assets come from SDL_GetBasePath; everything writable goes under SDL_GetPrefPath — the one directory every platform promises you can write.

  • SDL_GetPrefPath("sable", "canyon-dash") creates and returns the per-user writable dir
  • Load at boot, before the first screen: the menu needs master volume before it renders
  • Save on change, debounced ~500 ms — slider drags fire dozens of callbacks per gesture
  • Also save on exit and on SDL_EVENT_APP_WILLENTERBACKGROUND — mobile kills without warning
  • Write the whole file in one SDL_WriteIO pass — a half-written JSON fails to parse, defaults win
  • Settings and saves are separate files with separate schemas — options versus progress
Deep Dive — Why not the base path

SDL_GetBasePath is the install directory on desktop — read-only inside macOS bundles, Android APKs, and iOS containers. The pref path is per-user, per-platform, created on demand: a Library folder on macOS, AppData on Windows, app storage on Android. One call, every platform, done.

7.14 — Settings Serialization with cJSON

Chapter 2 sketched load-or-defaults with three keys; the settings window completes it — master bus added, cJSON building the write side, debounce on the save side.

key points
  • Same keys Ch 2 shipped — musicVolume, sfxVolume, fullscreen — plus the new masterVolume
  • Old files load clean: an unknown new key defaults, a missing old key defaults — the file self-heals
  • Volumes serialize as plain 0..1 numbers — the file stays human-editable, and players will edit it
  • SDL_free on both the file buffer and the printed JSON — cJSON allocates, you release
Common Pitfall — Trusting the file

A settings file is player input: someone will hand-edit master to 4.0 or delete half the braces. Clamp every value on load — volume back into 0..1 — parse defensively, and log what you ignored. Corrupt settings should mean one weird afternoon, not a support ticket.

7.15 — Save States: Progress, Not Preferences

Settings say how the game behaves; saves say how far the player got. Separate files, separate schemas, and a version field from day one.

  • saves.json: unlocked levels, high scores, total carrots — everything the player earned
  • Versioned: "saveVersion": 2 — the loader migrates 1 → 2 instead of wiping progress
  • High scores: a top ten per level — insert, sort, trim; the leaderboard is six lines
  • Unlock flags are booleans keyed by level id — no bit packing, JSON is cheap
  • Write on level complete, not every frame — progress changes are rare and important
  • Same pref path, different file: deleting settings must never cost a save
Deep Dive — Why version now

The first format you ship is wrong: you will add a stat, rename a field, split a category. A version integer plus a migration switch — case 1: copy across, case 2: read directly — turns a breaking change into a ten-line function. Without it, every format change ships as lost progress.

7.16 — SaveData: Scores and Unlocks

Insert, sort, trim, persist — the whole leaderboard. Everything the player earned, in one small type with one honest write path.

key points
  • Insert → sort → resize: the entire leaderboard algorithm, six lines
  • m_dirty + flush means no disk writes mid-level — only at safe moments
  • The version number travels inside the file: the loader branches on it first
  • A shared writePrefFile keeps the write path identical for settings and saves
Best Practice — Write at safe moments

Flush on level complete, on exit, and on app-background events — never inside the gameplay tick. A write stalls the frame on slow storage, and players experience it as a hitch during the exact moment they earned the score.

7.17 — The Pause Menu

Push, don't switch: PauseScreen goes on top of GameScreen, gameplay freezes itself in pause(), a dim layer keeps it visible — and pop() resumes exactly where the world stopped.

  • sm.push(makePauseScreen()) — GameScreen gets pause(), stops simulating, keeps state
  • The pause screen is not opaque (7.3): the manager renders the frozen world beneath it
  • Dim layer: one 60% black fill — the same translucent rect as the Ch 6 game-over overlay
  • Input flows to the top only: the player controller never sees the Escape that opened the menu
  • Resume = pop(); Quit to menu = set(...) — the stack unwinds or replaces, cleanly
  • The pause screen still ticks its own UI animations at menu speed while the world waits
Common Pitfall — Pausing by freezing the loop

Skipping update but still rendering feels right until audio keeps playing and the event queue backs up. Pause belongs to the screen contract: the covered screen simply stops simulating in pause(), while the app loop, events, and the pause screen itself keep ticking.

7.18 — The Navigation Graph

Every arrow in the flow is one ScreenManager call. The full graph fits on one slide — and Chapter 9 will animate exactly these edges.

happy path
Boot
set(menu)
Menu
set(game)
Game
push(pause)
overlays
Pause
pop · set(menu)
Settings
push over menu or pause
Game Over
set(menu) — replace
hooks
Ch 9 fades
wrap set/push/pop
Death timeline
Ch 6 gates input
Auto-pause
on window focus loss

Five screens, seven transitions, zero mode booleans — every edge is one manager call.

details
  • Menu → Game → Pause → Game → Game Over → Menu: the whole flow, no bools
  • Every transition is one call — set, push, or pop — later wrapped by a fade (Ch 9)
  • Window focus loss auto-pushes pause: mobile suspend and desktop alt-tab share one path
  • Settings pushes over whatever is beneath — the same widget tree serves menu and pause
  • Game over replaces the stack, not pops it: replay means a fresh world, not a resumed one
Best Practice — Auto-pause on background

On SDL_EVENT_APP_WILLENTERBACKGROUND, push the pause screen if a game is running. Mobile OSes suspend you mid-tick without asking; desktop alt-tab still fires window events. Players forgive a pause they did not request — they never forgive dying off-screen.

7.19 — Input on Menus

Menus are played with thumbs and gamepads as much as mice. Focus navigation, visible focus, and hold-to-repeat make keyboard and controller first-class.

  • Four directions move focus — the focus graph is data: each widget names its neighbors
  • Focus must be visible: the ring draws whenever focus exists — hidden focus is a bug
  • Confirm activates (gamepad SOUTH, ENTER, SPACE); back pops (gamepad EAST, ESC)
  • Hold-to-repeat: 0.4 s delay, then 12 Hz — nudging sliders and scrolling scores without tapping
  • Touch passes through: finger events hit-test the tree directly; focus follows the last touch
  • Mixed input is normal: one player steers with a pad while the mouse idles — both stay live
Common Pitfall — The invisible focus ring

A focus ring styled to near-invisibility passes review and fails couch play: the gamepad player cannot see what ENTER will hit. Contrast ratio, not subtlety, is the requirement — test the ring against the brightest background art you ship.

7.20 — Pitfalls Round-Up

Four failure modes own the bug tracker of every UI stack ever written. Check each one before shipping, not after.

  • Modality leaks: two screens consuming input — impossible with top-only routing, fatal without it
  • Focus traps: focus lands on a disabled or hidden widget and the menu dies quietly
  • Restart-to-apply: settings that demand a reboot — apply live through one apply() path
  • Stale state on resume: pause assumes things that changed while it was covered — re-read in resume()
  • All four share one cure: the screen contract, honored literally, on every path
Common Pitfall — The zombie screen

A covered screen that keeps ticking double-processes input and double-advances animations — if your manager ever updates a covered screen, modality is gone. The contract is the cure: top-only update, pause/resume honored, no exceptions for convenience.

Best Practice — A hundred lines of patience

Every pitfall on this slide is prevented by the same discipline: screens own their lifecycle completely. When show/hide/pause/resume stay symmetric and the stack routes input, the entire class of menu bugs — leaks, traps, zombies — becomes unrepresentable.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 7 Recap

  • Screens + ScreenManager stack: set replaces, push/pop overlays; top-only input and update
  • Widget tree: local rects, nine anchor points on 960×540, Rows; hit testing is the transform walk
  • Skin as data: one JSON reskins everything; widgets reference styles by name
  • Buttons, sliders, checkboxes — 44 px touch floor, visible focus, live-apply settings
  • Persistence: SDL_GetPrefPath("sable", "canyon-dash"), load-or-defaults, debounced writes
  • Saves are versioned and separate: insert-sort-trim leaderboards, unlock flags, flush at safe moments
Chapter 8 — Special Effects
Ch 8Chapter 8

Special Effects

01Game feel: why effects are features, not garnish
02Particles: emitters, pools, and data-driven presets
03Blend modes: add, blend, mod — and when each lies
04Procedural motion: wobble, wander, orbit
05Parallax scrolling and the full background stack
06Easing, critically-damped smoothing, and buoyancy

8.2 — Game Feel: Effects Are Features

A jump that lands without dust is data; the same jump with dust, a flash, and a score pop is a game. Effects are the feedback layer that tells the player the simulation noticed them.

  • Feedback first: every effect answers "did that matter?" — landing, collecting, taking damage
  • Landing dust confirms ground contact better than any collision response the player cannot see
  • Carrot sparks plus a Hud pop make the carrot value 10 feel earned, not merely counted
  • Hit flashes (SDL_SetTextureColorMod toward white) read in two frames; players react before numbers
  • The three pillars of this chapter: particles, motion smoothing, environment response
Deep Dive — Juice is compression

A 100 ms burst of dust substitutes for the thousands of collision details the player never sees — the brain reads it as "the game acknowledged my input". Effects are communication, so budget them like UI: every burst must answer a question the player just asked.

8.3 — Particle System Anatomy

Three concerns, three types: emitters decide when and where particles are born, particles carry per-instance state, the pool owns the memory all of them live in.

who spawns
ParticleEmitter
policy: rate · cone
Preset
data: dust · sparks
EventBus
trigger: player.landed
what moves
Particle state
pos · vel · life
ParticlePool
SoA + free-list
Curves
size/color over life
what draws
ParticleSystem
render pass
Blend mode
