ADD · BLEND
Camera2D
world to screen

A smoke vent and a landing puff differ only in their preset row — never in code.

details
  • ParticleEmitter — spawn policy: rate, bursts, velocity cone, gravity; it draws nothing
  • Particles — per-instance state only: position, velocity, life, size; no behavior of their own
  • ParticlePool — preallocated SoA storage plus a free-list; allocation never happens at runtime
  • Presets — plain data rows: one config per named effect, tuned like a spreadsheet
  • One ParticleSystem renders everything — draw order and blend modes live there, not in emitters
Best Practice — Split policy, state, and memory

Emitter code that also stores particle data and draws cannot be reused, tested, or tuned separately. Keep the trinity split: a new effect becomes a new preset row and maybe a new subscription — not a new class hierarchy.

8.4 — Data Layout: SoA vs AoS

Ten thousand particles at 60 fps is 600k state updates per second — arithmetic the CPU does in its sleep. The real bottleneck is which bytes travel from RAM to the core, and how many of them are wasted.

  • AoS — array of structs: each particle is 32-64 bytes, so the physics sweep drags size and color along with position
  • SoA — structure of arrays: one flat float column per field; the update pass reads x/y/vx/vy/life only
  • A cache line is 64 bytes: AoS wastes most of every line it pulls during the integrate sweep
  • 10k AoS particles is roughly 640 KB of live state — bigger than many L2 caches, streamed every frame
  • The same particles in SoA integrate through about 200 KB, and the render pass touches other columns
Performance Tip — SoA is prefetcher food

Linear sweeps over contiguous float arrays are the best case for hardware prefetch and auto-vectorization: the next particle is already in flight while the current one computes. AoS with interleaved hot and cold fields defeats both — and no compiler flag fixes a layout decision.

8.5 — The Particle Pool

The pool in one screen: seven parallel float arrays, a stack of free indices, and not one allocation after construction.

key points
  • Construction allocates once; acquire and release are a few instructions — no malloc in the loop
  • A full pool returns -1: emitters drop the newest particle, so effects degrade gracefully
  • The free-list is LIFO — recycled indices stay hot in cache while stale ones age out
  • Public columns, private bookkeeping: emitters and the renderer share data, not behavior
Common Pitfall — The vector that reallocates

If a late "just push_back one more" sneaks into the update path, std::vector reallocates and every pointer and reference into the pool dangles mid-frame. Capacity is fixed at construction; overflow means dropping, never growing.

8.6 — Emitter Configuration as Data

Everything an emitter does belongs in a config struct a designer could edit without a compiler — which conveniently doubles as the particle-editor file format.

  • spawnRate — particles per second as a float; bursts are spawnRate 0 plus a burst count
  • lifetime range — min/max seconds; variety in lifetime alone fixes most "fountain looks fake" complaints
  • velocity cone — base angle plus a half-angle; speed gets its own min/max pair
  • size over life — start and end size: growth reads as smoke, shrink reads as dust and sparks
  • color over life — two-stop gradient for tint, fading toward transparent at the end
  • gravity + drag — per-preset acceleration and velocity damping; smoke ignores gravity
Deep Dive — The editor is a saved struct

A particle tool is a property grid that edits this struct live, plus a preview canvas. Because the preset is plain data, the editor never links against the engine: it writes JSON, the game hot-reloads it, and the identical file ships to players.

8.7 — ParticleEmitter::update

One tick, three jobs: convert spawn rate into whole particles through an accumulator, integrate motion with the preset fields, retire expired slots back to the pool.

key points
  • The accumulator turns fractional rates into exact long-run averages — 40/s at 30 fps still spawns 40
  • Semi-implicit Euler again: velocity first, then position — the same order the player integrates with
  • Death is one compare per particle per tick; zero destructor traffic, zero allocation
  • spawnOne is pure config lookup: angle and speed scattered inside the preset ranges
Common Pitfall — Spawning whole particles per frame

Spawning "if (frame % 3 == 0)" ties the effect to the frame rate: the same emitter fires twice as often at 120 Hz. Multiply rate by dt and bank the fraction in an accumulator — effects must be properties of the game, not of the player monitor.

8.8 — ParticleSystem::render

Drawing is one loop: live particles become rotated, faded quads through the camera transform, with additive blending for glow.

key points
  • Per-particle angle from atan2f(vy, vx): sparks streak along their motion, dust ignores it
  • SDL_SetTextureAlphaMod fades each quad by the squared life ratio — fast-out reads softer than linear
  • Size shrinks over life here; start smaller than end instead, and the same code reads as smoke
  • The loop runs inside the world pass, inheriting the camera zoom scale Chapter 3 already set
Performance Tip — Alpha mod breaks the batch

SDL_SetTextureAlphaMod is texture state: changing it between two draws of the same texture flushes the render batch. Hundreds of particles mean hundreds of flushes. Quantize alpha into 16 buckets and draw bucket by bucket — visually identical, far fewer state changes.

8.9 — Blend Modes: Add, Blend, Mod, None

A blend mode is the arithmetic the GPU evaluates per pixel. Pick it per effect family, not per particle — it is state on the texture, so it belongs to presets.

  • SDL_BLENDMODE_BLEND — source over destination: the standard alpha path for dust, smoke, water overlays
  • SDL_BLENDMODE_ADD — source plus destination, clamped: glows, sparks, fire; brightens what it covers
  • SDL_BLENDMODE_MOD — source times destination: tinting and shadowing; darkens without hiding detail
  • SDL_BLENDMODE_NONE — copy, alpha ignored: opaque props, the fastest path, wrong for anything soft
  • Canyon Dash presets: dust and smoke blend, sparks add, the water overlay blends at alpha 140
  • Premultiplied-alpha art needs a custom one/one-minus-source blend — SDL3 can compose it, but author straight alpha first
Common Pitfall — ADD on bright backgrounds

Additive particles over a pale sky clamp straight to white: a noon spark burst reads as a hole in the scene. Tint embers toward saturated orange, or switch that preset to BLEND in bright biomes — test every effect against the lightest and darkest background it can cross.

8.10 — Presets: Dust, Smoke, Sparks

Three presets carry the whole game: dust for weight, smoke for place, sparks for reward. Each is one data row the emitter reads at spawn time.

  • dust — burst 22, life 0.30-0.55 s, upward cone 35 degrees, speed 60-110, shrink 10 to 4 px, BLEND
  • smoke — stream 6/s, life 1.2-2.0 s, drift upward at 15-25, grow 6 to 18 px, BLEND, peak alpha 90
  • sparks — burst 14, life 0.25-0.40 s, radial cone, speed 180-260, gravity 340, ADD, streaks on
  • Sizes are fractions of a 32 px TILE: dust starts under a third of a tile, sparks under a fifth
  • Tuning order: lifetime, then speed, then count — count multiplies cost, so fix feel before volume
  • Author tuning at the fixed 60 Hz tick: a preset tuned at 144 Hz lies about lifetime elsewhere
Best Practice — One knob at a time

Tune by changing exactly one number, watching one full spawn-to-death cycle, and reverting if it did not help. Two simultaneous changes interact — especially lifetime with gravity — and you will never know which one made the burst feel right.

8.11 — Presets in Code + Event Hookup

The presets as aggregate initializers, plus the wiring that turns a landing into dust without gameplay code ever calling the renderer.

key points
  • A preset is one aggregate initializer — diffable in review, loadable from assets/ later
  • The burst lands at the feet (e.y - 4), not the actor center — offsets sell contact
  • Gameplay emits events knowing nothing about particles; the screen translates facts into effects
  • The pattern scales: water splash, hit flash, checkpoint glow — each one new subscription
Deep Dive — Why events, not calls

If the player controller called burst() directly, every new effect would mean editing the controller and growing its dependency on the FX stack. The EventBus inversion keeps the emit site a bare fact ("player.landed") and the reaction a policy elsewhere — new effects ship as one subscription, zero simulation edits.

8.12 — Procedural Movement

Not everything that moves needs physics. A parametric function of time animates forever with zero state, stays deterministic for replays, and costs two trig calls.

  • Sine wobble — offset by sin(t · freq): signage, hanging ropes, idle collectibles
  • Random wander — two sines at incommensurate frequencies: critters and props that never visibly loop
  • Circular orbit — a cos/sin pair around a center: collectible halos, debris rings, drifting shadows
  • All three are pure functions: no velocity, no accumulator, no state to save or rewind
  • Determinism for free — the fixed-step loop replays the exact same wobble from the same tick count
  • They drive emitters too: a vent emitter riding wander becomes a smoke plume that searches

8.13 — Motion Helpers: Wobble, Wander, Orbit

Three tiny functions in sable/fx/motion.h — the entire animation budget for every decorative prop in Canyon Dash.

key points
  • The carrot bobs with sineWobble(t, 3.0f, 0.8f) — t is the level clock, shared by every prop
  • Seeds desynchronize: wander(i, t, amp) across ten props yields ten unrelated motions
  • The vertical squash (0.35) fakes perspective on the orbit — a full circle reads as a fly, not a halo
  • These are static inline: the compiler folds them into callers, no call overhead
Common Pitfall — Mixing clocks

Feeding these helpers wall-clock time breaks determinism: a replayed tick sequence would wobble differently than the original run. Pass accumulated fixed-step time (tickCount / 60.0f) — never SDL_GetTicksNS-derived seconds — into any function whose output the simulation can see.

8.14 — Parallax Scrolling

Depth from motion: when the camera pans, nearer layers slide faster than far ones. Six draw calls of tiled art buy an entire canyon of depth.

  • Each background layer scrolls at camera.x × factor — factor 0 is glued to the screen, 1 to the world
  • Canyon Dash factors: far mountains 0.15, mid rock formations 0.35, near cactus ridge 0.60
  • The mismatch between layer speeds is the depth cue — the eye reads relative motion, not absolute speed
  • Cheaper than it looks: each layer is one tile strip drawn two or three times — a handful of quads
  • Vertical parallax (camera.y × factor × 0.5) is optional; a subtle pitch on jumps sells height
  • Foreground occluders at factor above 1 move faster than the world — rare, cinematic, for whip-pans
Performance Tip — Parallax is a dozen quads, not a world

A three-layer stack with 512 px strips draws at most three strips per layer across the 960 px screen: about a dozen textured quads per frame, no matter how long the level is. The depth you sell costs less than one actor — spend the savings on particles.

8.15 — The Parallax Renderer

Infinite scrolling in a dozen lines: wrap the camera-relative offset into one tile width, then tile across the logical screen with no seam.

key points
  • fmodf wraps the scroll into one tile width — strip count never grows with level length
  • The negative start guarantees coverage of the leftmost column with zero seam
  • Factors live in one function: retuning depth means editing three numbers in render
  • Layers draw back to front before the world pass — the stack composites under everything
Common Pitfall — The one-pixel seam

Rounding wrapped x to whole pixels, or mixing NEAREST-scaled art with float offsets, occasionally leaves a 1 px gap between strip copies. Keep offsets in floats, size strips in whole pixels, and if a seam persists, draw each strip 1 px wider than its source — overlap is invisible, gaps are not.

8.16 — The Full Background Stack

Compose the frame back to front: a fixed sky, three parallax strips, then the camera-space world from Chapter 3 — one painter ordering, zero special cases.

sky · factor 0
Sky gradient
screen space, never scrolls
far · 0.15
Mountains
one 512 px strip, 2-3 draws
mid · 0.35
Rock formations
one strip, slightly faster
near · 0.60
Cactus ridge
closest, moves with intent
world · 1.0
Tiles · actors · particles
Camera2D space, zoom applies

This is the drawBackground(cam) stub Chapter 3 left in WorldRenderer — finally filled.

details
  • Sky gradient: a 1x64 gradient texture stretched to 960x540 — factor 0, immune to the camera
  • Layers two to four: parallax strips in screen space, offset by camera.x × factor
  • Layer five: the world pass — SDL_SetRenderScale(cam.zoom), then tiles, actors, particles
  • Draw order is depth: any reorder here is instantly visible as popping at layer boundaries
  • Zoom applies to the world pass only — stable backgrounds read as atmospheric distance
Best Practice — One composer, one order

Keep the entire back-to-front sequence inside WorldRenderer::render so the ordering is auditable at a glance. Draw calls scattered across systems are how HUD-under-particles and sky-over-actors bugs are born — the painter algorithm only works if one place owns the brush order.

8.17 — Lerp and Easing

Smoothing is one formula — interpolate between a start and an end as t goes from 0 to 1 — and easing is what shape you give t on the way there.

  • lerp(a, b, t) = a + (b - a) × t — the atom of animation; every curve below just bends t
  • linear — t straight through: mechanical; right for progress bars, wrong for anything a hand touched
  • quad / cubic — t squared, cubed: acceleration and deceleration, the default for physical motion
  • back — overshoots past 1 then settles: UI pops and punchy pickups, never for cameras
  • elastic — springs around the target several times: celebration moments and combo payoffs
  • Curves compose: easeIn for departures, easeOut for arrivals — "fast then settle" is easeOutQuad
Common Pitfall — Lerp with a constant alpha

pos += (target - pos) × 0.1f per frame is frame-rate-dependent lerp: the same stiffness is about 2.4x stronger at 144 Hz than at 60 Hz. Always derive alpha from dt — 1 - exp(-k · dt) — exactly the fix Camera2D already ships from Chapter 3.

8.18 — The Easing Library

Five curves and a clamp in one header — the whole library Sable needs for UI motion and effect choreography.

key points
  • Every function clamps first — an out-of-range t from a late frame cannot fling UI offscreen
  • easeOutBack peaks near 1.10: scale past the target, then settle — the entire "pop" vocabulary
  • Elastic is loud; reserve it for milestone payoffs like level complete, not routine UI
  • No classes, no state — pure math helpers, callable from C and C++ alike
Best Practice — Ease t, never the output

Compute progress linearly (elapsed / duration), then pass it through a curve — do not "ease" by scaling results. A normalized t means the same tween can pause, reverse, and scrub in debug tools without touching a single curve.

8.19 — Easing in Action: Damping and Pops

Two production uses: the camera-follow formula generalized into a critically-damped helper, and a score pop that overshoots on purpose.

key points
  • damp becomes the only smoothing call in Sable: camera, HUD bars, and zoom all route through it
  • Stiffness is readable tuning: 6 for the camera, 12 for UI, 2 for slow ambient drift
  • The pop peaks near scale 1.10 around t = 0.7 — one beat of overshoot reads as weight
  • Both run off the fixed tick, so a replay reproduces identical pop timing
Best Practice — One clock, one damper

When every smoothed value flows through one damp() helper, a frame-rate bug or tuning problem has exactly one place to live. Ten bespoke lerp sites mean ten subtly different feels — and ten places to forget the dt.

8.20 — Buoyancy: The Float Model

Floating props need to answer interaction, not just decorate: a restoring spring toward the water line plus drag gives bobbing that reacts when the player splashes through.

  • Cheapest: sineWobble around the water line — pure decoration that ignores the player entirely
  • Reactive: a spring toward the surface — force proportional to how deep the prop sits
  • The drag term is what makes it water: without it the prop oscillates forever like a dry spring
  • Real Archimedes scales with submerged volume; depth-proportional is indistinguishable at game scale
  • The water line comes from the Ch 5 translucent overlay region — props and visuals share one source
  • Entrance events fall out for free: crossing the line downward is exactly when to spawn the splash
Common Pitfall — Springs that explode

A stiff spring integrated with a large dt overshoots the rest position each tick and gains energy — the prop launches out of the water, forever. Keep stiffness × dt well under 1, clamp bounce velocity, or substep; jitter on entry is the tell that damping is too weak.

8.21 — Water Float Physics

The whole model in one update: a depth-proportional restoring force, velocity damping, sideways drag, and a splash burst on the exact frame of entry.

key points
  • Stiffness 26, damping 3.5: two slow bobs, then rest — pickups settle in under a second
  • Entry detection is one crossing test — no repeated bursts while riding the surface
  • Sideways drag (0.8 per second) makes the prop trail the current instead of sliding freely
  • The splash preset: burst 30, upward cone 60 degrees, BLEND, life 0.4-0.7 s — foam, not glow
Performance Tip — Floating is nearly free

A floating prop costs one spring evaluation per tick — a handful of float ops — and the splash only pays on the crossing frame. A canyon pool with a dozen drifting crates and 40 splash particles stays well under 1% of the frame budget; buoyancy scales without thought.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 8 Recap

  • Effects are feedback: particles answer "did that matter?" — presets make the answer cheap data
  • The trinity: emitters spawn, SoA pools store, one system renders — zero allocation after construction
  • Blend modes per family: BLEND for dust and smoke, ADD for sparks and glow, MOD for tinting
  • Parallax strips at camera.x × 0.15 / 0.35 / 0.60 behind the world pass sell depth for a dozen quads
  • Easing: clamp t, bend t — back pops UI, elastic celebrates, damp() smooths frame-rate-free
  • Buoyancy: depth spring plus drag, splash on the entry crossing of the water line
Chapter 9 — Screen Transitions
Ch 9Chapter 9

Screen Transitions

01Why transitions exist: hiding hitches, keeping continuity
02The ScreenTransition interface and the render-target technique
03The TransitionManager: timing, swapping, input blocking
04A repertoire: fade, slide, wipe, dissolve
05Chaining with loading screens for level swaps
06Timing, accessibility, pitfalls, and testing

9.2 — Why Transitions Exist

A hard cut between screens is a discontinuity the brain flags as an error; a transition is a designed 300 ms bridge that hides loading, preserves context, and signals that a boundary was crossed.

  • Hiding hitches: the first frames of a new screen stall on texture uploads and font rasterization — a transition covers them
  • Continuity: motion across the change preserves the mental map — where am I, what just happened
  • Semantics: fades read as time passing, slides read as travel, wipes read as a chapter turn
  • Polish: shipping games are judged on screen changes more than on any single frame of gameplay
  • A cut is still a tool: instant restarts and quick deaths in a fast game feel better without ceremony
Deep Dive — The brain treats cuts as events

An abrupt scene change interrupts visual flow, and viewers spend attention deciding whether it mattered. A short animated bridge spends that attention for them: the eye follows the motion, and the new scene arrives already accepted. That is why 300 ms of fade feels faster than 0 ms of cut.

9.3 — The Framework: Requirements First

Before writing any single effect, fix the contract all of them must satisfy — otherwise every new transition re-solves the same plumbing problems.

  • Any screen to any screen: menu to game, game to results, level to level — one mechanism, no special cases
  • Timed and dt-driven: a fixed duration in seconds, the same speed at 60 and 144 Hz
  • Input-blocked: gameplay and menus freeze for the duration — a transition is a cinematic, not a simulation
  • Composable: effects stack with a loading screen between two fades for level swaps
  • Engine-owned: TransitionManager and ScreenTransition live in sable; games only pick presets
  • Interface first: the next slide is the entire contract every effect must honor
Best Practice — Contract before effects

Write the interface, the manager, and a single fade; ship that; then add slides and wipes. Teams that start with the dramatic dissolve discover the dull problems — input leaks, double swaps, texture sizing — only after the fancy effect is welded in place.

9.4 — The ScreenTransition Interface

Four calls and two owned textures: the interface stays small because the manager does the scheduling and the effects only animate pixels.

key points
  • begin captures both frames up front — the old screen keeps its final pose, the new its first
  • update touches only t; every visible change happens in render as a pure function of t
  • The effect owns its two textures and frees them on destruction — leaks have exactly one owner
  • Duration is data: FadeTransition(0.30f) reads as intent at the call site

9.5 — The Render-Target Technique

SDL3 can redirect every draw into a texture: render each screen once into a 960×540 target, then the transition animates two static images — cheap, uniform, and effect-agnostic.

  • SDL_SetRenderTarget(renderer, tex) redirects all draws; passing NULL restores the window
  • Target textures require SDL_TEXTUREACCESS_TARGET at creation — ordinary textures fail the call
  • The size rule: targets match the logical 960×540 exactly, so captured frames composite 1:1, unscaled
  • Capturing freezes each screen as a texture: the effect composites images, never live scenes
  • Two captures, one per screen: the outgoing frame is the old screen as the player last saw it
  • This is why every effect can treat screens as interchangeable full-screen rectangles
Common Pitfall — Wrong target size

A target created at window pixel size (say 1920×1080) composites against logical 960×540 coordinates — letterboxing applies to the window, not your math — leaving stretched or clipped frames. Always size targets from the logical presentation and re-create them only if the logical size itself changes.

9.6 — captureScreen

The helper that freezes a screen: redirect, clear, render, restore — four calls, and the restore is the one people forget.

key points
  • Redirect, clear, render, restore — four calls, and the last one is load-bearing
  • A recycled target still holds the previous transition — SDL_RenderClear kills the ghost frame
  • Targets come from the manager pool created at startup: begin() performs zero allocation
  • Capture the incoming screen before its first update tick — first pose, not first simulation frame
Common Pitfall — Rendering into the wrong place

A stray SDL_SetRenderTarget left set means the rest of the frame — HUD, present, everything — quietly renders into your texture. Symptom: a blank window while the game keeps running. Restore NULL immediately, on every path including errors, exactly as above.

9.7 — Progress, Interpolation, Easing

Every effect reduces to t in [0,1] across its duration; the easing curve applied to t decides whether the motion reads as mechanical, eager, or cinematic.

  • Normalize once: t = elapsed / duration, clamped — effects never see minutes, only 0..1
  • Linear t reads mechanical and cheap — fine for progress bars, wrong for full-screen motion
  • easeOut family is "fast then settle": the new screen arrives quickly and docks — the default
  • easeIn departs: the outgoing screen leaves slowly, then hurries away — use on the exit half
  • Symmetric easeInOutCubic suits slides and wipes — both ends are visible motion
  • Overshoot curves (back, elastic) are celebratory; on full-screen frames they read as camera bounce
Deep Dive — Why easeOut reads as arrival

Fast-then-slow matches how real objects decelerate into place, so the brain accepts the incoming screen as something that landed rather than teleported. The inverse, easeIn, matches departure — things leave slowly, then are gone. Compose the two and a two-phase transition feels like one continuous hand-off.

9.8 — The TransitionManager

The scheduler: start an effect on a screen pair, advance it, render its composite while active, and commit the swap exactly once at the end.

key points
  • The manager owns the swap: screens change hands exactly once, at isDone, never mid-flight
  • While active, the two captured textures are the whole frame — screens freeze by design
  • start refuses to re-enter: a second press during a fade is ignored, not queued
  • The input gate is one boolean — the queue-draining half lives on the blocking slide
Best Practice — One owner for the swap

If both the manager and individual screens can call swapTo, you get transitions racing transitions and screens destroyed while still captured inside a texture. Route every screen change through one choke point — the flow diagram stays a straight line.

9.9 — The Fade Transition

The workhorse: phase one fades the outgoing frame to black, phase two fades the incoming frame back in — one overlay, two textures, thirty lines.

key points
  • Each phase is a full-screen blit plus one translucent fill — two draw calls on any hardware
  • The midpoint swap happens between frames: no cross-fade math, no double blending
  • SDL_SetRenderDrawBlendMode is the enabler — the draw color alpha is dead state without it
  • A cross-fade variant draws both frames with per-texture alpha mods — softer, double the compositing
Best Practice — Ship the fade first

The fade is the least likely to break, the easiest to test, and appropriate for 80% of screen changes. Ship it as the only transition; add others only where the game earns them — dramatic wipes on a menu hop read as insecurity, not polish.

9.10 — The Slide Transition

The incoming screen chases the outgoing one across the logical screen — one shared offset, eased symmetrically, reads as a single continuous belt.

key points
  • One offset drives both frames — perfectly synced motion is free when there is only one number
  • easeInOutCubic on the offset: both screens accelerate and decelerate together
  • Slides read as travel: level-to-level and map-to-game pair best
  • Draw order matters at t = 0 and t = 1 only — the belt never overlaps mid-flight
Performance Tip — Slides are two quads

The whole effect is two full-screen texture blits — the GPU composites them while the CPU idles. At 60 fps that leaves the entire 16.6 ms frame free for asset streaming behind the scenes, which is exactly why slides pair well with loading screens.

9.11 — The Wipe Transition

A directional reveal via the renderer scissor: the incoming frame draws only inside a rectangle that grows across the screen.

key points
  • The clip rectangle is a hardware scissor — pixels outside are discarded before blending
  • Order matters: draw the base frame first, then the clipped reveal on top
  • The reset is not optional: clip state persists on the renderer and would clip the next screen too
  • Edge treatment separates wipes: a hard edge is classic, a masked edge is modern — next slide
Common Pitfall — The clip that never cleared

SDL_SetRenderClipRect state persists across frames on the renderer. A wipe that forgets the NULL reset leaves every later draw — HUD, menus — clipped to the last sliver of reveal. The symptom (UI missing its left half) points far from the cause; always reset in the same function that sets it.

9.12 — The Texture-Masked Wipe

Replace the hard wipe edge with a pre-baked noise threshold: the incoming screen arrives through a spreading field of holes — the classic dissolve look, without a single shader.

  • Pre-bake a noise texture at authoring time: each pixel brightness is its reveal threshold
  • Quantize the noise into 8-16 bands: band k reveals every pixel whose threshold is below k
  • Runtime keeps a reveal target: start from the outgoing frame, blit incoming pixels onto it band by band
  • Each step draws the next band as small tile rects — a few hundred blits at the worst step, then fewer
  • The screen just shows the reveal target; band edges get a 1-2 px feather from the mask art itself
  • Sort tiles by threshold offline in tools/ — runtime never touches the noise texture at all
Deep Dive — Why bands, not pixels

Per-pixel masking needs a multiply of two textures — the 2D renderer cannot express it without custom blend plumbing. Band quantization approximates the same dissolve with plain blits: at 16 bands over 300 ms the eye cannot tell it from the shader version, and everything stays inside the API you already trust.

9.13 — Shader-Based Wipes

The per-pixel truth: a fragment shader compares noise against progress and outputs alpha directly — one quad, no bands, no approximation. SDL_GPU makes it possible; Chapter 11 makes it practical.

  • The dissolve in one line of GLSL: step(noise(uv), t) — each pixel switches exactly when t passes its threshold
  • An SDL_GPU graphics pipeline renders the two captured frames as textures with that shader bound
  • Cost model: a 20-line shader plus roughly 200 lines of plumbing — pipeline state, SPIR-V, samplers, uniforms
  • Honest advice: the banded mask is visually equal at transition speeds; shaders win on edge effects
  • Edge effects are the real prize: burn glow, refraction of the outgoing frame, liquid masks over time
  • The two captured 960×540 frames slot straight in as shader inputs — render targets compose with everything
Deep Dive — Where shaders pay off

A frame-rate-independent dissolve is table stakes; the reason to cross into GPU code is what the 2D API cannot fake: edge glow that samples neighbors, refraction, advected liquid masks. Budget a week of pipeline plumbing before the first of those lands — it is machinery, not a snippet.

9.14 — A GLSL Dissolve Shader

The whole effect as it will sit inside the Chapter 11 pipeline — illustrative, because the surrounding SDL_GPU plumbing is that chapter’s subject, not this one’s.

key points
  • d = progress - noise is the distance into the reveal — its sign decides which frame shows
  • The hard version is the commented step line; the ember edge adds three more
  • Uniforms arrive once per frame from C: eased progress and edge width — zero per-pixel CPU work
  • Everything else — samplers, sets, pipeline creation — is Chapter 11 machinery, deliberately out of frame

9.15 — Chaining: The Level-Swap Choreography

A real level change is three beats: fade out the gameplay, hold a loading screen while assets stream in, fade in the new level — each beat its own transition.

  • Beat 1 — fade (250-300 ms): the gameplay screen exits under the overlay, hiding the teardown stall
  • Beat 2 — loading screen: a progress bar driven by the async AssetManager queue from Chapter 4
  • Beat 3 — fade or wipe (300 ms): the new level arrives warm — textures uploaded, first tick pre-run
  • Between beats the loading screen owns the frame and may animate freely until the queue drains
  • Never block inside an effect: if assets are not ready, the loading beat lengthens, not the fade
  • The chain is plain sequencing in ScreenManager — transitions compose because each ends in a stable state
Best Practice — Make the load the pause

The loading screen is not an apology; it is the transition partner. Stream the level while the bar animates, and keep the final fade duration independent of disk speed — a slow SSD must lengthen the loading beat, never the fade, or the choreography stops being choreography.

9.16 — Choosing a Transition

Two families, two jobs: subtle bridges keep the player moving; dramatic reveals mark beats that deserve ceremony.

ASubtle — fade, short slide
  • Durations 200-300 ms; easeOut shapes that dock quickly
  • Fits: menu to game, pause to resume, settings and back
  • Invisible in the best sense — players feel flow, not the effect
  • Cheapest to test: one overlay or two quads, no edge cases
  • The default for anything traversed dozens of times per session
BDramatic — wipe, dissolve, long slide
  • Durations 400-500 ms; symmetric easeInOut or custom curves
  • Fits: level to level, chapter turns, finale to credits
  • Reads as a boundary crossed — the game says this mattered
  • Costs attention: at high frequency it becomes friction
  • Earn it with content: a new biome deserves a wipe, a settings toggle does not
Best Practice — Frequency decides

Ask how often the player crosses this boundary per hour. Dozens of times: subtle, under 300 ms, or an instant cut. A handful of times: the dramatic option is on the table. The screen after a 20-minute level is a ceremony; the pause menu is a hallway door.

9.17 — Timing, Pacing, Accessibility

Transitions live in a perceptual sweet spot: long enough to read as intentional, short enough to never be waited on — and optional entirely for players whom motion harms.

  • Sweet spot 250-400 ms — enough to register the motion, far from enough to reach for the phone
  • Under about 150 ms reads as a rendering glitch, not a transition
  • Over about 600 ms is for ceremonial beats only — players mash through anything longer
  • Reduced motion: respect the setting and offer instant cuts — the option belongs in the settings from Chapter 7
  • Durations are constants, not vibes: 0.30f at the call site, one table in the docs
  • Never block on async inside the effect — the transition draws; the loading screen loads
Best Practice — Accessibility is a deadline feature

Vestibular disorders make full-screen motion genuinely unpleasant, and platform certifiers increasingly check for a reduced-motion option. Because every transition is a duration plus a swap, the accessible path is one branch: skip the effect, run the cut. Cost: an afternoon, once.

9.18 — Input Blocking

During a transition the game is a movie: events must be consumed and discarded, or a queued press from the old screen detonates on the new one.

  • The manager consumes every event while active — one boolean gate at the top of the dispatch
  • The SDL event queue keeps filling while you ignore it: drain it, do not merely skip polling
  • Undrained queues replay later: the Start press from the results screen fires on the fresh gameplay screen
  • Double-trigger guard: if (m_active) return; in start — a second press cannot queue a second swap
  • Edge-triggered logic (the Chapter 3 jump pattern) protects anything that slips a single-frame gap
  • On completion, flush once more before handing control back — the last stale press dies there
Common Pitfall — The ghost button press

The player mashes Pause during a fade; the queue holds three KEY_DOWN events. The transition ends, dispatch resumes, and the new screen instantly pauses — or skips the level-complete screen. Drain the queue each frame while active and flush at completion: presses that happened during the movie never happened.

9.19 — Pitfalls of the Technique

Three failure modes own the bug tracker for render-target transitions: sizing, stale pixels, and first-frame hitches. All three are one-line fixes once you can name them.

  • Symptom guide: stretched frames means target size, ghosting means uncleared target, stutter at start means late allocation
  • Keep the two frame textures for the process lifetime; re-create only if the logical size itself changes
  • Capture before the present of the same frame — the outgoing pose must be the pose the player just saw
  • Check the bool returns: a failed SDL_SetRenderTarget leaves draws aimed at the window mid-transition
  • Log the failure with SDL_GetError() at the call site — the string is stale three functions later
Common Pitfall — Size mismatch after resize

Targets sized at window pixel size break under letterboxing and DPI scaling: the composite is drawn in logical 960×540 coordinates against a differently sized texture. Size targets to the logical presentation, and handle SDL_EVENT_WINDOW_RESIZED by re-creating only if the logical size changed.

Common Pitfall — Alpha accumulation

A captured frame with transparent pixels, composited onto a dirty target, accumulates: the last transition faintly ghosts inside the new one, growing every level swap. SDL_RenderClear with an opaque draw color before every capture — recycled targets are only clean if you make them clean.

Performance Tip — Pre-create the pair

Creating two 960×540 RGBA textures at begin() time allocates and uploads on the exact frame whose hiccup you built the transition to hide. Create the pair once at startup and reuse it forever: the effect then costs two blits and nothing else.

9.20 — Wiring It Into GameApp

One public call on the app: setScreen with an optional effect. Games state intent; the engine decides the plumbing.

key points
  • A nullptr effect is a cut: instant swap — the reduced-motion setting routes here
  • Mid-flight requests are refused, not queued: one transition at a time, always
  • Ownership is explicit: the manager takes the effect by unique pointer and frees it at isDone
  • Every screen change funnels through one call — the flow diagram stays a straight line
Best Practice — Choke points age well

A single setScreen is where throttling, analytics, autosave-on-exit, and the accessibility cut all attach later — each a two-line change. Ad-hoc screen swaps scattered through gameplay code turn each of those features into an archaeology project.

9.21 — Testing Transitions

Effects that live 300 ms are hard to watch and harder to debug — so stretch time, capture frames, and stress the swap path until it stops surprising you.

  • Time-scale key: a debug key runs the whole app at 0.25x — every curve shape becomes visible
  • Frame capture: dump the composite at fixed t values (0.25, 0.5, 0.75) — easing bugs show as uneven gaps
  • The 100-transition stress test: auto-loop menu to game to menu, watching texture count and memory
  • Leak signature: video memory climbing a fixed amount per loop — one 960×540 target per swap
  • Resize mid-transition: the window event must not corrupt the composite — a classic bug class
  • Test every pairing both ways; transitions are symmetric in code and asymmetric in bugs
Performance Tip — Automate the loop

A debug key that auto-loops the swap path takes a minute to write and two minutes to run, and it catches every leak the code review missed. Assert that the texture count returns to baseline after each iteration — determinism makes the assert meaningful instead of flaky.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 9 Recap

  • Transitions hide hitches, preserve continuity, and mark boundaries — cuts remain a deliberate tool
  • The technique: capture both screens into 960×540 render targets, then animate two static images
  • ScreenTransition is begin/update/render/isDone; TransitionManager owns the one true swap
  • Repertoire: fade (default), slide (travel), wipe (scissor reveal), banded dissolve, shader (Ch 11)
  • Timing: 250-400 ms sweet spot, reduced-motion cuts, never block async inside the effect
  • Block and drain input for the duration — queued presses must not outlive the movie
Chapter 10 — Managing Music and Sound Effects
Ch 10Chapter 10

Managing Music and Sound Effects

01The SDL3 audio model: one logical device, mixed streams
02Sound effects: decoded banks and fire-and-forget voices
03Music: threaded streaming without underruns
04Volume, pitch and panning on live streams
05Recording, device-stream callbacks and taps
06Procedural audio: the AudioManager closes the loop

10.1 — Two Audio Budgets, One AudioManager

Chapter 2 drew the logical-device picture and promised a SfxVoice pool and a MusicStreamer. This chapter builds every box — behind one facade the game already knows how to talk to.

Game layer
gameplay code
playSfx · playMusic · setVolume
Facade
AudioManager
device · bank · voices · routing
SFX path
SFX bank
decoded at boot
SfxVoice pool
16 fire-and-forget streams
Music path
MusicStreamer
worker · chunked decode
music stream
long-lived · gain · ratio
SDL3
logical device
mixes every bound stream

One device, two feeding disciplines, zero custom mixing code.

details
  • SFX budget — latency: fully decoded into RAM at boot; a trigger pushes bytes and walks away
  • Music budget — memory: decoded in small chunks from disk, minutes of playback at flat RAM cost
  • AudioManager owns the device, the SFX bank, the voice pool, the feeder thread and the gain buses
  • Gameplay calls audio.playSfx("jump") — no SDL3 type ever appears in src/game/
  • Both budgets meet at one bound-stream device: same mixer, two feeding disciplines
Common Pitfall — The 45 MB song

A four-minute stereo track at 48 kHz S16 decodes to roughly 45 MB — several times the entire SFX bank. Load effects like a database and stream music like a faucet; the moment one song costs more RAM than every effect combined, the split is no longer optional.

10.2 — The SDL3 Audio Model: Devices Mix for You

SDL3 replaced the open-a-callback-and-pray contract with logical devices: bind any number of SDL_AudioStreams and SDL converts and mixes them all. The mixer you used to write is gone.

  • Open one logical device with an SDL_AudioSpec — the spec describes what your streams speak; SDL adapts the hardware
  • Each stream carries its own input spec; rate, format and channel conversion are automatic
  • Every bound stream is mixed by SDL — summing, clamping and scheduling are the runtime's job
  • Per-stream dials: gain, frequency ratio, queued bytes — no shared mixer state to lock
  • The callback era is still reachable (slide 10.18) — but now it is opt-in, not the toll booth
Deep Dive — Why automatic conversion matters

A 44.1 kHz mono WAV and a 48 kHz stereo device coexist without one line of resampler code. In the SDL2 era you matched specs exactly or chained conversions by hand — and every mismatch surfaced as a runtime buzz, never a compile error. The stream model moved that entire bug class into the runtime.

10.3 — AudioManager::init: Opening the Device

The device setup is one spec and one call — plus one SDL3 habit: devices open paused, so bind your starting streams first and resume deliberately.

key points
  • SDL_AUDIO_DEVICE_DEFAULT_PLAYBACK lets the platform pick its default sink
  • S16 / 2 channels / 48 kHz is the comfortable target: CD-grade, cheap to sum, universally mixable
  • Devices open paused in SDL3 — bind your first streams, then resume once
  • One playback device for the whole game; recording (slide 10.16) opens its own
Common Pitfall — Ids are not pointers

SDL_AudioDeviceID is a Uint32, and failure is 0, not NULL. if (device == NULL) compiles clean and then never fires — the game runs mute while the log stays empty. Audio ids are numbers: compare against zero.

10.4 — SFX Design: Decode Once, Fire and Forget

A jump that sounds 100 ms after the button feels broken. So every gameplay sound is fully decoded before the first frame — and triggering one is pure memory work.

  • Decode every WAV at boot into a bank: name → {spec, data, len}, resident for the session
  • A trigger does no IO and no decoding: make a stream, push bytes, return
  • Voices end themselves — queued bytes drain to zero, the slot recycles
  • Voice cap 16 — ample for a platformer, invisible to the mixer
  • Only music and long ambience stream from disk; everything else lives in RAM
Performance Tip — Decode-on-play is the classic hitch

One SDL_LoadWAV mid-jump stalls long enough to hear it. Pay that cost during the loading screen, where Chapter 4 already owns a stall — never during play. Stalls at boot are invisible; stalls mid-air are reviews.

10.5 — The SFX Bank: SDL_LoadWAV at Boot

One call per file fills the bank. The returned buffer is raw PCM you keep for the whole session — and it is SDL's allocation, so SDL takes it back.

key points
  • The spec describes the returned PCM — a 44.1 kHz mono file next to 48 kHz stereo is fine
  • Buffers are SDL's allocation: pair every load with SDL_free, never plain free
  • A missing sound at boot is a hard stop — it should never be a runtime surprise
  • Dozens of Canyon Dash effects fit in a few MB — the bank is the cheap half of audio
Common Pitfall — Mixing allocators

A buffer from SDL_LoadWAV freed with libc free works on one platform and corrupts the heap on another — the crash lands in an unrelated malloc weeks later. Whoever gave you the memory takes it back: SDL's memory, SDL_free, every time.

10.6 — Play: A Fresh Stream per Trigger

The pattern that replaces a mixer: every play creates its own SDL_AudioStream, pushes the whole clip once, and lets it drain. Polyphony falls out as a side effect.

key points
  • N overlapping sounds = N streams: SDL sums them; there is no playing-voices array to maintain
  • Pushing a few KB is non-blocking — the main thread never waits on the mixer
  • Lifetime by query: SDL_GetAudioStreamQueued hitting zero means the clip finished
  • Stream creation is cheap — microseconds against a 16-voice ceiling
Best Practice — Own no audio state after the push

After SDL_PutAudioStreamData the main thread holds nothing the mixer needs — no locks, no per-frame mixing, no callback math. The device drains streams while you render frames. Fire-and-forget is not laziness; it is the design working.

10.7 — Voice Budgets: Drop, Steal, Duck

Sixteen voices sound infinite until a waterfall of golden carrots asks for seventeen. A drop policy chosen on purpose beats one chosen by the first crash.

  • Cap at 16 voices — beyond that a mix turns to mud, not richness
  • Pool exhausted: drop the new sound, steal the quietest, or steal the oldest
  • Canyon Dash steals the oldest — except priority voices like the level-clear jingle
  • Ducking on big hits: music gain dips for ~200 ms, ramps back over ~600 ms
  • Ducking looks like mixer magic; it is one SDL_SetAudioStreamGain on the music stream
Common Pitfall — Unbounded polyphony

Two hundred simultaneous footstep streams clip the sum while the mixer burns CPU resampling silence. The failure is gradual — it never crashes, the soundtrack just gets worse every level. Choose the cap, choose the drop, ship both.

10.8 — Streaming Music: Feed It, Do Not Hold It

A theme outlives any loading screen. Music decodes in small chunks on a worker thread and is pushed ahead of playback — memory stays flat no matter how long the song runs.

  • Never hold a decoded song: ~45 MB per track versus the SFX bank's few MB
  • The feeder thread decodes ahead: push when queued bytes run low, sleep otherwise
  • Aim for ~500 ms of cushion — rides out scheduler spikes without lagging track switches
  • Too little cushion: underruns — clicks, gaps, the OS starved your thread
  • The music stream is long-lived: gain, ducking and pitch all ride it
Performance Tip — Chunk math worth memorizing

16 KB at 48 kHz stereo S16 is about 85 ms of audio — six chunks in flight cover the 500 ms cushion with under 100 KB of RAM. The whole music subsystem costs less memory than one Chapter 4 sprite atlas.

10.9 — MusicStreamer: The Feeder Thread

One thread, one mutex, one rule: keep the stream fed. The underrun guard is nothing more exotic than watching how many bytes stay queued.

key points
  • feedThreshold in bytes is the only tuning knob: 96 KB ≈ 500 ms at 48 kHz stereo S16
  • Chapter 2's golden rule holds: the worker touches files and memory, never video
  • readChunk hides the format — a raw PCM reader here; a codec is a dependency decision
  • stop() is flag → join → destroy — the same order as AsyncLoader::stop() in Chapter 2
Common Pitfall — Teardown races the feeder

Destroying the stream while the feeder is mid-push is a use-after-free. The mutex covers shared flags, but the join is what guarantees the thread is gone before the stream dies. Flag, join, then destroy — never reorder it, and never skip the join.

10.10 — Volume Is Gain, and Gain Is Per Stream

SDL3 has no master volume dial — and that turns out to be a gift. Every stream owns a gain, so master, music and SFX levels are three numbers and two multiplications.

  • SDL_SetAudioStreamGain(stream, 0.5f) — linear, default 1.0, effective immediately on a playing stream
  • No mixer rebuild, no restart: slider drags map straight to one call
  • Bus model: master × music and master × sfx — every sound routes through two floats
  • Chapter 7's settings sliders persist 0..1 values; this chapter is where they land
  • Ducking reuses the machinery: save the music level, dip, ramp back
Best Practice — Two update paths, on purpose

Short-lived SFX bakes its gain in at play time — streams die young, so new triggers hear new levels instantly. The long-lived music stream takes live SDL_SetAudioStreamGain calls — slider drags never restart the song, and gaps never happen.

10.11 — Routing: Master, Music, SFX

The example wiring: master 0.8, music 0.6, SFX 0.9 — the shipped Canyon Dash balance. Three sliders, two multiplication sites, zero rebuilds.

key points
  • SFX gains are baked at play — streams die young, new triggers hear new levels
  • Music gain is applied live — the song never stops, no gap ever opens
  • Master mute is masterGain = 0 — one field every route already respects
  • Values persist through the Chapter 7 settings file in SDL_GetPrefPath("sable", "canyon-dash")
Deep Dive — Why per-stream gain beats a global master

Pause menus duck only music, cutscenes duck only SFX, a low-health state muffles everything — each effect is one stream's gain, not a global three systems fight over. Category buses fall out of per-stream gain for free, which is why SDL3 never needed a master dial.

10.12 — Pitch: The Frequency Ratio Dial

SDL_SetAudioStreamFrequencyRatio bends time and pitch together on a playing stream — the cheapest juice in the game, and it stacks with gain.

  • SDL_SetAudioStreamFrequencyRatio(stream, 1.25f) — consume 25% faster: pitch up, clip gets shorter
  • Power-ups: the ratio drifts toward 1.3 as the meter fills — the world speeds up with the player
  • Game over: 0.6 on the music for a slow-motion tail while the camera pulls out
  • Ratio changes are live on playing streams: no restart, no reload, no mixer
  • Musical results live around 0.5–2.0; beyond that, artifacts grow faster than the effect
Common Pitfall — Pitch is not loudness

A pitch-up reads louder because of your ears, not the mixer — and a ratio also shortens the clip, so tight effects can vanish mid-blend. Follow big pitch rides with a small gain trim and check that the release still lands where you intended.

10.13 — Pitch Bends: Ramp the Ratio

A stepped ratio sounds synthetic; a ramped one sounds alive. The bend runs from the same update loop that moves actors — thirty seconds of code for a signature feel.

key points
  • The bend is ramped interpolation — the interesting part is the curve you choose
  • Ease-out sells "charge up"; linear sells "machine"; steep exponential sells "doom"
  • One live call per bent voice per frame — pocket change next to the mix itself
  • The same trick on the music stream: a 1.0 → 0.85 dip as the timer runs out
Best Practice — Bend the music, not just the effects

A 4% ratio droop over the final seconds of a level builds tension with zero new assets. Players feel it long before they can name it — and that unnameable feeling is exactly what polish is.

10.14 — Panning Without a Mixer

A carrot pinging off-screen left should come from the left. SDL3 has no pan parameter — a stream's gain scales every channel it produces — but two small data tricks build stereo placement anyway.

  • No pan dial exists: SDL_SetAudioStreamGain scales all channels of its stream equally
  • Trick one — in-place mixing: bake L/R into a stereo buffer at trigger; one stream, pan frozen at fire time
  • Trick two — the split: L-only and R-only stereo buffers on two streams; gains steer, pan moves live
  • The split costs 4× the mono bytes and two voice slots — spend it only on sounds that must track
  • Listener-relative X feeds either trick every frame — the Camera2D follow habit, in audio
Deep Dive — Constant-power panning

L = cos(θ), R = sin(θ) keeps total energy flat as a sound sweeps the stereo field. A naive linear crossfade dips audibly in the middle — one trig pair and the mix stays loud edge to edge. The same law drives physical mixing consoles.

10.15 — Panning a Voice: The Split in Code

The split in code: interleave one mono clip into L-only and R-only stereo buffers, bind two streams, then steer with gains — data laid out once, position updated live.

key points
  • The buffers isolate the sides; the gains move the sound — data untouched after trigger
  • A panned voice occupies two of the 16 stream slots — budget accordingly
  • For short blips, bake instead: one stereo buffer, one stream, pan fixed at fire time
  • setPan runs from the update loop with the same listener-relative X as Chapter 3's camera
Performance Tip — The split does not scale

One interleave pass and 4× the mono bytes is trivial for a handful of positional sounds, ruinous for hundreds. Spatial audio at scale is middleware territory — a Chapter 11-sized dependency decision, not a hand-rolled trick stretched past its design.

10.16 — Recording: Microphones Are Devices Too

The same logical-device model reads audio as easily as it plays it: enumerate, open, bind, pull. Games use it sparingly — but it is one API away, not one engine away.

  • SDL_GetAudioRecordingDevices(&count) — a snapshot list of microphones
  • Open the default with SDL_AUDIO_DEVICE_DEFAULT_RECORDING, or a chosen id from that list
  • Recording is pulled: bind a stream, drain it with SDL_GetAudioStreamData
  • Use cases: voice annotations on save files, loopback visualizers, audio-reactive menus
  • Mobile and web gate it behind permission prompts — ask early, fail soft
Common Pitfall — The queue nobody drains

Recording hardware buffers whether you read or not: skip the drain and the stream's queue grows silently — megabytes per minute of RAM held for nothing. Pull every frame you consume, or pause the device when you do not.

10.17 — Record, Write, Replay

A complete toy: open the mic, pull raw PCM into a file on a steady cadence, close it — then replay the memo through the default playback device.

key points
  • Same model, opposite direction: the device feeds the stream, main pulls
  • Raw PCM files carry no header — the spec must live next to the bytes or replay guesses
  • A steady pull cadence is the whole engineering: queue growth is the only failure mode
  • A real feature writes into SDL_GetPrefPath and asks permission before opening
Common Pitfall — Raw PCM is not a WAV

SDL_LoadWAV expects a RIFF header your raw capture does not have. Store the spec beside the file, or write the 44-byte header yourself — replaying bytes at the wrong rate is the chipmunk-voice bug, and it is fully preventable.

10.18 — Beyond Push: Device Streams and Taps

When the simple model runs out, SDL3 meets you halfway: one call opens a device with a callback attached, and streams stay inspectable, clearable and flushable at runtime.

  • SDL_OpenAudioDeviceStream(SDL_AUDIO_DEVICE_DEFAULT_PLAYBACK, &spec, callback, userdata) — device and stream in one call
  • Pass a NULL callback and it behaves like the push model — the door opens both ways
  • A real callback runs on SDL's audio thread: fill the buffer, return, never block
  • Stream surgery on live audio: inspect with SDL_GetAudioStreamQueued, flush with SDL_ClearAudioStream
  • Filters and taps are your code between decode and push — SDL has no DSP graph, by design
Common Pitfall — The real-time thread rules

The audio callback is a real-time thread: no allocations, no locks, no file IO, no SDL_Log. One slow callback and the audience hears the glitch forever. That is precisely why this chapter lives in the push model and visits the callback only when a design truly demands it.

10.19 — Procedural Audio: Synthesize, Do Not Ship Files

Every clip so far came from a file. The last one comes from math: oscillators and envelopes synthesize chiptune-grade audio at boot with zero assets on disk.

  • An oscillator is the raw wave: square for punch, triangle for soft, noise for texture
  • An ADSR envelope shapes loudness over milliseconds: attack, decay, sustain, release
  • Chiptune aesthetics: hard waveforms, fast envelopes, arpeggios — the tracker heritage
  • Sable bakes blips into the SFX bank at boot: same voices, same caps, no synthesis thread
  • Full tracker support (MOD, XM) is a dependency decision — deliberately skipped for Canyon Dash
Deep Dive — The tracker heritage

FastTracker, ProTracker and the Amiga scene shipped music as data: tiny samples plus speed and arpeggio commands, replayed by a tracker. Every piece of that machine is already in this chapter — buffers, streams, gain, ratio. Building one is a weekend project, not a rewrite.

10.20 — Tiny Synth: A Pickup Blip from Math

Roughly forty lines replace a WAV: a square wave sweeps up an octave while an ADSR envelope snaps it off — pushed through the same voice path as any loaded clip.

key points
  • The blip lands in the same bank as loaded WAVs — voices, caps and gains do not care
  • ±12000 is ~37% of full scale: loud, with headroom for a pile of simultaneous voices
  • Piecewise-linear envelopes read clearly; exponential curves are the homework
  • Boot-time synthesis: bake once, play forever — zero runtime cost
Best Practice — Level discipline applies to math too

SDL clamps the mixed sum rather than letting it wrap, but a bank full of full-scale squares still saturates into mush. Pick peaks with the voice budget in mind — synthesized clips deserve the same mastering care as recorded ones.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 10 Recap

  • One logical device, many SDL_AudioStreams — SDL converts and mixes; we never wrote a mixer
  • SFX: SDL_LoadWAV at boot, one stream per trigger, a 16-voice cap with a deliberate drop policy
  • Music: MusicStreamer feeds a long-lived stream on a worker — watch SDL_GetAudioStreamQueued
  • Gain, frequency ratio and panning are per-stream and live — three sliders, two multiplies
  • Recording, device-stream callbacks and boot-time synthesis complete the AudioManager
Chapter 11 — Advanced Programming Techniques
Ch 11Chapter 11

Advanced Programming Techniques

01Why physics: rotation, stacking, emergent gameplay
02Rigid bodies, the simulation pipeline, body types
03Box2D v3 in Sable: worlds, bodies, shapes, transforms
04Contact events, collision filtering, sensor triggers
05Spawners, goal zones and level progression
06Shading languages and the SDL_GPU pipeline
07Post-processing, tilt input, virtual joysticks

11.1 — Why a Physics Engine at All

Chapter 6 answered "do these two AABBs overlap?" — a real physics engine answers "what happens next?" This chapter earns its weight by what it gives back for free.

  • Hand-rolled AABB collision answers a yes/no question — nothing about rotation, mass or settling
  • Rotation: tumbling crates and tipped towers need oriented boxes, not axis-aligned ones
  • Stacking: objects that settle, jostle and topple require an iterative constraint solver, not intersection tests
  • Restitution and friction: material behavior without 400 lines of per-object special cases
  • Emergent gameplay: designers place one crate; players invent towers, dominoes and chain reactions
  • When NOT to bother: tile-precise platformers, lockstep determinism requirements, tiny budgets — Ch 6 still runs our tile grid
Deep Dive — The physics dividend

The payoff is not fewer lines of code — it is behaviors you never specified. A crate bridge that sags, a hazard that ricochets: physics converts level design into systems that surprise even you. Budget an afternoon to just drop things and watch.

11.2 — Rigid Bodies: Mass, Force, Torque

A rigid body is six numbers and two laws: mass resists force, rotational inertia resists torque. Understanding the model tells you why the solver behaves the way it does.

  • State: position, angle, linear velocity, angular velocity — plus mass and 2D rotational inertia
  • Forces accumulate into linear acceleration (F = ma); torques spin the body around its center
  • An impulse is an instant velocity change: jumps, one-shot kicks, and every contact resolution
  • Integration: semi-implicit Euler — advance velocity first, then position with the new velocity
  • Order matters: velocity-first is why engine stacks settle instead of slowly exploding
  • Determinism: same inputs plus same dt sequence gives identical trajectories on one build — the basis of replays
Deep Dive — Semi-implicit beats explicit

Explicit Euler (x += v·dt with the old velocity) injects energy every step — springs oscillate louder, stacks self-destruct. The symplectic (semi-implicit) variant approximately conserves energy for the cost of swapping two lines. Every serious physics engine integrates velocity-first.

11.3 — The Body-Type Trichotomy

Every body in every physics world is one of exactly three kinds: static, dynamic or kinematic. Choosing wrong is the root of half of all "physics feels broken" bugs.

  • Static — never moves, infinite mass, nearly free: floors, walls, canyon geometry
  • Dynamic — a full citizen: forces, gravity, contacts, sleeping: crates, debris, the player body
  • Kinematic — moved only by your code via velocity; ignores forces and plows through dynamics: platforms, doors
  • The player is dynamic + `fixedRotation`: the controller writes velocity, so coyote time stays authored while crates still get shoved
  • Rule of thumb: static for scenery, kinematic for scripted motion, dynamic for anything the world may move
  • Ch 6 tile collision does not die: solid tile runs become static bodies at level load
Best Practice — Authored feel, physical presence

Keep jump arcs, coyote time and variable jump height in PlayerController; express them as velocity writes and one jump impulse on a dynamic body. You keep platformer feel while the world gains a body that can push crates and ride platforms.

11.4 — Static vs Dynamic vs Kinematic

Static bodies — immovable, infinite mass, the free floor under everything — are the boring third of the trichotomy. The interesting question is the two kinds that move, and who does the moving.

ADynamic — the world moves it
  • Driven by forces, impulses and gravity; contacts push back
  • Mass computed from shape area x density — geometry IS the weight
  • Tumbles, stacks, bounces, sleeps when idle
  • Canyon Dash: crates, falling rocks, the player body
  • Cost: full solver participation — budget them in level data
BKinematic — you move it
  • Driven only by velocity you set; the world integrates position
  • Immune to forces and to contact response — nothing knocks it off its path
  • Pushes dynamics it meets: riders get carried for free
  • Canyon Dash: water platforms, sliding canyon doors
  • Cost: cheaper than dynamic, still touched every step
Best Practice — Platforms ride on velocity

Move kinematic platforms with b2Body_SetLinearVelocity once, and Box2D carries riders correctly. Teleporting with b2Body_SetTransform every frame slingshots passengers — the platform arrives before its riders do, every tick.

11.5 — Shapes: Geometry and Material

Bodies own motion; shapes own everything else — geometry, weight, friction, bounce. Box2D v2 called them fixtures; v3 flattened the concept into plain shapes attached to bodies.

  • One body, many shapes: the player is a box plus a small circle sensor at the feet
  • Circle — the cheapest contact in physics: one distance test. Balls, pickups, foot sensors
  • Polygon — convex, up to 8 vertices: crates, platforms, slopes (b2MakeBox, b2CreatePolygonShape)
  • Chain — linked segments tracing canyon contours; keeps terrain seams smooth
  • Material trio per shape: density (mass), friction (grip), restitution (bounce)
  • Sensors are a shape flag, not a type: isSensor = true means events without forces
Common Pitfall — Density multiplies area

Mass is density x area, per shape. A 2x4 m platform at density 1 outweighs a 1 m crate 8:1 with identical "density". Tune through geometry first; reach for density knobs only after shapes are final — or your tuning table lies every level.

11.6 — Inside the Simulation Pipeline

Every physics step is the same four stages, in the same order. Learn the shape of the pipeline once and every engine you touch afterward looks familiar.

Each step
Broadphase
AABB tree: candidate pairs
Narrowphase
contacts: points + normals
Solver
iterative constraints
Integrate
velocity, then position
Plumbing
Fixed dt 1/60
Ch 3 accumulator
b2World_Step
8 substeps inside
Contact events
gameplay reads after

Only the solver and integrator touch velocities — everything upstream exists to make that work cheap and correct.

details
  • Broadphase — an O(n log n) sweep of AABBs discards distant pairs without touching real geometry
  • Narrowphase — exact tests: polygon clipping produces contact points and normals
  • Solver — iteratively relaxes constraints: many small corrections until velocities agree
  • Integrate — semi-implicit Euler advances velocities, then positions, then sleeps the still
  • The pipeline slots straight into Ch 3: the accumulator already produces exact 60 Hz ticks
Deep Dive — Fixed dt was a physics requirement all along

Solver stability and restitution behavior are functions of the timestep. Variable dt makes stacks pump and bounce heights drift — which is why Chapter 3 built the accumulator loop before any physics existed. b2World_Step(worldId, dt, 8) assumes you kept that promise.

11.7 — Box2D v3 vs Chipmunk vs Custom

Three credible roads: two mature C libraries and the tempting custom solver. Our pick is Box2D v3 — its C API with id handles slots into Sable without a binding layer.

ABox2D v3 — our pick
  • The reference 2D solver: substepped constraints, rock-solid stacks
  • v3 is a from-scratch C rewrite: b2* functions, id handles — no C++ glue
  • Contact events and filter bits are first-class C API
  • Long maintenance record; shipped in countless commercial games
  • Heavier core to vendor — FetchContent makes it one paragraph
BChipmunk2D — the classic alternative
  • Small, clean C library — readable end to end in an afternoon
  • Body/shape/constraint model transfers directly to Box2D knowledge
  • Simpler solver; fewer knobs for exotic stacking behavior
  • Beloved in indie and mobile scenes; permissive MIT license
  • Perfectly viable for Canyon Dash — the wrapper isolates the choice
Deep Dive — The custom road

Writing your own solver is the best physics education money cannot buy — do it once, on a weekend branch. Then ship a library: stable stacking, rotation and restitution are each research-grade problems, and players do not grade you on the engine you authored.

11.8 — Fetching Box2D v3 with CMake

Box2D v3 joins the build exactly the way SDL3 did in Chapter 1: pinned FetchContent, one link target, zero manual installs.

key points
  • v3 installs as plain C — #include <box2d/box2d.h> and link box2, no C++ runtime needed
  • Pin the tag and cache the fetch, same discipline as the SDL3 declare in Chapter 1
  • Sable wraps it as PhysicsWorld — the only file that ever includes the header
  • The engine/game boundary survives: src/game never sees a b2 name
Common Pitfall — v2 tutorials everywhere

v3 is a rewrite, not a version bump: ids replaced pointers, fixtures became shapes, b2World_Step grew a substep count. Most Box2D content online is v2 — it will mislead you silently. Bookmark the v3 migration notes before copying any sample.

11.9 — PhysicsWorld: Sable Meets Box2D

One thin wrapper class owns the world id, the unit conventions and the step. Everything else in Sable touches physics only through this face.

key points
  • WorldController::update already receives STEP = 1/60 from Ch 3 — pass it straight through
  • Meters, not pixels: a 32 px tile is 1 m — solver constants stay numerically sane
  • 8 substeps is the stacking tax; drop to 4 for sparse scenes, restore 8 when crates pile
  • b2DestroyWorld reclaims every body — no per-body cleanup loop at level end
Common Pitfall — The two y-axes

Box2D points +y up; SDL renders +y down. Convert in exactly one place — these two helpers — or crates fall upward off the top of the screen. A flip scattered across gameplay code is a flip that is wrong an odd number of times.

11.10 — Building Bodies: Ground and Crate

The two archetypes of every physics level: an immovable floor and a movable crate. Everything else in Canyon Dash is a variation on these two recipes.

key points
  • Static bodies skip the solver — level geometry should be overwhelmingly static
  • The player reuses the crate recipe plus fixedRotation = true — controller writes velocity, jump is an impulse
  • Kinematic platforms use the same b2BodyDef with b2_kinematicBody and a set velocity
  • One body can carry several shapes — the player box plus a foot-sensor circle
Common Pitfall — b2MakeBox takes HALF extents

b2MakeBox(0.5f, 0.5f) is a full 1 m crate. Double-size geometry that "somehow" overlaps its neighbors is this bug nine times out of ten — check the half-extent convention before you touch density, friction or anything fancier.

11.11 — Physics Owns Position

After each step, sprites read their bodies back. Data flows one direction per frame — the body is the truth, the sprite is a view of it.

key points
  • One-way flow: body → sprite. The sprite never writes position back into the world
  • Gameplay nudges bodies via velocity, force or impulse — b2Body_SetTransform is for teleports only
  • Per-frame teleports fight the solver: contacts flicker, resting stacks shudder
  • Player motion: b2Body_SetLinearVelocity from the authored controller; jump via b2Body_ApplyLinearImpulseToCenter
Best Practice — The single-writer rule

Exactly one system writes a body transform: the solver, plus rare explicit teleports (spawn, recycle, reset). When gameplay and physics both write position, you get rubber-banding actors and a week of "jitter" bugs nobody can reproduce.

Deep Dive — Interpolating 60 Hz onto 144 Hz

Store last and current positions per body; at render time lerp between them using the accumulator leftover as alpha (Chapter 3). The solver still ticks at 60 Hz — the display gets buttery in-between frames. This is the exact trick the 2D renderer never needed.

11.12 — Contact Events

Box2D v3 tells you what happened after it happens: step the world, then read the contact event arrays. Polling, not callbacks — and that difference shapes everything.

  • After every b2World_Step, call b2World_GetContactEvents(worldId) — it returns the fresh arrays
  • beginCount / endCount: a pair started touching, or stopped touching — that is the whole vocabulary
  • Sensors fire the same events; they simply never resolve forces while overlapping
  • Poll once per tick: after stepping, before gameplay updates read state
  • Events describe pairs of shape ids — mapping ids back to actors is our job (next slide)
  • The arrays are world-owned scratch: consume them in the same tick you read them
Common Pitfall — Begin fires once

A begin event fires when contact starts — not every frame it persists. "Still touching" is state you maintain yourself, from begin until the matching end. Gameplay that waits for repeated events is a silent bug that only shows on hill crests.

11.13 — Pumping Contacts into the EventBus

The pump translates physics vocabulary into game vocabulary: shape ids become Actor pointers, and touches become the same events Ch 6 wired everywhere else.

key points
  • bind(shapeId, actor) fills m_shapes when props spawn — the carrot and goal zone use the same call
  • One pump per tick, immediately after b2World_Step — the ordering is part of the contract
  • Damage, pickups, footsteps, goal crossings: all ride the same ContactEvent
  • Past a few hundred shapes, swap the scan for a hash on the id bits — measure first
Performance Tip — Bail early on boring pairs

In a crate avalanche, events dwarf shapes. Ground-vs-crate pairs nobody registered exit at the first nullptr check — publish only what has subscribers. The bus stays quiet and the tick stays flat, even mid-avalanche.

11.14 — Collision Filtering: Categories and Masks

Left unfiltered, everything collides with everything — spikes knock carrots off shelves, crates squash the goal flag. Sixteen bits of policy fix all of it declaratively.

  • Every shape carries a filter: categoryBits, maskBits, groupIndex
  • The AND rule: A meets B only when each mask contains the other category — both directions
  • groupIndex overrides masks: same negative never collides, same positive always does
  • 16 category bits = 16 layers; Canyon Dash needs exactly five
  • Our layers: CAT_LEVEL, CAT_PLAYER, CAT_HAZARD, CAT_PICKUP, CAT_SENSOR
  • Sensors obey the same rules — a carrot that ignores hazards costs zero extra code
Deep Dive — The two-sided test

The engine evaluates (A.maskBits & B.categoryBits) != 0 AND (B.maskBits & A.categoryBits) != 0. One-sided masks are the classic "invisible wall" bug: your side is listening, the other side never reports the pair at all.

11.15 — Wiring the Filter Bits

Filtering is three assignments at shape creation — but only if the bits live in exactly one header that everything else includes.

key points
  • One header is the single source of truth — a mask typo has exactly one place to live
  • Same negative groupIndex for entity-self pairs: a carried lantern never collides with its owner
  • The comment table is the design doc — keep it beside the bits, not in a wiki that rots
  • The player mask deliberately omits nothing — every layer legitimately interacts with it

11.16 — Sensors as Triggers

A sensor is a shape that answers "when?" instead of "stop?": full contact detection, zero physical response. Pickups, goal zones and volume triggers all hang off this one flag.

  • isSensor = true: overlap detection with no push, no forces, no blocking
  • Sensors generate the same begin/end events — the 11.13 pump needs no changes
  • The golden carrot: static body + circle sensor + pickup filter bits
  • Goal zones: invisible box sensors at level end — walk-through triggers
  • Water volumes: one sensor region drives Ch 8 splash particles and Ch 10 splash SFX
  • The rule: sensors are for when, colliding shapes are for stop
Common Pitfall — Sensors never block

Anything the player must not pass through — spikes, walls, water you drown in — is a colliding shape. A sensor exerts exactly zero force. Goal zones are meant to be walked through; the flag is a trigger, not a fence.

11.17 — The Golden Carrot as a Sensor

The collectible becomes three short functions: spawn a static sensor, guard the begin event, publish the pickup. Physics provides the "when"; the game provides the meaning.

key points
  • Static body: bobbing is a Ch 8 visual effect, not physics — the body never moves
  • A 0.5 m radius forgives near-misses — pixel-perfect pickups feel punishing, not skillful
  • CAT_PICKUP + MASK_PICKUP: crates and hazards pass straight through the carrot
  • The HUD adds 10 and plays the Ch 10 chime — it never touches a single b2 call
Common Pitfall — Destroying bodies mid-event-wave

Collecting by destroying the body leaves every other queued shapeId pointing at a freed slot — later handlers read garbage ids. Teleport it below the level instead: one b2Body_SetTransform parks it off-stage until recycling (11.20 pools exactly this way).

11.18 — Visual Physics Editors and Level Data

Typing body definitions by hand stops scaling at about ten objects. Designers need to drag, drop and tune — so physics joins the Ch 4 asset pipeline as data.

  • Dedicated physics editors (RUBE-class tools): drag bodies, joints and chains, tune friction per object, export JSON
  • Generic tile editors cover 90%: object layers carry body type, half-extents, category, sensor flag
  • The export schema is ours to define — flat, versioned, sitting beside assets/levels/level-01.json
  • Ch 4 extends, never replaces: LevelLoader gains a bodies array; AssetManager serves it like any asset
  • Level data drives spawn: "bodies": [{ "type": "static", "half": [60, 1], "at": [60, 0] }]
  • Validation belongs in a build tool: budgets, overlapping spawns, unknown categories — fail at build, not at runtime
Common Pitfall — No physics budget

Designers will happily place 5,000 dynamic bodies per level. Enforce a body-count cap in the validation tool before the 3 fps playtest teaches them — a build-time error message is a design conversation; a frame spike is a bug report against you.

11.19 — Spawning Mechanics and Body Pools

Canyon Dash drops crates into the ravine on a timer — the Cascade set piece. Doing that at 60 Hz without hitches is a pooling problem, not a spawn problem.

  • Spawn points are data: { "x": 12, "y": 9, "type": "crate", "interval": 2.5 } objects in level JSON
  • Timed spawners reuse one body template — parameters differ, the recipe does not
  • Creation cost: allocation plus broadphase insert. Destruction cost: world bookkeeping and id churn
  • Pooling: pre-create bodies at load; recycle with teleport plus velocity reset — zero allocations in the tick
  • Destroy when rare or one-off (boss debris); pool anything repeated (drops, projectiles)
  • Rule of thumb: anything spawned faster than once a second must come from a pool
Performance Tip — Create and destroy are the expensive ops

Outside the solve itself, body create/destroy is the costliest thing you can do to a Box2D world — and a burst of destroys in one tick is a visible hitch. Pool ahead at load, recycle in the tick, and spread large cleanups across frames.

11.20 — A Pooled Crate Spawner

The spawner is a timer plus a pool of pre-built bodies. Ticks only ever teleport — the garbage collector never notices a physics level exists.

key points
  • The whole tick is allocation-free: worst case is one scan over poolSize slots
  • Recycle is the sanctioned teleport: b2Body_SetTransform plus b2Body_SetLinearVelocity
  • Pool size is level data: "crateSpawners": [{ "x": 12, "y": 9, "pool": 8 }]
  • Exhaustion is silent by design — a skipped drop beats a mid-level hitch
Best Practice — Build the pool behind the loading screen

Every body creation happens during level load, where a hitch is invisible. The tick only ever teleports existing bodies. Same pattern as Ch 4 assets and Ch 10 resident SFX: pay loading costs at load, never during play.

11.21 — Goal Triggers and Win/Loss

Victory is a sensor at the end of the canyon; defeat is three hazard touches. Both arrive as the same contact events Ch 6 made first-class — the arc completes itself.

  • The win: player overlaps the flag sensor at level end → LevelComplete event
  • The loss: lives depleted — canon max 3 — hazard contacts are the same ContactEvents
  • Every condition is an event subscriber: damage, pickup, goal — one pipeline since 11.13
