  • Conditions live in level data: goal rect, lives count, optional carrot minimum
  • Screen flow: Playing → LevelComplete overlay → next level; Playing → GameOver → title
  • The Ch 6 arc completes: gameplay moments became data-driven events, not if-chains

11.22 — GoalZone and Level Complete

The flag is a box sensor wired exactly like the carrot — but what it publishes reaches the ScreenManager, and unlocks the next level before the fade finishes.

key points
  • The goal rect comes straight from level JSON — designers move the finish line, not code
  • Publish-and-return: the world may not be torn down inside the event wave
  • SDL_max on the unlock index makes replaying finished levels harmless
  • The overlay pushes through ScreenManager; the fade is a Ch 9 transition, untouched
Common Pitfall — Level swap inside the tick

LevelComplete fires deep inside the physics tick. Swapping levels right there destroys the world mid-wave and dangles every b2BodyId later handlers still hold. Publish now; let the ScreenManager act between frames — event systems are for scheduling, not doing.

11.23 — Level Progression and Unlocks

One number — the highest unlocked level — chains the campaign together. The Ch 7 save system already knows how to persist it; this chapter just decides when it changes.

  • Progress persists the instant it happens: progress.json beside Ch 7 settings.json in the pref path
  • Unlock rule: finishing level N unlocks N+1 — carrots feed score, never gates
  • The level-select screen greys locked entries; the unlocked count is the only gate
  • Chaining: ScreenManager swaps LevelScreen N → N+1 behind a Ch 9 wipe
  • Failure preserves progress: GameOver → title; unlocked levels stay unlocked
  • Three files now: settings.json, progress.json, and the pack in assets/levels/
Best Practice — Save at the moment of unlock

Write progress when the event fires, not when the player quits. Mobile platforms terminate apps without warning (Ch 2 lifecycle) — a player forgives a lost run far faster than a lost level. One 200-byte write is cheaper than the anger.

11.24 — Shading Languages: GLSL, HLSL, MSL

SDL_GPU sits above Vulkan, Metal and D3D12 — and each backend speaks a different shader dialect. Portability is a build-time decision you make before you write a single shader.

  • GLSL compiles to SPIR-V for Vulkan; HLSL to DXIL for D3D12; MSL for Metal
  • SDL_GPUShaderFormat says which byte formats a device accepts — you ship what it wants
  • The course asks for one: SDL_CreateGPUDevice(SDL_GPU_SHADERFORMAT_SPIRV, ...)
  • Strategy: author once, cross-compile offline to every format, ship artifacts beside assets
  • Per-backend sources are the maintenance trap; per-backend artifacts are the escape
  • The 2D renderer never needed this — shaders are the admission price of SDL_GPU
Deep Dive — SPIR-V as the canonical artifact

SPIR-V is an intermediate bytecode, not source: Vulkan consumes it directly, and offline toolchains translate it toward DXIL and MSL. You author one language, ship one artifact per shader per backend, and validate all of them in CI — nobody debugs GLSL on a player machine.

11.25 — The SDL_GPU Pipeline Anatomy

The mental model that makes SDL_GPU click: build immutable state once at load, record a script of work every frame, hand the whole script to the GPU in bulk.

Build once, at load
Shaders
SDL_CreateGPUShader x 2
Pipeline
SDL_CreateGPUGraphicsPipeline
Resources
buffers, textures, samplers
Record every frame
Command buffer
SDL_AcquireGPUCommandBuffer
Swapchain texture
WaitAndAcquire the target
Render pass
Begin, bind, draw, End
Fire and present
Submit
SDL_SubmitGPUCommandBuffer
GPU executes
the whole batch in order
Present
vsync makes it visible

Pipelines are frozen state bundles; command buffers are per-frame scripts. Variety costs pipelines; frequency costs nothing.

details
  • Record then submit: the CPU writes a script of GPU work, then hands it over in one batch
  • A pipeline bundles shaders, topology, blend and target formats — immutable once created
  • A render pass wraps draws that share the same targets; passes live inside command buffers
  • SDL_WaitAndAcquireGPUSwapchainTexture brings in the frame destination before the pass
  • Submit fires the batch — the CPU is free until it actually needs GPU results
  • Contrast with Ch 3: same discipline as the 2D renderer, but we now own the state machine
Performance Tip — Sort by pipeline

Every pipeline switch rebinds a bundle of GPU state. The 2D renderer batched this silently; in SDL_GPU it is your job. Sort draws so pipeline binds are rare — quad, then sprites, then the post pass, never interleaved.

11.26 — Creating a Pipeline (Sketch)

Two creation calls carry the whole pattern: compile shaders to artifacts, then freeze them plus all fixed state into one pipeline object. Everything else is filling forms.

key points
  • Creation order mirrors dependency: shaders exist before the pipeline that consumes them
  • Bytecode arrives from the asset pipeline — AssetManager loads it like any other file
  • The elided fields are the tuning surface: blend for the vignette, topology for the quad
  • One pipeline per shader pair plus state combo — count them, budget them, name them
Common Pitfall — Pipelines built per frame

The classic SDL_GPU porting bug: constructing pipelines inside the render loop. Creation validates state and talks to the driver — it is a loading-screen activity. A frame that creates pipelines is a frame that hitches; build at load, bind per pass.

11.27 — A Fragment Filter in GLSL

The entire post-process is one fragment shader over one fullscreen quad: sample the scene, compute grayscale, multiply a vignette, done.

key points
  • Input is one texture sample at vUV — the whole scene, already rendered off-screen
  • The luma weights come from color science: green dominates perceived brightness
  • Vignette math is squared distance from center, clamped — no branches, no costs
  • Constants are knobs: hoist 0.9 into a uniform to animate a low-health pulse
  • The same source cross-compiles to SPIR-V, DXIL and MSL artifacts at build time
Best Practice — Compile offline, ship artifacts

Never compile GLSL at load time. Offline builds validate once in CI and fail loudly where you can fix them; runtime compiles fail on player machines with drivers you have never seen. Shader source lives in the repo; shader bytecode ships with the game.

11.28 — Applying Post-Processing

The Ch 9 pattern transfers wholesale: render the world into an offscreen target, run an effect pass over it, present the result. Only the vocabulary changes — render targets become GPU textures.

  • Ch 9 skill reused conceptually: scene → offscreen target → effect pass → screen
  • In SDL_GPU the scene lands in an SDL_GPUTexture; the filter pass samples it as uScene
  • The fullscreen-quad trick: one quad, UVs 0..1 — the fragment shader does all the work
  • Chain passes for bloom: bright-pass target → blur target → combine onto the screen
  • Feedback loops: sample last frame while writing this one — trails, heat haze, motion blur
  • 2D-renderer ceiling: SDL_SetTextureColorMod tints; real filters require SDL_GPU
Common Pitfall — Two texture worlds, no bridge

An SDL_Texture from the 2D renderer and an SDL_GPUTexture from SDL_GPU live in different worlds — there is no call that converts one into the other. Decide your rendering path before adding post-processing; retrofitting a hybrid mid-project is a rewrite.

11.29 — Tilt Input: The Sensor API

SDL3 treats accelerometers and gyroscopes like any other device: init, enumerate, open, read. Tilt steering is one small filter away from the raw samples.

  • Pass SDL_InitSensor at startup — sensors are opt-in like gamepads
  • Enumerate with SDL_GetSensors(&count), open with SDL_OpenSensor(id)
  • Two read paths: SDL_EVENT_SENSOR_UPDATE events, or poll SDL_GetSensorData each tick
  • SDL_SENSOR_ACCEL streams gravity plus motion in m/s² — tilt is the gravity direction
  • Handheld design: tilt steering, large touch targets, short sessions, one-thumb reach
  • SDL_SENSOR_GYRO tracks rotation for aiming — out of scope for Canyon Dash
Common Pitfall — Accelerometer noise as gameplay

Accelerometers report hand tremor as physics. Without a dead zone plus exponential smoothing (alpha around 0.1-0.2), a tilt-controlled cart jitters at rest and drifts on a bus. Recalibrate the neutral pose when the level starts — players do not hold devices the way you hold yours.

Best Practice — Gate the option on device presence

Desktops enumerate zero sensors. Hide the tilt option when the sensor list is empty rather than shipping a control scheme that silently does nothing — an absent feature reads as polish; a dead one reads as a bug.

11.30 — Virtual Joysticks and Gestures

Touch screens have no sticks — so we synthesize them. The Ch 2 input abstraction earns its keep: gameplay reads virtual axes and never learns which device filled them.

  • Ch 2 InputManager funnels every device into one queue — virtual devices join right there
  • Stick: finger-down anchors the base; the drag delta, clamped to a radius, becomes moveX/moveY
  • Dead zone: ignore the inner 15% of the radius — the same rule as gamepad sticks
  • Swipe: down-point to up-point under 350 ms and past a distance threshold → jump or dash
  • Pinch: two-finger distance ratio drives Camera2D zoom — the Ch 3 camera already lerps it
  • Gameplay reads axes and gestures — never a raw event.tfinger coordinate
Best Practice — The abstraction is the feature

Whether moveX came from keys, a gamepad axis or a virtual stick is an InputManager implementation detail. That single boundary is what lets Canyon Dash ship desktop, handheld and TV builds from one gameplay codebase — design it before you need it.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 11 Recap

  • Physics earns its keep: rotation, stacking, restitution — emergent behavior far beyond AABB tests
  • Box2D v3: a C API of ids and handles; static/dynamic/kinematic bodies; shapes carry geometry and material
  • Ch 3 fixed ticks feed b2World_Step; sprites read transforms back — physics owns position
  • Contact events plus filter bits drive pickups, hazards and goal zones through the EventBus
  • Spawners pool bodies at load; ScreenManager chains unlocked levels with Ch 7 saves
  • SDL_GPU: pipelines, passes, offline-compiled GLSL filters; sensors and virtual sticks widen input
Chapter 12 — Animations
Ch 12Chapter 12

Animations

01Animation as data: the declarative turn away from per-frame busywork
02TweenEngine: pooled actions, lifecycle, completion callbacks
03The action vocabulary: tweens, Sequence, Parallel, Delay, Repeat
04Easing curves from Chapter 8 plugged into every tween
05Juice: menu entrances, carrot pickup ceremony, button reflexes
06Sprite-sheet clips and the SpriteAnimator player
07Play modes and the player state machine: idle, run, jump, fall
08Screen feel: shake, score roll-ups, and the classic pitfalls

12.1 — Animation as Data

Hand-rolled timers work — once. The moment two effects overlap, per-frame busywork becomes a phase enum you debug forever. The declarative turn: describe the outcome, let the engine produce the frames.

  • Imperative habit: a t counter, an if (t < 0.3f) branch, copy-pasted into every actor that ever faded
  • Declarative turn: move here in 0.3 s, easeOutQuad — one sentence of intent, zero per-frame code
  • An action is a small object that advances itself by dt and reports when it is done
  • Tweens, sprite clips, particle bursts (Ch 8) — one shape: state plus update(dt)
  • Composition is the payoff: Sequence(Parallel(a, b), c) turns choreography into data
  • Transitions (Ch 9) move screens between each other; this chapter animates everything inside them
Deep Dive — Actions are a tiny language

Delay, tween, sequence, parallel, repeat: five combinators with names, nested like expressions. Once the vocabulary exists, choreography reads like code and tunes like data — retiming a menu becomes editing constants, not rewriting logic.

12.2 — TweenEngine: One Manager, Every Action

One manager owns every running action in the game: it ticks them in spawn order, fires completions after the walk, and returns the dead to a pool. Spawners only describe.

Spawned by
Actor
pickup ceremony
Screen
menu entrance
Hud
score chase
Button
hover reflexes
TweenEngine
Active list
spawn order · stable
Free pool
recycled actions
Completion queue
onDone · post-tick
Action types
Tween
value A → B, eased
Sequence
children in order
Parallel
children together
Delay · Repeat
time itself

Spawners describe; the engine iterates. One clock, one pool, zero allocations mid-frame.

details
  • Actors, screens, widgets spawn actions; the engine alone ticks them — one clock for the whole game
  • Pooled actions are re-initialized in place: spawning is a pointer pop, never a mid-frame heap hit
  • Stable spawn order means deterministic playback — same inputs, same motion, every run
  • Completion callbacks queue up and fire after the tick, so cascades can kill and spawn safely
Performance Tip — Pool or perish

A 60 Hz game allocating two action objects per pickup chews the heap all level long — allocator spikes, cache misses, fragmentation. The pool makes spawning a pop and completion a splice: the same GC-free discipline Chapter 8 gave particles, aimed at time.

12.3 — TweenAction and the Engine Tick

The whole system rests on one contract: an action advances by dt and says when it is finished. The engine owns starting, ticking, completing, and recycling — nothing else ever touches time.

key points
  • update(dt) returns true exactly once — finishing is the engine's business, not the action's
  • The engine starts, ticks, completes, retires — actions never reach back into the engine
  • onDone fires after the walk: callbacks may spawn, kill, or remove actors mid-cascade
  • retire() splices and recycle()s the action into the pool — the heap is never involved
  • killAll(owner) flags, never splices — safe to call from inside any callback
Best Practice — One clock, zero exceptions

The moment an actor ticks its own tween inside Actor::update, the game has two timelines — and one of them lies during pauses and hitches. GameApp calls TweenEngine::update once per frame, after the controller and before the renderer, and that is the only place time advances.

12.4 — The Movement Tween

The canonical action: glide a value from where it is to where it should be, shaped by an easing curve. Every other tween in this chapter is this class pointed at something else.

key points
  • The tween writes through a pointer — the owner never knows an animation is running
  • start() snapshots the live value at first tick, so spawn-time and tick-time can differ safely
  • Snap to target on the last tick: eased curves promise ease(1) == 1, floating point does not
  • EasingFn is a plain function pointer — every Ch 8 curve slots in without adaptation
  • ScaleTo is this same class pointed at one float — write the lerp once, reuse forever
  • Animate presentation fields (fx->pos, fx->scale), never physics state — 12.30 expands
Common Pitfall — The zero-second tween

u = m_t / m_dur with m_dur == 0 yields 0/0, which is NaN — and every NaN comparison is false, so the finish test never fires and the action ticks forever. Validate durations at spawn: treat zero and negative as instant, and log loudly in dev builds.

12.5 — The Alpha Fade Tween

Fades are the most-used tween in any UI-heavy game. Sable drives SDL_SetTextureAlphaMod from one small action — with two hard rules about who owns the texture and who restores it.

key points
  • The mod is texture-wide state: every draw of that texture uses it until someone changes it
  • The caller supplies from — pooled actions stay pure data, and current alpha is never a guess
  • A faded-out texture must be restored to 255 before anyone reuses it — pools reset alpha on release
  • Fades land on dedicated textures (logos, ghosts, glows) — read the callout before touching the atlas
Common Pitfall — Fading the atlas

Canyon Dash packs tiles, player, pickups and HUD into one atlas (Ch 4). SDL_SetTextureAlphaMod on it fades the entire screen. Fade only textures with a single visible user — or first blit the region into its own small target texture, the ghost trick on 12.13.

12.6 — Sequence: Actions in Order

Sequencing is an index pointer and a while loop. The subtlety is ownership: children belong to the sequence, and the engine stops seeing them the moment they are adopted.

key points
  • The index pointer is the state — "3 of 5" is all a sequence remembers
  • Children belong to the sequence: the parent wakes them, ticks them, recycles them
  • The engine never sees the children — engine.sequence() adopts them out of the active list
  • Zero-duration children chain within one tick — no frame of dead air between steps
Best Practice — Compose at spawn

Build the entire chain once, when the effect begins. Per-frame branching about "what happens next" is exactly the hand-coded habit this system exists to retire — if an if-statement is deciding the future, a Sequence should be holding it instead.

12.7 — Parallel: Actions Together

The ensemble action: every child receives the same dt, and the parallel survives until the last one finishes. Fast children simply ride along as passengers.

key points
  • Every child receives the same dt — the ensemble ages together, frame for frame
  • Done when all children are done — a slow fade holds the fastest pop captive, on purpose
  • Finished children ride along as passengers: no removal, no reshuffling, no early teardown
  • Stagger is built, not special-cased: Sequence(Delay, X) inside a Parallel is a late joiner
Deep Dive — The stagger identity

A stagger is arithmetic, not a feature: button i begins at i × 60 ms. Express that as one Parallel of small Sequences, each opening with its own Delay, and the engine needs no stagger concept at all — composition covers it. 12.11 cashes this identity in for an entire menu.

12.8 — Delay, Repeat, Forever

Three primitives that build every timeline shape you will ever need: pure waiting, bounded repetition, and the endless loop that keeps menus breathing until killed.

key points
  • Delay is nothing but time — the pause that turns two tweens into choreography
  • Repeat(child, n) re-runs one pooled child: recycle, start, go — no allocation between passes
  • Zero or negative count is forever: bobbing glints, pulsing prompts — until killAll retires them
  • Nest freely: Repeat(Sequence(up, down), -1) is a heartbeat in one expression
  • One restart per tick, maximum: a zero-length child can never wedge the loop

12.9 — Easing: Curves with Intent

Chapter 8 built the curve library; tweens are its best customer. The curve is the personality the motion gets — pick it by intent, apply it consistently.

  • A tween is from + (to - from) × ease(u) — the curve shapes the middle; the endpoints stay exact
  • easeOutQuad for motion: camera nudges, pickups, counters — fast start, gentle settle
  • easeOutBack for UI: the few-percent overshoot reads as playful, physical arrival
  • easeInOutCubic for ceremony: slides and wipes — departures and arrivals that both earn attention
  • Linear is not neutral — it reads mechanical; save it for lasers and conveyor belts
  • Consistency across the game is what reads as polish — a per-feature zoo of curves reads as noise
Best Practice — One library, every consumer

Particles (Ch 8), tweens, camera smoothing, audio envelopes — all pull curves from easing.h. The day a second easing implementation appears, two systems tuned "the same" drift apart silently. One library, one vocabulary, one tuning session.

12.10 — Choreographing Menu Screens

First impressions are choreography: the logo drops with a bounce, buttons pop in staggered, the footer fades last. One entrance sequence, built once, runs on every menu entry.

  • The logo drops with easeOutBack — the overshoot reads as weight, and it lands the eye
  • Buttons pop in, staggered: about 50 ms apart, scale 0 to 1, each arriving with easeOutBack
  • The footer fades last and slowly — it is metadata, and metadata never upstages controls
  • Transitions (Ch 9) carry screens in; the entrance decorates whatever arrived
  • Keep the whole show near one second — long entrances turn first impressions into first obstacles
  • Skippable beats beautiful: an early input fast-forwards everything to its settled pose

12.11 — The Menu Entrance, One Sentence

This is the slide the whole system was built for: a four-part entrance — drop, staggered pops, late fade — expressed as a single nested composition with no timers and no phase enum.

key points
  • The whole entrance is one sentence — no timers, no phase enum, no per-frame branches
  • Stagger is arithmetic: button i starts at i × STEP — retiming the menu means editing constants
  • Buttons 2 and 3 each ride a Sequence(Delay, ScaleTo) inside the shared Parallel
  • The parallel ends when the last button lands — the footer then fades, unattended
  • The footer label fades on its own cached text texture — alpha mod is texture-wide (12.5)
  • About 1.0 s cold open to settled: DROP + 2·STEP + POP + fade
Best Practice — Gate input until it settles

A pointer-down 200 ms into the entrance hits a moving button: the click misses, the player retries, the menu feels broken. Swallow input until the sequence finishes — or fast-forward every tween to its end values on the first press. Polish that fights the player is friction.

12.12 — Collectible Juice: The Carrot Pickup

The golden carrot is worth 10 points and half a second of ceremony. Pickup juice is where Canyon Dash stops looking like a debug build and starts feeling like a game.

  • Scale pop: ×1.4 over 0.15 s with easeOutBack — the pickup announces itself
  • Rise: 24 px upward across the whole 0.40 s — motion the eye can chase to nothing
  • Fade: only the final 0.20 s — shine first, dissolve last
  • Burst: Chapter 8 golden sparkles at t=0 — the emitter manages its own lifetime
  • The 0.4 s rule: total ceremony under half a second — juice is seasoning, not the meal
  • Rules resolve instantly — score, sound, state; only the visual lingers
Performance Tip — Budget the juice

Chain a 12-carrot pickup line and dozens of ceremonies overlap: each is one pooled sequence plus one ghost texture from a small ring. Anything that allocates per pickup shows up in the frame graph at exactly the moment the game feels best — pool it all upfront.

12.13 — The Pickup Animation, End to End

Chapter 8 wired carrot.picked to a spark burst; this slide grows that same subscription into the full farewell — a tiny visual entity, a ghost texture, and one nested composition.

key points
  • The carrot actor died the tick it published (Ch 6) — the ceremony is a separate visual entity
  • Sound, burst, and ceremony all land at t=0 in one subscription — a single event, three reactions
  • The ghost blit isolates the fade — one pooled 32×32 target; the pool restores alpha on release
  • PickupFx carries pos and scale only: presentation fields, never simulation state (12.30)
  • Every number is a constant away from retuning: 0.40 s total, 24 px rise, 1.4× pop
Deep Dive — The one allocation we keep

The completion lambda heap-allocates its captures — one small block per pickup, by design. If profiles ever disagree, swap std::function for a typed slot (function pointer plus userdata) and the pool discipline is whole again.

12.14 — Character State Animations

Tweens animate values; characters animate themselves. A small state machine decides which sprite clip is playing — the bridge between Chapter 6's controller and the renderer.

  • The controller already computes the facts — grounded, velocity, input; animation just reads them
  • Four states ship: idle, run, jump, fall — hurt arrives as the one-shot lockout example
  • Tweens still handle everything around the frames: landing squash, hurt tint, pickup pops
  • One SpriteAnimator per actor: it owns the current clip and its clock, nothing else
  • Transitions are guards over live state — an animation never drives gameplay, ever
  • Same inputs, same state sequence, same frames: the animator stays replay-friendly (Ch 3)

12.15 — Sprite Sheets: Clips from the Atlas

Chapter 4 packed the sprites; now we name what is inside. A clip is a list of atlas region indices plus how long each frame holds — that is all an animation is.

  • Frames are sub-rectangles of the atlas: SDL_FRect source rects in atlas pixel space
  • A clip = frames[] + per-frame duration: 8 run frames at 80 ms is a 0.64 s cycle
  • Canyon Dash frame budgets: idle 4, run 8, jump 3, fall 2 — drawn into the 32 px grid
  • Uneven durations carry personality: contact frames hold; passing frames flash by
  • The same data plays in every mode — Normal, Loop, Ping-Pong, Reversed are playback, not art
Deep Dive — Tight packing, clean sampling

Source rects are floats, so the packer can place frames anywhere — but linear filtering samples beyond rect edges when a sprite scales or rotates. The one-pixel gutter between regions is what keeps neighboring sprites from bleeding in; the clip data never needs to know it exists.

12.16 — The Animation Class

A clip is deliberately dumb: borrowed region pointers, durations, a play mode, and nothing else. It never updates itself — playback is the animator's job, next slide.

key points
  • Pure data: an Animation never updates itself — playback belongs to SpriteAnimator
  • Frames borrow SpriteRegion pointers: the Atlas map is node-based, stable for the process lifetime
  • Fixed MAX_FRAMES array: clips are built at load, iterated at play — no heap in the hot path
  • Per-frame durations — not one fps — let art hold contact frames and flash passing ones
  • Build once at load, then read-only: every critter of a kind shares one clip forever

12.17 — SpriteAnimator: The Clock and the Frame

The animator accumulates time into the clip and consumes frame durations until the clock fits. A hiccup dt skips ahead honestly — animations never catch up by stalling the game.

key points
  • Accumulate, then subtract durations — a long dt skips ahead honestly instead of stalling the loop
  • play() is idempotent per clip: re-calling it every tick (the lazy pattern) changes nothing
  • Frame changes are an index bump — the common tick is one add, one compare, one subtract
  • Paused animators still answer currentRegion(): pause is display state, not destruction
  • Guard at build time: every duration > 0, or the consume loop spins forever
Performance Tip — One clock per actor, and it is nearly free

The steady-state tick of an animator is three arithmetic ops and a branch; a frame change adds an index bump and a mode switch. Ten thousand animators cost less than one particle emitter — spend the optimization budget on draw batching and text, not here.

12.18 — Naming Regions in the Packed Atlas

The atlas answers where every sprite lives; region names now answer which sprites belong together. One naming convention turns the atlas into an animation library.

  • Convention: player_run_00 through player_run_07 — <actor>_<clip>_<frame>
  • Zero-padded two digits: lexicographic order equals numeric order — 10 never sorts before 2
  • The Atlas (Ch 4) maps names to regions via find(); a prefix scan collects a clip in one pass
  • Durations ride the data too: a sidecar JSON per atlas, or one duration per clip
  • Names are the contract between art and code — pixel rects never appear in source
Common Pitfall — Names that rot

Art exports drift: "run (1).png", "run_final2.png", a renamed "sprint_00". The prefix scan silently finds fewer frames — the run cycle plays at half length and nobody gets an error. Validate clip lengths at load time and log every short or empty scan.

12.19 — Building Clips from Region Names

Scan, sort, emit: three plain steps at load time. The loader re-reads Chapter 4's plaintext region table, sorts the matches, and resolves each through the same find() the renderer uses.

key points
  • Load-time work, once per clip — play-time never scans, sorts, or string-matches
  • The loader re-reads the plaintext table from Ch 4 — the packer wrote it; animation data rides the same contract
  • Insertion sort is correct here: n is the frame count (≤16), not the region count
  • startsWith is literal — player_run also grabs player_run_fast; pass player_run_ or name clips uniquely
  • Return by value: the caller stores the clip in the animation library beside the Atlas

12.20 — Play Modes: What Each Is For

Same clip data, four playbacks. The mode is a readability decision: what does the eye need to believe the motion?

  • Normal — run once, hold the last frame: one-shots like hurt, and attack later
  • Loop — wrap to frame 0: idle, run, spinning pickups — cycles with no seams
  • Ping-pong — bounce between the ends: glints, wobbles, wings — no return-trip art
  • Reversed — play backward: unwinds and dissolves; reuses a squash as a stretch
  • A loop is only a loop if the last and first frames read as neighbors
  • Mode is clip data, not actor code — every user of the clip shares the shipped setting

12.21 — Animation Play Modes: Loop vs Ping-Pong

Two ways to play a cycle, and a rule for choosing: match the mode to the seam. Normal and Reversed live outside this axis — they are one-shots that finish and hold.

ALoop — wrap around
  • Last frame jumps straight to frame 0 — no direction state at all
  • For seamless cycles: run, idle, spinning pickups
  • Cheapest wrap in code: (frame + 1) % count
  • Demands seam-free art: the last and first frames must read as neighbors
  • Reversed is its sibling: walks the indices down, finishes, holds
BPing-pong — bounce between ends
  • Direction flips at both ends — there is no wrap at all
  • For clips whose ends differ: wings up vs wings down, glint left vs right
  • No return-trip art: the same frames play backward for free
  • Watch the turnaround: a naive bounce dwells on the end frames (12.22)
  • Normal stays outside this axis: one-shots finish and hold their last frame
Best Practice — Let the seam decide

If the first and last frames are near-twins, loop — the wrap is invisible. If they are opposites, ping-pong — a wrap would snap. The clip is geometry; it already knows the answer. Taste only breaks ties.

12.22 — Implementing the Play Modes

Four modes, one switch, zero math libraries. The only subtlety is ping-pong: flip direction and step inward in the same tick, so end frames never dwell twice.

key points
  • Ping-pong flips direction and steps away in the same tick — end frames never dwell twice
  • A one-frame clip is static: guard it, or the bounce walks straight off the array
  • Normal and Reversed raise m_finished; looping modes never do
  • All of ping-pong is one signed int: m_dir, +1 rising, −1 falling
  • No allocations, no iterators, no math library — indices and comparisons only
Common Pitfall — The double-dwell bounce

Ping-pong implementations that restart the return pass AT the end frame hold it for two durations — the eye reads a hitch at every turnaround. The fix is structural: flip direction and move inward in one step, as above. Rhythm problems are almost always frame-booking problems.

12.23 — The Player State Machine

Idle, run, jump, fall — four states, guarded by live simulation facts. The rule that keeps it debuggable: every edge has exactly one trigger, and air has exactly one entrance.

Grounded
idle
4 frames · loop
run
8 frames · loop
Grounded → Air
jump pressed
grounded · edge-detected
ground lost
ledge walk-off · crumble
launch pose
one visual entrance
Air
jump
3 frames · vy < 0
fall
2 frames · vy > 0
Air → Grounded
land still
→ idle
land moving
→ run

No idle→fall edge exists: every trip into the air passes through the launch pose, so the eye always sees the leaving-the-ground cue.

details
  • Guards read live facts: grounded, vel.y, |vel.x|, jump edge — never animation time
  • One entrance into air: the launch pose, whether you leapt or the ground left
  • A deadzone on |vx| stops idle/run flicker when the controller bleeds velocity
  • Landing routes by speed: still → idle, moving → run — two edges, no third
  • The table stays small enough to debug at 2 AM — that is the design goal

12.24 — PlayerAnimator: State to Clip

The animator is a translator: it reads PlayerState each tick, guards through the machine, and switches clips. One-shots claim the machine until they finish — nothing interrupts a hurt clip.

key points
  • Reads PlayerState, writes pixels — the animator never writes gameplay state back
  • Lockouts: hurt (and attack, later) finish before yielding — one-shots outrank cycles
  • The just-left-ground tick always shows the launch pose — 12.23's one-entrance rule
  • Switching costs a pointer copy and a clock reset — clips themselves are shared and immutable
  • A deadzone on vel.x keeps idle and run from flickering at standstill
Common Pitfall — Animations that grab the controls

The moment a clip refuses to yield for gameplay reasons, it has become gameplay: invulnerability hidden in a hurt animation, inputs swallowed mid-attack. If the design needs those windows, put the timing in the controller where it is testable — the animator paints, it does not govern.

12.25 — Blending vs Snapping

3D engines blend poses; sprite games snap frames. At 60 Hz with short cycles, snapping reads as crisp — blending is a discretionary spend.

  • Snapping: the new clip starts at frame 0 the tick the state flips — deterministic, free
  • A real crossfade is two draws with two alphas for the whole blend duration
  • Atlas sprites need the ghost trick (12.13) to crossfade — one texture per layer
  • Spend blends on big shifts only: death, transformations — 100-150 ms, then never again
  • Canyon Dash snaps everywhere; the tween layer (squash, tint) supplies the softness
  • When a snap reads harsh, first try a one-frame overlap — a shared frame costs nothing
Deep Dive — Why 3D blends and 2D snaps

A 3D pose is continuous — joint angles interpolate into plausible in-between poses. Two sprite frames are just two images; there is no pose between them, so a "blend" is really a double-draw dissolve. The eye forgives a hard snap far more readily than a mushy dissolve — spend accordingly.

12.26 — UI Button Micro-Interactions

Chapter 7 gave buttons states; this chapter gives them reflexes. Hover grow, press shrink, focus glow — the whole budget is about 100 ms per gesture.

  • Hover: scale to 1.06 over ~100 ms, easeOutQuad — the interface says "I see you"
  • Press: scale to 0.94 over ~60 ms, then spring back on release
  • Focus: the gamepad glow ring fades in over 120 ms — Chapter 7 focus state gets a visual voice
  • The budget rule: ~100 ms — slower micro-interactions read as lag, not polish
  • Interrupts must reverse from the current value — never restart from nominal 1.0
  • Three tweens serve every button on every screen: the data is written once

12.27 — Button Hover and Press Tweens

Hooking Chapter 7 widget states into the TweenEngine is two small hooks and one retarget helper. The disciplines: kill the previous tween before spawning, and scale the art around its center while the hit rect never moves.

key points
  • Retargeting is free: start() captures the live value, so a press mid-grow reverses smoothly
  • Kill before spawn — two live tweens writing one scale is a strobe, not an animation
  • Press-release returns to 1.06 while hovered, 1.00 otherwise — the state ladder decides
  • Scale anchors at the center; the hit rect never scales — the 44 px floor stays honest
  • The glow sprite is its own texture under the crisp ring — the alpha mod law from 12.5

12.28 — Game-Screen Animations

The last layer of feel is the screen itself: shake on damage, counters that roll, banners that slide — all event-driven, all on the one TweenEngine.

  • Screen shake: a trauma value tweens 1→0 over ~0.25 s; the renderer adds decaying noise offsets to the camera
  • Shake lives in the render transform only — the simulation, the camera state, and replays never move
  • Counter roll-ups: the HUD score chases its truth — digits that teleport read as errors (12.29)
  • Banner slides: level-start banner, checkpoint toast — one Sequence(move, fade) each
  • Event-driven, never polled: the controller emits damage, score, checkpoint; screens translate to tweens
  • Sound lands in the same tick as the motion (Ch 10) — cohesion is half the felt impact

12.29 — The Score Counter Roll-Up

Not every animation is a tween. The display score is an open-ended chase — no fixed end pose — so it converges with Chapter 8's damp while the Chapter 5 text cache re-renders only when the digits change.

key points
  • The display value is a converging lie: truth is m_realScore; shown is the chase
  • Open-ended chases want damp() — a bounded tween needs a destination nobody knows
  • Stiffness 12 reads eager then calm — 8.19's table: 6 camera, 12 UI, 2 ambient drift
  • Chained carrots stack cleanly: the chase just keeps converging — no restarts, no snapping
  • The 5.13 cache survives intact: TTF runs only when the rounded digits change
Performance Tip — Roll the number, not the texture

A chase changes its float every tick, but only digit changes should ever reach TTF. Gate the re-render on the rounded value, not the raw one — otherwise the roll-up multiplies the classic 5.13 stall by exactly the frames it was supposed to feel good on.

12.30 — Pitfalls: Where Animation Systems Die

Four traps catch nearly every young animation system. Each has a mechanical fix — and each fix is cheaper than the bug it prevents.

  • Per-frame allocation: spawning actions with new mid-frame — pools (12.2) or frame-time sawtooth
  • Units: SDL_GetTicksNS() is nanoseconds; dt and durations are seconds — convert once, in the loop (Ch 3)
  • Animating gameplay state: a tween writing the physics position corrupts tests and replays — animate visual fields only
  • Zombie tweens: actor dies mid-ceremony, the callback fires into freed memory — killAll(owner) in every dispose
  • Audit trick: watch activeCount() across a level — a count that only grows is a leak in disguise
Best Practice — Dispose is symmetric

Whatever spawns must retire: actors kill their tweens, screens kill their sequences, buttons kill their hover. Make killAll(owner) the first line of every dispose path and zombie callbacks become structurally impossible, not merely unlikely.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 12 Recap

  • Animation as data: small actions with update(dt), one TweenEngine, pooled — never allocated mid-frame
  • The vocabulary: MoveTo, ScaleTo, FadeTo, Sequence, Parallel, Delay, Repeat — nesting builds any choreography
  • Easing from Chapter 8: easeOutQuad for motion, easeOutBack for UI — curves are personality, applied consistently
  • Juice: 0.4 s carrot ceremony, ~1 s menu entrance, 100 ms button reflexes, rolling score counters
  • SpriteAnimator: clips of atlas regions plus durations; Normal, Loop, Ping-Pong, Reversed playback
  • Player machine: idle, run, jump, fall with guard-driven switches — one entrance into air, lockouts for one-shots
  • Animate visuals, never simulation; kill tweens on owner death; re-render text only when the digits change

06The 3D playground Chapter 14 will simulate

13.1 — From Sprites to Vertices: What Changes

Chapter 3's loop — input, update, render, present — survives untouched. What changes is everything behind the draw call: positions gain an axis, and a projection decides which pixels they become.

  • 2D: pixel rectangles at (x, y); 3D: vertices at (x, y, z) in a shared world space
  • A projection maps world to screen — perspective foreshortens, orthographic stays parallel
  • Depth replaces painter's order: a depth buffer resolves occlusion per pixel, per frame
  • Lighting stops being painted in — normals and lights compute shading in the shader
  • Engine core carries over wholesale: loop, assets, input, screens, audio — only rendering deepens
Deep Dive — The 2D renderer was 3D all along

SDL_RenderTexture internally builds a quad, applies a camera transform and rasterizes it — with an orthographic projection and no depth test. Learning 3D is learning what that convenience was quietly hiding: the pipeline is the same machine with the safeties off.

13.2 — SDL3 Options for 3D

Three viable routes from an SDL3 window into 3D. The course takes SDL_GPU for its portability and modern pipeline thinking — the other two matter the day you inherit a codebase.

ASDL_GPU — the new route
  • First-class SDL3 API over Vulkan, Metal and D3D12 — one code path
  • Modern vocabulary: command buffers, render passes, pipelines, transfer buffers
  • Portable by construction — the same promise that carried the 2D chapters
  • Cost: you own buffers, pipelines and passes — more plumbing per draw
  • Sable's 3D chapters build here; Chapter 11 adds the shader depth
BClassic GL / external renderers
  • A raw OpenGL context attached to an SDL window, then straight GL calls
  • Battle-tested and tutorial-rich; driver quality varies, macOS deprecates it
  • Third-party renderers (bgfx, Ogre, Diligent) bring full pipelines at dependency cost
  • Inherited engines and older textbooks live here — the math is identical
  • Choose it when porting, not when starting
Common Pitfall — Two backends, one window

Each backend expects to own the window's presentation: an SDL window driven through both an OpenGL context and SDL_GPU is not a hybrid, it is a support ticket. Pick one route per project and stay on it — the math transfers, the window does not.

13.3 — The Math You Actually Need

Two vector types, one matrix type and one multiplication chain carry all of basic 3D. We roll a mini library precisely so none of the pipeline stays magic.

  • Vec3 — positions, directions, normals: dot, cross, length, normalize
  • Mat4 — 4×4 transforms: rotation, scale, translation and projection in 16 floats
  • Column-major storage, the GL and SDL_GPU convention: m[col][row], vectors multiply on the right
  • The chain: model → world → view → clip — object matrix, camera, projection
  • glm is excellent; ~200 hand-written lines are better for learning — same math, no mystery
Best Practice — Roll it once, then freeze it

perspective, lookAt, multiply, transform — extend the mini library mid-project and every system subtly disagrees about conventions. The day you truly need quaternions you will know exactly why, and glm will still be there waiting.

13.4 — Mat4 Essentials: perspective, lookAt, multiply

Three functions are the spine of every 3D frame. Compact and standard — worth typing by hand once, because the rest of the chapter only ever multiplies them.

key points
  • perspective: fov + aspect + near/far — five entries, everything else stays identity
  • lookAt builds a camera basis (right, up, back) and bakes the eye offset into column 3
  • Depth maps to 0..1 on SDL_GPU backends, not GL's -1..1 — a classic port bug
  • Vulkan, Metal and D3D all agree on 0..1; only old GL disagrees — one entry changes
Common Pitfall — Transposed matrices render confetti

A row/column mix-up produces valid-looking matrices with wrong math, and no error anywhere — things rotate wrong, the camera flies. One-line sanity check: translate a point with your matrix; if the translation did not land, you stored rows where columns go.

13.5 — Lights: Ambient, Directional, Point

Three light types cover nearly every scene, and the Phong model prices each with the same three terms — ambient, diffuse, specular.

  • Ambient — a constant floor so shadows are not pure black; no direction, no distance
  • Directional — the sun: one direction for every pixel, position irrelevant
  • Point — a bulb: radiates from a position and dims with distance
  • Phong per shaded point: ambient + diffuse·max(dot(N,L),0) + specular·pow(dot(N,H),shininess)
  • The playground: one warm directional plus faint ambient — a desert reads in two lights
Deep Dive — Why the half-vector exists

H = normalize(L + V) is why Phong highlights look right: dot(N,H)^shininess approximates mirror-glare geometry without computing an actual reflection. Cheap, published 1975, and still the default in half the industry.

13.6 — Materials: What Surfaces Are Made Of

Light defines the scene; material defines what each surface does with it. One small struct per submesh drives every term the shader needs.

  • Albedo — the base color, an RGB triple lighting math never rewrites
  • Specular strength — 0 is chalk, 1 is chrome: how much glare returns
  • Shininess — highlight focus: 2 is dull plastic, 128 is polished metal
  • A submesh pairs one material with one index range — draws per material, not per triangle
  • An emissive flag for glowing carrots: skip lighting, output albedo directly
Best Practice — Materials stay plain data

Plain structs upload with a memcpy, diff for hot-reload, and serialize through the same JSON pipeline as levels. The moment materials grow virtual functions you lose all three — the same discipline Chapter 4 applied to atlas regions.

13.7 — Perspective vs Orthographic

Two projections, two feelings: perspective says "you are there", orthographic says "here is the diagram". Working games keep both in the drawer.

APerspective — FOV and depth
  • Parallel lines converge; near objects loom — the default scene camera
  • FOV is drama: 60–70° for play, wider for speed, narrow for cinematics
  • Depth is nonlinear: dense near the camera, coarse far away — z-fighting lives far
  • Chase cameras, first person, cutscene framing
  • Near/far choice drives precision — near stays as large as tolerable
BOrthographic — parallel rays
  • No convergence: size is independent of distance — no vanishing points
  • Isometric games, minimaps, level editors, HUD elements in 3D
  • Uniform depth precision along the whole range
  • Zoom is a scale, not an FOV; motion feels like sliding a map
  • Our Chapter 7 screens were effectively an ortho camera all along
Common Pitfall — The too-tiny near plane

The depth buffer spends most of its precision near the camera: a 0.01 near plane starves everything beyond arm's length and invites z-fighting at distance. Raise near until it starts clipping, then stop — that is the entire tuning procedure.

13.8 — Camera3D: The View-Projection Battery

The 3D twin of Chapter 3's Camera2D: hold the pose, derive matrices lazily, cache the product. Every draw, cull and pick this chapter makes asks this one object for one matrix.

key points
  • Same habits as Camera2D: one authoritative matrix, updated on resize, never cached at boot
  • dirty batching: 60 camera tweaks per frame still pay one multiply
  • Aspect refreshes from SDL_EVENT_WINDOW_RESIZED — Chapter 2's rule, verbatim
  • Draw, cull and pick consume viewProjection() — a single source of truth
Best Practice — Multiply once per frame

Pipelines that rebuild lookAt per draw call burn three times the math for identical pixels. The camera is a cache, not a calculator — dirty flags exist so nobody re-derives what one multiply already settled.

13.9 — Meshes: Vertices, Indices, Submeshes

A mesh is three flat arrays and a material list: interleaved vertices, an index buffer, and ranges mapping material to draw call.

  • One interleaved vertex: pos, normal, uv — 32 bytes, one shader layout for every mesh
  • Indices reference vertices: a cube is 8 positions and 36 indices, never 36 vertices
  • Sharing vertices cuts memory and upload bandwidth before culling even starts
  • A submesh is an index range + material — batching happens per submesh
  • Normals ride along because lighting needs them — they also decide flat vs smooth shading
Performance Tip — The dedup arithmetic

A naive cube is 24 vertices (per-face normals); an indexed cube is 8. A ten-thousand-prop scene saves 160,000 vertex uploads before the first cull even runs. Indices are the cheapest optimization in 3D — and OBJ gives them to you for welding.

13.10 — The Mesh Struct and Its Vertex Layout

The whole format in one screen: a POD vertex, an index vector, submesh ranges. This exact layout uploads to GPU buffers verbatim — no re-packing step.

key points
  • The 32-byte vertex keeps uploads aligned and shaders single-layout
  • Material sits in the same header — plain data, hot-reloadable, JSON-friendly
  • One mesh uploads as one vertex buffer + one index buffer regardless of materials
  • The bounding sphere is baked at load and never changes — culling's fast path
Best Practice — Freeze the vertex format early

Shaders, pipelines and the OBJ parser all bind against the vertex format: a "flexible" one is three weeks of adapter code you will eventually delete. Sable chose 32 bytes and moved on — boring is a feature.

13.11 — Instances: One Mesh, Many Transforms

A level repeats its meshes hundreds of times — rocks, cacti, crates. Instances pair a mesh with a transform, and the batch renderer culls, sorts, then draws as few times as possible.

  • Instance = mesh handle + Mat4 transform + optional material override
  • Per frame: cull against the frustum, sort by material and depth, draw per batch
  • Material sorting collapses thousands of instances into dozens of draw calls
  • True GPU instancing — one draw, transforms in a buffer — pays off past ~1000 draws
  • The 3D playground decorates with instanced rocks and glowing carrot clusters
Performance Tip — Order matters

Cull → sort → draw, never sort-then-cull: sorting the 300 survivors costs a fraction of sorting all 3000. Chapter 6's actor grid taught this exact lesson in 2D — the frustum is just the 3D camera's rectangle.

13.12 — OBJ: The Anatomy Worth Knowing

OBJ is the lingua franca of 3D tools: a text format you can read in a text editor — which makes it the one model loader worth hand-writing in a course.

  • v x y z positions; vt u v texture coordinates; vn x y z normals — three pools
  • f v/vt/vn v/vt/vn v/vt/vn — a face: three 1-based indices into those pools
  • The same position reappears with different normals — that is how sharp edges survive
  • A .mtl sidecar carries materials: albedo map, specular — the Phong inputs, file-side
  • Text parses slowly, which is fine at load time; parse once and cache your own binary
Deep Dive — The independent-pool wrinkle

OBJ's pools are independent, so a cube's 8 positions expand into 24 unique v/vt/vn triples — each corner belongs to three faces with three different normals. The parser's real job is welding those triples into the interleaved vertices of slide 13.10.

13.13 — A Mini OBJ Parser

Roughly forty lines that demystify every asset loader you will ever inherit: stream lines, tokenize, pool the three index sets, weld faces into the interleaved buffer.

key points
  • The weld map is the whole trick: repeated triples become one vertex, one index
  • Faces may carry 3 or 4 corners — this parser assumes triangulated exports
  • Materials from the .mtl sidecar become submesh ranges; scope here is one material
  • Paths still root at SDL_GetBasePath() — the same asset rules since Chapter 2
Common Pitfall — OBJ counts from 1

OBJ indices are 1-based and may be negative (relative to the last pool entry). A missed subtraction reads one entry past the pool's end: garbage that still renders, just wrong. Subtract on parse, assert the bounds — both bugs are silent otherwise.

13.14 — GLTF and FBX: The Industry Formats

OBJ is for learning; shipping needs scenes, skinned characters and animation clips. That is GLTF and FBX territory — and the moment you decide to take a dependency.

  • GLTF 2.0 — the royalty-free standard: JSON scene graph, binary buffers, skins, animations
  • FBX — the proprietary DCC exchange format: ubiquitous in studios, opaque in a hex editor
  • tinygltf: a single-header GLTF reader; assimp: dozens of formats behind one C++ API
  • The trade: a thousand lines you never write, versus a build dependency you now own
  • Sable stays hand-rolled for this course — adopt tinygltf the day skinned actors appear
Deep Dive — PBR is Phong's grown-up cousin

GLTF's PBR materials (base color, metallic, roughness) replace specular/shininess with physically grounded terms — same pipeline, better physics. The plain Material struct from slide 13.10 is the bridge: fields change, the submesh draw path does not.

13.15 — The SDL_GPU Draw Path

Every SDL_GPU frame tells the same story: upload once at load, acquire a command buffer, open a pass, bind pipeline and buffers, draw, submit. The order is the API.

  • Upload: vertex and index data travel through an SDL_GPUTransferBuffer, never straight into GPU memory
  • Frames open with SDL_AcquireGPUCommandBuffer and SDL_WaitAndAcquireGPUSwapchainTexture
  • SDL_BeginGPURenderPass opens the work; SDL_BindGPUGraphicsPipeline fixes the state
  • Buffers bind to slots; the indexed draw consumes a submesh's index range
  • Pass ends, command buffer submits — the GPU replays the recorded work asynchronously
Performance Tip — Upload once, at load

The transfer path exists so asset bytes cross the bus once. Anything genuinely per-frame — a debug line overlay, a UI quad — earns a small dynamic buffer and a comment saying why it is allowed to exist. Everything else is uploaded at load and never touched again.

13.16 — One Indexed Draw, Start to Submit

The journey of one submesh, sketch level: create the pipeline once at load, then each frame record a pass that binds buffers and draws from the index range.

key points
  • Order is the API: acquire → target → pass → bind → draw → submit — never reorder
  • Pipelines are expensive state objects: created at load, bound per pass
  • The command buffer records; the GPU replays — nothing above blocks the CPU
  • More submeshes = more draws inside one pass; material changes are small per-draw data
Common Pitfall — Reusing a submitted command buffer

Recording into an already-submitted command buffer is undefined behavior — and it compiles fine, because the handle still points at memory. Acquire fresh every frame and let SDL manage the ring; "reusing last frame's buffer" is a crash you scheduled in advance.

13.17 — Frustum Culling: Six Planes from One Matrix

The camera cannot see behind itself, yet a naive renderer transforms every mesh anyway. Six planes extracted from the view-projection matrix reject most of a level before any vertex work begins.

  • The frustum is the visible pyramid: six planes — left, right, top, bottom, near, far
  • Gribb & Hartmann: each plane is a row sum of the VP matrix — no geometry involved
  • Sphere test: signed distance from center to plane versus radius — four floats per mesh
  • AABB test: the "positive vertex" corner decides per plane — slide 13.19 implements it
  • Cull per instance or per cluster — the playground culls whole rock batches by sphere
Performance Tip — The arithmetic is lopsided

Rejecting a mesh costs a handful of float ops; drawing it costs a draw call plus thousands of GPU cycles. The cheapest triangle is the one never transformed — cull before anything else touches geometry, every frame, no exceptions.

13.18 — Extracting the Six Planes from VP

Row sums of the view-projection matrix ARE the frustum planes — the trick feels too short to work, then it works every frame for the rest of your career.

key points
  • A plane is (a, b, c, d); inside the frustum means a·x + b·y + c·z + d ≥ 0 for all six
  • Cost: 6 planes × 4 adds — once per frame, after the VP rebuild
  • The near-side plane is slightly generous with 0..1 depth — culls late, never wrongly
  • The same vp that draws the frame culls it — no second camera state to keep honest
Deep Dive — Why rows are planes

A point sits on the screen's edge exactly when its clip coordinate saturates: x equal to ±w is the border projected back into world space. Gribb & Hartmann's insight was noticing that |x| <= w is linear in the point — so its boundary can be read straight off the matrix that defines it.

13.19 — visible(): AABB vs the Frustum

The hottest function in the 3D pipeline: one box against six planes, answered in about thirty operations. Everything this chapter built funnels into this yes/no.

key points
  • The positive-vertex trick: pick the farthest corner by the sign of each normal
  • Reject on the first failed plane — most invisible objects exit at plane one
  • Answers are conservative: "certainly invisible" skips; "maybe visible" draws
  • Batch renderer flow: visible() per instance → material sort → draw per batch
Best Practice — The failure modes are asymmetric

Cull whole meshes by sphere and placed instances by AABB — the coarsest volume that never under-rejects. A wasted draw costs milliseconds; a wrongly culled mesh pops in front of the player and reads as a bug. Bias generous, always.

13.20 — Ray Casting: Clicks Become 3D Lines

The oldest 3D question: what did I just click? A ray from the camera through the pixel, tested against boxes first and triangles last.

  • Mouse to NDC: x = 2·mx/w − 1, y = 1 − 2·my/h — the viewport is a window into clip space
  • Unproject two points (z = 0 and z = 1) through the inverse VP; subtract for the ray direction
  • Ray-AABB slab test: each axis clips the ray to an interval; overlapping intervals mean a hit
  • Ray-triangle Möller–Trumbore: one determinant, barycentric coordinates — the precise contact
  • Editor: drag-select cacti. Game: tap a glowing carrot in the 3D playground to collect it
Deep Dive — Picking is rasterization in reverse

Möller–Trumbore computes the same barycentric weights the rasterizer uses to blend vertex attributes — so the hit point inherits the triangle's normal, UV and material in one multiply. Picking and drawing share the math, which is why they share the camera.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 13 Recap

  • The 2D loop survives; vertices, projection matrices and depth buffers replace sprites
  • Route: SDL_GPU — transfer-buffer uploads, one pipeline per material, one pass per frame
  • Mini math library: Vec3 and Mat4 (perspective, lookAt, multiply) feed Camera3D's cached VP
  • Meshes: interleaved 32-byte vertices, welded OBJ parsing, materials per submesh
  • Gribb & Hartmann planes and AABB tests reject the invisible; rays turn clicks into world math
Chapter 14 — Advanced Physics and Simulation
Ch 14Chapter 14

Advanced Physics and Simulation

01Why 3D physics is a different beast — and why Bullet
02Rigid bodies, inertia tensors, and motion states
03Collision shapes: primitives, hulls, triangle meshes
04Constraints as gameplay: ropes, hinges, 6-DOF doors
05World assembly, contact events, rays, and triggers
06The acid tests: stacking, shadows, one full playground

14.1 — Why 3D Physics Is a Different Beast

Chapter 13 renders a 3D world; this chapter makes it react. Volumetric gameplay needs props to fall, topple, hinge, and collide — on every axis at once.

  • The new needs: full 3D collision, angular motion, jointed constraints, continuous sweeps
  • A 2D solver does not stretch: Box2D's math assumes one plane — one tilt axis, no mesh geometry
  • Choosing Bullet: mature, zlib-licensed, pure C++, proven from indie games to film tooling
  • It slots beside Chapter 13's renderer as a second backend — not a rewrite of the engine
  • Sable wraps it exactly like Box2D in Chapter 11: one thin PhysicsWorld3D seam
Best Practice — Wrap, don't absorb

Keep Bullet behind one seam class, as Chapter 11 did for Box2D. The day you swap in Jolt or another solver, it is one module of work — not a rewrite of every gameplay file that ever touched a force.

14.2 — 2D Physics (Box2D) vs 3D Physics (Bullet)

Both engines earn their keep in this course. The question is when the third dimension starts paying rent — and what it charges.

ABox2D v3 — Chapter 11
  • C API: b2WorldId handles, plain functions, no classes
  • 3 degrees of freedom per body: x, y, angle — one tilt axis
  • Polygons, circles, segments; sensors built in
  • Contact events in the box: b2ContactEvents begin/end arrays
  • Canyon Dash gameplay: platforms, water, golden carrots
BBullet — Chapter 14
  • C++ class API: pointers, construction info, virtual callbacks
  • 6 degrees of freedom: position plus a full quaternion orientation
  • Primitives, convex hulls, compounds, static triangle meshes
  • Contacts are polled or ghost-driven — we build the event layer
  • 3D playground: crate towers, hinged planks, ray picking
Common Pitfall — Escalating early

If the game plays on a plane, 3D physics buys quaternion math and a heavier solver for zero player-visible gain. Escalate when gameplay is genuinely volumetric — stacking, tumbling, jointed props — not because the renderer went 3D.

14.3 — Rigid Body Dynamics in Three Dimensions

A 2D body carried three numbers of freedom; a 3D body carries six — and angular motion stops being a scalar trick and becomes real mechanics.

  • Linear half is old news: position, velocity, forces — integrated exactly as in Chapter 11
  • Angular half is the new cost: orientation quaternion, angular velocity, torque
  • The inertia tensor is rotation's mass: a 3x3 map of how mass is distributed
  • Bullet derives it per body: shape->calculateLocalInertia(mass, localInertia)
  • Sleeping bodies leave the active set until activate() wakes them — free stability
Deep Dive — Why a long plank wobbles

The tensor encodes spin resistance per axis: a plank resists end-over-end turns far more than twists. It is why a diver tucks mid-air to spin faster — angular momentum conserved over a reshaped tensor — and why calculateLocalInertia needs the shape, not just the mass.

14.4 — Collision Shapes: Primitives, Hulls, Meshes

Shapes are cheap stand-ins for expensive art. Picking the primitive is a performance decision before it is a fidelity one.

  • btBoxShape (half-extents), btSphereShape (radius), btCapsuleShape (radius + height)
  • The capsule is the character-actor shape: rounded ends never snag on geometry seams
  • btConvexHullShape: shrink-wrap any prop — convex only, but fully dynamic-safe
  • Static world geometry: btBvhTriangleMeshShape — arbitrary triangles over a BVH tree
  • Doctrine: primitives for dynamics, triangle meshes for the immovable world
Common Pitfall — Dynamic triangle meshes

A concave mesh on a dynamic body breaks the solver's assumptions — convex pairs only. Bullet treats such shapes as static; gameplay then wonders why the boulder never falls. Hulls for anything that moves.

14.5 — Creating Shapes in Code

Three primitives cover ninety percent of dynamic props. Every size below is in meters, measured the Bullet way.

key points
  • Sizes are half-extents and radii, measured from the center — never full widths
  • The capsule's height is the cylinder section; the hemisphere caps add 2 * radius
  • btStaticPlaneShape is infinite — one line is the entire floor of the playground
  • Compounds weld primitives under per-child transforms: one body, many shapes
Best Practice — Share shapes, instantiate bodies

A shape is stateless data; a body carries the state. Keep a small shape cache and hand the same btBoxShape* to every crate on screen — memory and the pair cache both thank you.

14.6 — Motion States: Simulation Meets Rendering

Somebody has to own each transform — the physics engine or the scene graph. Bullet refuses to decide for you: transforms cross a seam called btMotionState.

  • The interface's job: Bullet pushes simulated transforms out, and reads teleports back in
  • btDefaultMotionState is the passive default — you poll getWorldTransform() after stepping
  • Custom subclasses can write straight into scene nodes — the zero-copy option
  • Bullet interpolates between substeps through the motion state — smooth at any render rate
  • It pairs with Chapter 3's alpha: simulation at 60 Hz, presentation at vsync, no fighting
Best Practice — One-way dataflow

Simulation writes, rendering reads. Never scribble render-space transforms back into a live body mid-step; if gameplay must move something, do it between ticks and let the motion state carry it out again.

14.7 — Building a Dynamic Body

One factory function is the whole body pipeline: shape, inertia, motion state, construction info, world registration — then the per-frame read-back.

key points
  • btRigidBodyConstructionInfo bundles mass, motion state, shape, inertia — build it right
  • Friction and restitution ride on the body, not the shape — two crates can differ
  • getMotionState()->getWorldTransform() is the render feed: one call per body per frame
  • tr.getRotation() returns the orientation quaternion — straight into the model matrix
Common Pitfall — Zero inertia, real mass

Skip calculateLocalInertia and a dynamic body spins with no resistance: every graze imparts absurd angular velocity. Bullet will not warn you — your crates will, by cartwheeling off-screen.

14.8 — Constraints: Joints as Gameplay

Constraints are the physics vocabulary of furniture: a door is a hinge, a rope is a ball joint, a drawbridge is a motorized limit.

  • A constraint is a solver promise: these two bodies stay related in exactly this way
  • btPoint2PointConstraint — ball-and-socket: ropes, chains, hanging lamps
  • btHingeConstraint — one axis with limits and an optional motor: doors, wheels, flippers
  • btGenericSixDofConstraint — lock or bound each of six axes: the precision instrument
  • They live in the world: addConstraint(c) registers them with the same solver as contacts
Deep Dive — Constraints share the solver budget

Every joint adds equations to the same iterative pass that resolves contacts. A scene of hundreds of chained links spends its convergence budget across all of them — heavy constraint webs and stable stacks compete for the same iterations.

14.9 — Ropes and Doors: Constraints in Code

Two joints, two gameplay sentences: a crate swinging on a rope, and a saloon door that swings through exactly ±69 degrees.

key points
  • btPoint2PointConstraint holds two local-space pivots coincident — the ball joint
  • 6-DOF means six independent limits: three translational, three rotational
  • A welded axis is setLimit(i, 0, 0); a swinging axis gets real bounds in radians
  • addConstraint(c, true) also disables collision between the two linked bodies
Best Practice — Joints want limits

An unbounded hinge can swing its door clean through the wall it is mounted in. Real furniture in real games always carries limits — set them before tuning anything else about the joint.

14.10 — Assembling the Physics World

One constructor takes four collaborators. Each has a precise job — and the pipeline they form is our Chapter 6 collision grid, one dimension up.

One tick inside stepSimulation
Broadphase
btDbvtBroadphase · AABB pairs
Dispatcher
narrowphase · manifolds
Solver
sequential impulse
Integrate
motion states advance
The Sable seam
PhysicsWorld3D
owns all four collaborators
WorldController

EventBus
contacts and triggers flow out

Same shape as Chapter 6: cheap broadphase candidates, expensive narrowphase confirmations — one axis and one rotation richer.

details
  • Gravity is a world property: setGravity(btVector3(0, -9.8, 0)) — +Y up, meters per second squared
  • The world owns bodies, constraints, and ghosts — and executes the tick
  • PhysicsWorld3D wraps it like Chapter 11's PhysicsWorld wrapped b2WorldId
Performance Tip — The broadphase is the crowd controller

A hundred bodies mean thousands of possible pairs; the AABB tree keeps actual narrowphase work near linear. Skip it and the frame dies before the solver even starts — the same lesson our Ch 6 spatial grid taught in 2D.

14.11 — World Setup and the Fixed-Step Handshake

Assembly is four allocations and one constructor. The interesting part is the handshake: Bullet meets Chapter 3's accumulator, and neither owns the other.

key points
  • STEP from Chapter 3 is also Bullet's fixedTimeStep: 60 Hz in, 60 Hz out
  • Bullet runs its own mini-accumulator — our fixed dt means exactly one substep per tick
  • maxSubSteps = 5 mirrors the spiral cap: if a tick runs long, debt is dropped, not life
  • Same wiring as Chapter 11: the physics seam receives ticks, it never takes them
Best Practice — One clock, one authority

Never feed Bullet raw frame deltas. Chapter 3's accumulator owns time; stepSimulation receives an already-fixed tick, and its substep machinery becomes a safety net instead of a second, competing clock.

14.12 — Contacts, Filtering, and Triggers

Gameplay runs on events; Bullet ships raw manifolds. Building the event layer is our job — the third event layer this course has built.

  • Poll manifolds after each step, or subclass ContactResultCallback and drive contactTest
  • Diff pair sets tick-over-tick and begin/end events fall out — Chapter 11 had them built in
  • Filtering: collision groups and masks decide who can ever pair with whom
  • Triggers: ghost objects overlap without response — the 3D sensor, two slides ahead
  • Identity rides on setUserPointer — stash the Actor* at spawn, read it back on contact
Common Pitfall — Contact spam

A resting crate stack emits a handful of manifolds every single tick. Route raw contacts into gameplay and the EventBus drowns in begin/end noise — filter at the physics seam, publish only what a listener can act on.

14.13 — A Contact Callback for the EventBus

Bullet hands us raw contacts; the EventBus wants typed events. One subclass bridges them — the same bridge Chapter 6 built for AABBs.

key points
  • contactTest sweeps one body against the world and calls addSingleResult per point
  • getUserPointer() is the identity channel — the Actor* we stashed at spawn
  • The return value throttles collection: 0 reports everything Bullet found
  • Box2D gave begin/end for free in Chapter 11; in 3D we diff pair sets ourselves

14.14 — Ray Casting the Physics World

The ray is the universal query of 3D gameplay: picking, line of sight, weapon traces, spawn placement — one primitive answers for all of them.

  • rayTest(from, to, callback) sweeps a segment through the entire world
  • ClosestRayResultCallback returns the first hit; AllHitsRayResultCallback returns every one
  • A hit carries point, surface normal, and the btCollisionObject it belongs to
  • The callback's collision group and mask filter what the ray can even see
  • The ray itself is Chapter 13's camera math — reused against a new database
Performance Tip — Rays ride the tree

A ray test walks the same AABB tree as the broadphase — full-scene picks cost microseconds. Fear a thousand rays per frame, not one per click; and prefer closest-hit over all-hits unless gameplay truly needs the list.

14.15 — Ray Picking: Click to Spawn

Chapter 13 built the ray from the camera; Bullet answers where it lands. A click becomes a hit point, a normal, an Actor — then a boulder.

key points
  • The ray is Chapter 13's camera math aimed at Chapter 14's database — zero new math
  • Rays are segments: to = from + direction * reach — 100 m covers the playground
  • m_hitPointWorld and m_hitNormalWorld orient effects: sparks, decals, spawns
  • Click-to-spawn drops a sphere above the hit and lets gravity finish the sentence
Common Pitfall — The silent zero-length ray

If from equals to, or an un-normalized direction shrinks the reach to millimeters, every pick misses with no error at all. Draw the segment as a debug line for one afternoon — it pays for itself the first week.

14.16 — The Stacking Test

A tower of crates is the acid test of a physics engine: it exercises pairing, manifolds, friction, and sleep all at once — and it fails loudly.

  • Symptoms of a weak setup: jitter, slow sinking, or the tower catapulting itself apart
  • First lever: friction — crates under ~0.5 slide off each other under their own weight
  • Second lever: solver iterations — getSolverInfo().m_numIterations, try 10 to 20
  • Third lever: smaller fixed steps — 120 Hz buys convergence at twice the CPU bill
  • The payoff: a settled tower sleeps, leaves the active set, and costs nearly nothing
Deep Dive — Why solvers jitter

Sequential impulse resolves contacts iteratively: each pass reduces error but never fully zeroes it. Shimmer is leftover penetration correction fighting gravity, one tick at a time. Iterations, friction, and sleep are your three dials against it.

14.17 — Trigger Volumes in 3D

btPairCachingGhostObject is the 3D heir of Chapter 11 sensors: an object that overlaps, remembers, and never pushes.

  • A ghost is a full collision object with zero response — it overlaps, it never shoves
  • The pair cache remembers current overlaps: diff it for begin/end events
  • Uses: pickup zones, level gates, water volumes, camera hint regions
  • Registered like any object: addCollisionObject(ghost, group, mask) — filtered from birth
  • Query after each step: getNumOverlappingObjects() and getOverlappingObject(i)
Common Pitfall — A ghost is not a wall

Players walk straight through trigger volumes — that is the feature. If you need blocking, that is a static body; if you need blocking plus an event, layer a ghost onto a solid, never instead of one.

14.18 — Dynamic Shadows

Shadow mapping is a two-pass trick with one idea: render the scene's depth from the light's point of view, then compare against it in the fragment shader.

  • Pass 1: depth-only render from the light's view into a depth texture — the shadow map
  • Pass 2: shade normally; a fragment is shadowed when its depth exceeds the stored value
  • One directional light, one cascade, one 2048 map — plenty at the playground's scale
  • Chapter 11's shader pass generalizes: same pipeline, light's matrix in, shadow factor out
  • Physics needs it: a crate floating 2 cm off the ground is invisible without a shadow
Deep Dive — Shadow acne and peter-panning

Comparing depths quantizes, so surfaces start shadowing themselves — acne. Bias the comparison to cure it; over-bias and shadows detach from their casters — peter-panning. Tune bias against the light's angle: steep light needs more.

14.19 — The Complete Test Scenario

Everything in this scenario is a slide you have already seen. Assembly is the only new skill: ground, stack, hinge, gate, spawn — in that order.

key points
  • Every piece is a slide already behind you — assembly is the only new skill here
  • The 2 cm seam between crates lets the solver settle the stack instead of fighting it
  • The hinge pivots at the plank's left end: constraint space is local, like all pivots
  • The ghost gate and spawned boulders publish to the bus — gameplay reacts, physics never knows
Best Practice — Build the scenario in pieces

Ground first, then one crate, then the stack, then the hinge — testing at every step. If the tower explodes later, exactly one recently added suspect changed; assemble everything at once and every line is a suspect.

14.20 — Tuning and Pitfalls

The gap between physics that works and physics that feels right is a short list of hard-won defaults. These are the ones that bite every 3D project exactly once.

  • Bullet speaks meters, kilograms, seconds — raw pixel coordinates mean 960 m cliffs
  • Rescale at the seam: our TILE 32 world maps to 1.0 m tiles entering PhysicsWorld3D
  • Tunneling: fast bodies skip thin geometry — enable CCD on bullets, not on boulders
  • Sleep tuning: too eager freezes conveyor belts; too lazy cooks the CPU for nothing
  • Determinism: fixed ticks keep a run repeatable; float drift still varies by compiler
Common Pitfall — The unit import

Feeding a 2D level's pixel coordinates into Bullet is the classic first crash: gravity acts 100x too strong and stacks explode on frame one, while nothing looks wrong in the code. Convert at the boundary, once.

Performance Tip — CCD is a scalpel

Continuous collision runs swept tests per body per step. Enable it for the handful of genuinely fast objects — projectiles, falling debris — and let ordinary crates live with plain discrete steps.

Best Practice — Wireframe before art

Turn on Bullet's debug draw from day one: world-space shape outlines, contact points, constraints. Floating bodies, wrong inertia, ghost gaps — all confess instantly in wireframe while staying invisible in textured renders.

Recap — lock it in

Chapter 14 Recap

  • 3D physics earns its keep only when gameplay is volumetric — otherwise stay on Box2D
  • A body is mass + shape + inertia + motion state; transforms cross the seam, ownership does not
  • Shapes: primitives for dynamics, hulls for props, triangle meshes for the static world
  • Constraints are gameplay furniture — ropes, hinges, and 6-DOF doors, always with limits
  • stepSimulation slots into Chapter 3's fixed tick; contacts, rays, and ghosts ride the bus
  • The test scenario ships: ground, stack, hinge, gate, spawn — with shadows to prove it

details

Deep Dive — Seams matter more than systems

The 3D chapters bolted on in two chapters precisely because the seams already existed: the fixed tick, the EventBus, the asset loader, the camera. Architecture is what you buy before you know what feature fourteen will be.

The Master Patterns

Features age; patterns compound. Five ideas carried every chapter — and they will carry the next engine you touch, whoever wrote it.

  • The fixed-step game loop — measure, clamp, bank, tick at 60 Hz, render with alpha
    • —Ch 3 built it; Ch 11's Box2D stepping and Ch 14's stepSimulation both hang off the same tick
  • Layered architecture — engine never includes game; renderer never simulates
    • —Ch 1 drew the boundary as folders; every chapter since widened it without crossing it
  • State machines — one table-driven pattern, three different jobs
    • —Screens (Ch 7), actor brains (Ch 6), sprite animations (Ch 12)
  • Data-driven design — levels, atlases, presets, and settings as files, not code
    • —Ch 4's JSON levels and settings.json: content changes ship without a recompile
  • Single ownership of resources — one owner, reverse-order teardown, no orphans
    • —AssetManager owns textures; AudioManager owns streams; PhysicsWorld3D owns bodies
Best Practice — Name the pattern before the feature

When a new system arrives, ask which of the five it is before writing anything. Nine times out of ten one already fits — and the tenth time, you have earned the right to invent a sixth.

Where to Go Next — Resources

The course ends; the ecosystem does not. These are the sources worth your evenings, roughly in the order you will need them.

  • SDL3 wiki — wiki.libsdl.org/SDL3: the full API reference, migration notes, and FAQ
  • SDL3 examples — examples.libsdl.org: runnable snippets for nearly every call in the API
  • Community: the SDL forums and Discord — maintainers answer, if you bring a minimal repro
  • Engine internals, now readable as a fellow author: the Box2D docs and the Bullet manual
  • Web target: the Emscripten docs — the asyncify and packaging pages you met in Chapter 2
  • Classic reading: Game Programming Patterns, Abrash, Sanglard's code-review essays
Best Practice — Reading another engine's source

Start at the main loop, pick one frame, and follow it end to end. You know every station it passes — input, events, simulation, render, present — because you built them. That map is the real diploma.

The Practice Roadmap

Skills decay without projects. Four capstones, graded by difficulty — each one a complete vertical slice through the stack you just built.

  • Easy — add one Canyon Dash mechanic end-to-end
    • —design → JSON data → actor → bus events → HUD → audio → polish; nothing skipped
  • Medium — port Canyon Dash fully to the web with the async asset loader
    • —Ch 2's toolchain + Ch 4's threaded loading + Ch 9's preloader screen
  • Medium-hard — a 3D mini-playground: picking, stacking, a hinged prop
    • —Ch 13's renderer + Ch 14's world; the test scenario is your starting line
  • Hard — a level editor that saves the Chapter 4 JSON level format
    • —SDL3 grid editing, cJSON serialization, then load your own levels in-game
Best Practice — The feature-slice method

Never "learn a system" in the abstract: pick a player-visible outcome and cut vertically through every layer to deliver it. The system teaches itself on the way down, and the slice ships — so motivation never starves.
